en: Viśvanātha Kavirāja: The First Chapter of the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
At the beginning of the work, desiring the completion of what he has begun without obstacle, he brings about the presence of the Goddess of Speech by virtue of her presiding over speech:
"May that Goddess of Speech, whose splendor is as beautiful as the autumnal moon, having dispelled the continuous darkness from my mind, illuminate all meanings. (VisSd 1.1)
Since this treatise is an auxiliary to poetry, it bears fruit through the very fruits of poetry; thus, he states the fruits of poetry:

"Because the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life comes from poetry itself, even for those of limited intelligence, through its mere enjoyment, therefore its essential nature is here described. (VisSd 1.2)

The attainment of the fruits of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) is indeed well-established through the instruction on engaging in what ought to be done and desisting from what ought not to be done, such as: "One should proceed like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others.
And it has been said by Bhāmaha:
"Expertise in virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as in the arts..."
The cultivation of excellent poetry produces both fame and joy.”
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, the attainment of dharma through poetry is well-established both through the hymns to the lotus feet of Lord Nārāyaṇa and by Vedic statements such as: "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world."
The attainment of wealth is established by direct perception;
the attainment of sensual pleasure occurs solely through the medium of wealth; and the attainment of liberation results from not pursuing the fruits of the dharmas produced by these [other two].
Furthermore, it is because poetry imparts proficiency in those statements that are useful for liberation.

For the attainment of the four aims of human life arises from the Vedic scriptures only through hardship due to their lack of aesthetic flavor, and only for those whose intellects have reached maturity.
However, because it generates a multitude of supreme joys, it arises even from poetry alone, and through pleasure itself, even for those of tender intellect.
In that case, one should not even say: "Why should those of mature intellect, when the Vedic scriptures exist, exert effort in poetry?
For if a disease that must be cured by bitter medicine could instead be cured by white sugar, which patient would not consider the application of white sugar to be more excellent?
Furthermore, the worthiness of poetry as something to be adopted is also stated in the *Agni Purāṇa*:
“Human birth is difficult to obtain in this world; knowledge therein is very difficult to obtain;
poetic talent is difficult to obtain therein; and creative power therein is very difficult to obtain.”
Thus it is said:
"Drama is the means for accomplishing the three aims of life.
And likewise in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
“Whatever poetic compositions there may be, and all songs as well—
these are portions of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound.”
Thus,
by that reason, the nature of that poetry is defined;
by this, its subject matter is also demonstrated.

In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of poetry (*kāvya*) is, someone says: "It consists of word and meaning that are free from defects, endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇas*), and sometimes further adorned with figures of speech (*alaṃkāras*). This, however, is to be examined.
To explain:

if one were to accept that only a work free from defects constitutes poetry, then consider this verse: “This is indeed my humiliation that there are enemies; moreover, that they are ascetics; furthermore, that they are destroying the race of Rākṣasas right here; and oh, that Rāvaṇa still lives!”
"Fie, fie upon Chakrājita! What is the use of Kumbhakarṇa, who has merely been awakened? And what is the use of these arms, puffed up in vain for the purpose of plundering the mere hamlet of heaven?"
Thus,
because this verse is marred by the defect of failing to discern what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it would lack the status of poetry;
on the contrary, it possesses *dhvani* (suggestive power).
Since the status of this [work] as the highest poetry has been accepted by you,
there is therefore the fault of the definition being under-extensive (*avyāpti*). If it is argued that "only a certain portion here is defective, and not the whole," [the response follows].
In that case, since the portion where a defect exists would be the cause of its being non-poetry (*akāvya*),

while the portion where *dhvani* exists would be the cause of its being excellent poetry (*uttamakāvya*), this work— being pulled from both sides by these two portions— would be neither poetry nor non-poetry.
Furthermore, defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (harsh to the ear) and so forth do not corrupt the entire work of poetry, but rather only certain specific parts.
Rather, all of it is indeed poetry;
for instance,
as long as they do not detract from rasa— which is the very soul of poetry— even their status as defects is not admitted.
Otherwise, even the distinction between permanent defects (*nityadoṣa*) and non-permanent defects (*anityadoṣa*) would not exist.
As stated by Dhvanikāra: "The defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* and others which have been shown are non-permanent (*anitya*)."
"These [defects] are to be avoided specifically in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) which consists of suggestion (dhvani); thus they have been illustrated."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in this way, poetry would have either a very limited scope or no scope at all, because a work that is entirely free from defects is in every respect impossible.

If it is argued that the negative particle *nañ* is used here in the sense of "slight," then by saying "poetry consists of word and meaning with slight defects," it would follow that works free from defects could not be considered poetry.
If it is argued that "with slight defects" is meant only when defects are possible [but not present], then this too should not be stated as a definition of poetry.
The characteristics of a gem and so forth are like the avoidance of insect-boring and other defects;
for indeed, insect-boring and the like are not capable of negating the gem-nature of a jewel, but rather only serve to determine its degree of desirability.
Likewise, here, defects such as those offensive to the ear [do not negate the nature of poetry, but affect its quality].
And it has been said:

"Poetic quality (kāvyatā) is held to exist even in defective works, provided there is a clear presence of rasa and so forth, just as the status of being a gem is common to a stone pierced by an insect."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore,
the qualification that both word and meaning possess qualities is logically consistent.

This is because he himself has established that the qualities have rasa as their sole property, stating: "Those which are the properties of the principal rasa, such as heroism and so forth, are like [the qualities] of the self," and so on.
If it is argued that this is justified through metaphorical usage because they manifest the rasa, even so, it is incorrect.
To explain: does rasa exist or not in those two—word and meaning—which are intended as the very nature of poetry?
If it does not exist, then the possession of poetic qualities (guṇa) does not exist either.
Because the qualities (guṇas) follow the positive and negative concomitance of that [substance].
If it exists, why was the qualifier "possessing flavor" (rasavantau) not stated?
If it is argued that this is obtained through the principle of the impossibility otherwise (anyathānupapatti) of the possession of qualities?
In that case, it would be more appropriate to say "endowed with moisture" (sarasau) rather than "endowed with qualities" (saguṇau);
for no one ever says, "regions possess living beings."
If it is argued that the statement "word and meaning are possessed of qualities" intends to mean that word and meaning which manifest the qualities (guṇas) are to be employed in poetry—
no; for the possession of words and meanings that manifest qualities merely bestows excellence upon poetry, but does not constitute its very essence.
For it has been said:
"The word and the meaning are the body of poetry, while rasa and so forth are its soul."
Qualities (guṇas) are like bravery and so forth;
defects (doṣas) are like being one-eyed and so forth; and styles (rītis) are like specific configurations of limbs.
"Ornaments are like bracelets, earrings, and so forth.
By this, that which was stated— "but [the figure] is sometimes without ornament"— is also refuted.
The meaning of this is as follows: poetry consists of word and meaning that are everywhere possessed of ornament (*alaṅkāra*), though in some cases they may even lack manifest ornaments.
This is because, within poetry, even words and meanings that possess ornament contribute to its excellence.
By this, the statement of the author of the *Vakroktijīvita*, namely that "oblique expression (*vakrokti*) is the life-force of poetry," is also refuted.
Because *vakrokti* (indirect expression) is itself the nature of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
And as for that which was cited in some instances where the ornament is not manifest:
"He who took away my maidenhood is indeed that same bridegroom; those very nights of the month of Caitra; and those mature breezes from the Kadamba trees, fragrant with blossoming Mālatī flowers."
And yet, though I am that very same person, my heart yearns for the playful performance of amorous dalliance there on the bank of the Revā, beneath the cane tree.
Thus [it is said].
This is to be considered:

for here there is the clear manifestation of the figure of speech *saṃdehasaṅkara* (the commingling of doubt), which is rooted in *vibhāvanā* (peculiar causation) and *viśeṣokti* (peculiar assertion).
By this [it is meant]: “The poet, composing poetry that is free from defects, endowed with qualities, adorned with ornaments,
and permeated by aesthetic flavor (rasa), attains both fame and pleasure.”
Thus, the status of these and other such [theories] as definitions of poetry is also refuted.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*— namely, "Suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry"— does that *dhvani*, characterized by the forms of matter (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and so forth, constitute the soul of poetry?
Or is it merely that which consists of rasa (flavor) and so forth?
Not the first, because it would over-extend to riddles (*prahelikā*) and the like;
if the second, we say "yes."
Now, if *dhvani*—consisting merely of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth—is the soul of poetry, then consider this:
"The mother-in-law sleeps here; I am here. Look well for the day, O traveler! Lest you, blinded by the night, fall into my bed."
If it is asked, "In such cases, since only the literal matter (*vastumātra*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), how can there be the designation 'poetry' (*kāvyavyavahāra*)?", we reply:
No; for here too, we maintain that there is indeed the presence of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).

Otherwise, even in the sentence "Devadatta goes to the village," there would have to be the status of poetry because of the comprehension of the suggested meaning consisting of his servant's following him.
If it is argued that this should be so, we say no; for we accept that only that which possesses *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) is poetry (*kāvya*).
Indeed, the purpose of poetry is to provide a mass of bliss through the tasting of *rasa* to those of tender intellect who are averse to the Vedas and the technical sciences.

For it has been stated by the ancients as well that [this work] provides instruction on the engagement in what is to be done and the avoidance of what is not to be done for those to be trained, such as princes and others, saying: "One should behave like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others.
Likewise, it is also said in the Āgneya Purāṇa:
“Even though verbal ingenuity is predominant here, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone is the lifeblood.
Thus it has also been stated by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*: “In poetry, which has as its soul the dominant factor (*aṅgin*),”
“No one disagrees that [the poem] consists of rasa and so forth.
The author of the Dhvanyāloka has also said: “A poet does not attain his status merely by successfully narrating a story.”
“Because that [status] is established through history (*itihāsa*) and so forth,” and so on.
Now, one might object: “In that case, would certain flavorless verses occurring within a literary work (*prabandha*) not possess the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*)?
No; for just as words lacking rasa within a verse containing rasa are [still part of] the verse by virtue of the rasa of the verse itself, [so too are such passages part of the poem].
This is because their possession of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattā*) is accepted as being due to the flavor of the composition itself.

As for the fact that the designation "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) is applied even to works lacking rasa—due to the presence of letters that manifest the *guṇas*, the absence of defects, and the presence of figures of speech—that is merely secondary (*gauṇa*), based on the similarity to the composition of poetry that possesses rasa and so forth.
As for what was stated by Vāmana:
As for the statement that "style (rīti) is the soul of poetry," that is not correct; for style is a particular kind of composition (saṃghaṭanā),
and composition consists in the arrangement of constituent parts.
And because that [meaning] is distinct from the self;
and as it was stated by the author of the *Dhvani*: "The meaning which is praised by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) and established as the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*)."
Its two divisions are traditionally known as the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (pratīyamāna).

Thus, in this context, the view that the essence of poetry consists in the denotative meaning (*vācyātmatva*) is already set aside by the contradiction of one's own statement, namely: "The essence of poetry is *dhvani*.
Therefore, what then is poetry? It is said:
"Speech whose essence is rasa"—
we shall define the nature of rasa.
Rasa itself is the soul (*ātman*), that which, by virtue of being the core essence, provides life to it.
For without that [rasa], its status as poetry would not be admitted.
By virtue of the etymological derivation "that which is relished is *rasa*," *bhāvas*, their semblances (*tadābhāsas*), and so forth are also included therein. An example of *rasa* is as follows:
Having observed the bedchamber empty, she rose slightly and slowly from her bed; then, feigning sleep, she gazed for a long time at the face of her husband who had approached it.
Having kissed her confidently and seeing the region of her cheek covered in horripilation, the young woman, her face bowed with shame, was long kissed by her lover who smiled.
For here, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is that called the erotic in its aspect of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*).
As for the emotional state (*bhāva*), it is as described by the great vessel Raghavananda Sāndhivigrahika:
"In whose scales the ocean dissolved, and upon whose back the circle of the worlds lay..."
The earth was on his tusk,
the lord of the sons of Diti was on his claw, and heaven and earth were at his feet.
In his anger is Kṣapaṇaka; in his arrow, Daśamukha;
in his hand, the Asura Pralamba.
Salutation to this one, in whose meditation the entire world of the unrighteous family [is dissolved].
In this case, the emotion (*bhāva*) is a lack of interest regarding the Blessed One.
An example of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) is as follows:
"The bee, following its own mate, drank honey from the flower's single petal."
And the black antelope scratched with his horn the doe, whose eyes were closed from the sensation of touch.
In this case, because the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) has animals as its object, it is a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
Other cases are similar.
Furthermore, what is the nature of defects (*doṣa*) in poetry?
Thus it is said: "The defects (doṣas) are those which detract from it,
such as being corrupted by Vedic rules, lack of substantial meaning, and so forth, just like being one-eyed, lame, and so on."
By way of the word and its meaning, or by way of the body [of the poem],

factors such as the direct verbal expression of transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) and so forth— just like [the mention of] stupidity and the like— diminish the rasa which is the very soul of poetry; therefore, they are called "defects" (apakarṣaka) of poetry.
We shall state specific examples of these. As for what the nature of the *guṇas* and so forth is, it is said:
"The *guṇas*, *alaṅkāras*, and *rītis* are declared to be the causes of excellence. (VisSd 1.3)
The *guṇas* are like bravery and other such qualities; the *alaṅkāras* are like bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments; the *rītis* are like specific arrangements of limbs.
By means of the body [of the poem]—that is, by means of word and meaning—they enhance the *rasa* which constitutes the very soul of that same poetry; thus they are called "enhancers of poetry.
Although, in this context, the qualities (*guṇas*) are properties of *rasa*, the term "quality" is here used metaphorically for the word and meaning that manifest those qualities.
Therefore, as was stated previously, it follows that "the words manifesting the qualities are the enhancers of *rasa*."
We shall also state specific examples of these.

Thus [ends] the work composed by Śrī Viśvanātha Kavirāja, the Great Minister (Mahāpātra) and Diplomat (Sāndhivigrahika), who was a bee at the lotus-feet of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, a helmsman in the ocean of poetics, the supreme teacher who established the school of Dhvani, a mine of jewels of poetic utterances, a master of eighteen languages, and a lover of the courtesans of speech.
The first chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "Definition of the Nature of Poetry," is concluded.
The second chapter states the nature of the sentence (*vākya*).

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words (*padoccaya*) endowed with semantic competency (*yogyatā*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and contiguity (*satti*). Semantic competency is the absence of contradiction when the meanings of the words are related to one another.
If this [competency] were absent, even a collection of words would be a sentence; thus, even "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*) and the like would constitute a sentence.
Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the absence of the completion of comprehension;
furthermore, it takes the form of the listener’s desire to know.
If a collection of words were considered a sentence even when devoid of expectancy, then such utterances as "cow, horse, man, elephant" would also have to be sentences.
Proximity (*āsatti*) is the non-interruption of cognition.

Even if [the sentence] were a sentence despite an interruption in cognition, there would be a connection between the word "Devadatta" uttered now and the word "goes" (*gacchati*) uttered three days later.

Here, although expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*) are properties of the self and its objects, they are figuratively attributed as properties of the collection of words (*padoccaya*).
A collection of sentences is a "great sentence" (mahāvākya) precisely when it is endowed with compatibility, expectancy, and proximity;
thus, a sentence is considered to be of two kinds.
The word *ittham* refers to [sentences] both as individual sentences and as great sentences (*mahāvākya*).
And it is stated in the *Tantravārttika*:
"For those [sentences] which are complete in the communication of their own meaning, there arises a mutual dependence based on the relationship of principal and subordinate."
Furthermore, the unity of sentences arises through their being combined together.
Thus it is said.
In that regard, an example of a sentence (*vākya*) is: “The chamber is empty,” and so forth (p.
22). An example of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is as follows:
The *Rāmāyaṇa*, *Mahābhārata*, *Raghuvaṃśa*, and so forth are collections of words (*padoccaya*); it has been stated that a sentence (*vākya*) is such a collection.
To this, one asks: what is the definition of a word (*pada*)? In response, he says:
Phonemes (varṇas) are those which, when not combined and capable of being used in linguistic usage, convey a single meaning;
for example, *gha-ṭa*.
The term "capable of being used" (*prayogārha*) serves to exclude nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
The term "non-sequential" (*ananvita*) refers to sentences and great sentences (*vākya-mahāvākya*).
The term "single" (*eka*) refers to multiple words and sentences that possess mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*).
The term "signifying meaning" (*arthabodhaka*) refers to [isolated sounds] such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth.
The plural number in the word "varṇāḥ" (phonemes) is not intended to be significant.
Meaning is considered to be threefold: the expressed (vācya), the indicated (lakṣya), and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
He states their essential nature:

"The meaning to be expressed is understood through denotation (*abhidhā*); that which is indicated is considered [understood] through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and that which is suggested is [understood] through suggestion (*vyañjanā*). These are the three powers of a word. (VisSd 2.3)
These are Abhidhā and the others.
Among them, *abhidhā* (denotation) is the foremost because it conveys a conventional meaning.

When an elder says to another elder, "Bring the cow," and the child observes that the latter proceeds to bring the cow, [the child concludes] that the meaning of this sentence is "the bringing of an object possessing a dewlap and so forth."
Thus one first arrives at this understanding;

immediately thereafter, through the processes of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*) in instances such as "Bind the cow" and "Bring the horse," one determines the convention that the word *go* has the meaning "that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," and the word *ānayana* has the meaning "bringing.
In some cases, this occurs through the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a well-known word, for example:
In the case of [the statement], "Here, within the interior of a blossomed lotus, the bee drinks honey," [it arises] from some authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*), as for example in the case:
"This is what is denoted by the word 'horse'."
And that power of a word which, unmediated by any other power, brings about the understanding of that conventionalized meaning is called *abhidhā* (denotation).
Convention is grasped with respect to universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), and actions (*kriyā*). (Viśadā 2.4)
A universal (*jāti*) is, for example, "cowness" (*gotva*) in individual cows and the like.
A quality (*guṇa*) is an established property of a thing that is the cause of producing a distinction;
for instance, whiteness and so forth differentiate a cow from others of its own class, such as black cows.
Substance-words (*dravyaśabda*) are those denoting a single individual, such as *hari*, *hara*, *ḍittha*, *ḍavittha*, and so forth.
Actions (*kriyā*) are properties of things (*vastudharma*) whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*), such as cooking (*pāka*) and the like.

For in these cases, the collection of operations (*vyāpārakalāpa*) consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off, is what is denoted by words such as "cooking."

For it is precisely in these limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individuals that the convention is grasped, and not in the individuals themselves, because that would entail the fallacies of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Now, as for the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇā*):

When the primary meaning is sublated, that power by which another meaning connected to it is understood—whether through conventional usage (rūḍhi) or for a specific purpose (prayojana)—is the imparted power of indication (lakṣaṇā). 2.5.
In expressions such as "The Kalingas are violent," the word *Kaliṅga* and others, being impossible [to apply] to their own primary meaning— the specific region and so forth—
convey through a certain power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) the men and others associated with that region. Likewise,

in cases such as "A hamlet on the Ganges," the word *Gaṅgā* and others, because they denote an object consisting of water and the like, being impossible in the present context, convey through another power the bank and so forth, which are related to them by a relation such as proximity.

That power of a word which is applied [to another meaning], being other than its own inherent [denotative] power, and is either established by convention or brought forth by a specific purpose, is called *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
In the former case, the cause is *rūḍhi*, which is simply conventional renown.

In the latter case, it is the purpose (*prayojana*) consisting of the communication of an excellence of coolness and purity that cannot be obtained through the literal expression "the hamlet is on the bank of the Gaṅgā."

It has been stated that, were there a definition of a related term even in the absence of a [logical] reason, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): "This [definition] arises from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or from a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
Some, however, cite "skilled in action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*) as an example of conventional usage.
Their intention is as follows:

they hold that the primary meaning, which consists of "one who grasps *kuśa* grass" as derived from its etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), being impossible in the present context, conveys the sense of "one who is dexterous" (*dakṣa*) through a relationship based on common properties such as discernment (*vivekatva*);
others do not accept this.

Although the meaning of *kuśagrāhin* (one who grasps *kuśa-grass*) is obtained through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) is specifically that of one who is skillful (*dakṣa*).
For the basis of a word's etymological derivation (*vyutpattinimitta*) is one thing, while the basis for its actual application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is another.

If that which is obtained through etymological derivation were the primary meaning, then even in the case of the expression "the cow lies down" (*gauḥ śete*), there would have to be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Because the word *go*, derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍe* according to *Uṇādi-sūtra* 2.67 (*gamer ḍeḥ*), is employed at the time of lying down;
he states its various types:
When the primary meaning implies another meaning for the sake of establishing its connection within the sentence-meaning—even by including itself—this is *upādāna-lakṣaṇā*. (VisSd 2.6)
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it is an indication based on the material cause (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*), as in:
"The white one runs.
In the case of a motive (*prayojana*), it is as follows:
In the expressions "the spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*) and [“the men run”],

since the spears and so forth, as well as the white objects and so forth, being insentient and devoid of consciousness, cannot by themselves be construed as the agents of the actions of running and entering, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of horses and the like, or men and the like, who are related to them, in order to establish this.

In the former case, the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) prevails due to the absence of a specific purpose; in the latter case, however, the purpose is the extreme density of the *kunta* trees and so forth.
And here, there is also the inclusion of the primary sense, namely the Self (*ātman*).
However, in the case of *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*, there is only the indication of another; this is the distinction between the two.
This very [type of indication] is called *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning).
It is the "offering" (*arpaṇa*) of one's own [meaning] into the sentence-meaning for the sake of establishing the connection of another.
Because it serves as the cause for secondary observation, this is the definition of the definition (lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā).
The definition of indication based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and purpose (*prayojana*) is as follows:
"Kaliṅga is a brave man" and "A hamlet on the Ganges.
For in these two cases, the words *Kaliṅga* and *Ganges* surrender their own primary meanings in order to establish the connection of the person and the bank with the sentence-meaning.
Or as it is said:
"Much harm has been done there; what more can be said? Yet, O friend, you have displayed supreme goodness toward me. Always acting in this very same way, [may you remain so]."
"Therefore, may you remain happy for a hundred autumns."

In this case, for the purpose of establishing the connection of "injury" (*apakāra*) and so forth with the sentence-meaning, words such as "benefactor" (*upakṛta*) surrender their own literal meanings. Because the presentation of "benefit" and so forth is directed toward one who has actually caused injury, there is a subversion of the primary meaning characterized by contrariety; the relationship [between the literal and indicated meanings] is that of contrariety, and the result is the intensification of the injury.
This very [type] is called *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning).
Through superimposition (*āropa*) and determination (*adhyavasāna*), each of those is also twofold.
Those aforementioned [types] possess fourfold characteristics.
It is produced by the perception of identity with something else, while the object itself is not swallowed up [by that thing].

It is considered that *sāropā* occurs when [the object] is swallowed, while *sādhyavasānikā* occurs when it is not. *Sāropā* is that which brings about the cognition of identity between the object (*viṣaya*)—which is not swallowed by the subject (*viṣayin*)—and that very subject.
This alone is the seed of the poetic figure *rūpaka*.
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is a superimpositional indication based on the material cause (*upādānalakṣaṇā sāropā*), as in:
"The white horse runs.
For here, the horse, possessing the quality of whiteness, is perceived without its own nature being swallowed up, through its identity with the quality inherent in itself.
As for [implication] by purpose—for example: "These spears enter.
Here, because the word "these" (a pronoun) refers to the persons who carry the spears.
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), that is *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā* (indication based on indication), as in:
"The Kaliṅga man fights.
Here, the relationship between the Kaliṅga and the man is one of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
As for [the indication] by purpose (*prayojana*), for example: "Clarified butter is longevity" (*āyur ghṛtam*).
Here, although clarified butter is merely a cause of longevity, it is understood as being identical with longevity through its relation as a member of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
The purpose [of the metaphor] is longevity that is non-deviant due to its distinction from all other things;
or, for example, when a king's servant is walking, one says, "The king is walking."
In this case, the relationship is characterized by that between owner and owned;
or, for example, when one says "this is a hand" with respect to a portion consisting of only the tip of a limb.
In this case, the relationship is characterized by that of part and whole (*avayavāvayavin*).
In the expression “this carpenter is also a Brahmin,” the relationship is characterized by the performance of a function (*tatkarmya*).
Regarding pillars intended for Indra, [the expression] is "these are Indras.
Here, the relationship is characterized by being for the sake of that (tādarthya).
The same applies elsewhere as well.
*Adhyavasāna* (superimposition) consists in the cognition of the swallowed object as being identical with something else.
Its four varieties have already been illustrated by the previous examples.
Thus, *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is of eight kinds.
All those [cognitions], whether complete or otherwise, are pure when their relations are other than similarity.
However, secondary indication (gauṇī) is considered to arise from similarity; thus, it is divided into sixteen types.
These are the eight previously mentioned varieties of indication (lakṣaṇā), along with those based on relationships other than similarity, such as the relation of cause and effect and so forth.

In this context, the examples for the pure [types] are the same as those previously cited. Regarding conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the metaphorical indication based on the relation of material cause (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) is the "slightly impure" (*sārepa*) secondary indication (*gauṇī*), as in:
"These oils are pleasant in winter."
In this context, the word *taila* (oil) functions with respect to oils such as mustard oil only by taking its primary meaning—namely, a fatty substance derived from sesame—as its basis.
As for its usage based on purpose (*prayojana*), it is as when, while princes and those similar to them are walking, one says: "These princes are walking."
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is a secondary metaphor (*gauṇī*) characterized by appropriation (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) with complete identification (*sādhyavasānā*), as in:
"Oils are pleasant in winter.
In the case of a motive (*prayojana*), it is as follows:
In the conventional usage "the princes are going," it is a secondary indication based on a characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*). As for the purposeful indication (*prayojana*), as in:
"The King cleanses the thorn that is the Lord of Gauḍa. As for the purposeful indication: [example follows].

In the case of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) "The Vāhīka is an ox," there is a secondary indication (*gauṇī lakṣaṇā*) based on a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*) that is "determinative" (*sādhyavasānā*). For example:
"The king cleanses the thorns.
Regarding purpose (*prayojana*), for example: "The ox speaks."
On this point, some say: "The qualities such as dullness and slowness, which accompany the cow, are indicated; and these serve as the basis for the word 'cow' denoting the Vāhīka. This is incorrect.

Because it is impossible for the word "cow" (*gośabda*) to denote the meaning "Vāhīka" when the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) has not been grasped, and because it only brings about the cognition of the word's own [primary] meaning; and because the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) has ceased, and that which has ceased does not arise again;
furthermore, the meaning "Vāhīka" is not denoted by the word "cow."

However, it is argued that by virtue of the similarity between the qualities associated with the primary meaning and those residing in the *vāhīka*, it is precisely these qualities themselves that are indicated (*lakṣyante*).
Others do not accept even this; for instance:
In this case, is the meaning "Vāhīka" understood from the word *go* itself, or not?
If it is, is it understood from the word *go* alone,
or from a quality indicated [by it]?
Or is it due to invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)?
In that regard, it is not the first [option], because this [word] has not been conventionally designated (*asaṃketita*) with respect to the meaning of a Vāhīka.
Not the second [alternative],
because an object obtained through inseparable connection (avinābhāva) cannot enter into a verbal syntactic relation;
for a verbal expectancy is fulfilled by a word alone.
Not the second [alternative];
for if the meaning "Vāhīka" were not understood from the word "go," then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between this [word] and the word "vāhīka" would be inconsistent.

Therefore, in this case, the word "cow" (go), failing to obtain syntactic connection with the word "Vāhīka" through its primary function (mukhyā vṛtti), indicates the meaning of "Vāhīka" by virtue of the relationship of similarity consisting in qualities such as ignorance. The purpose is to convey the Vāhīka’s excellence in ignorance and so forth.
And this [indication] is called "secondary" (gauṇī) because of its connection with a quality (guṇa).
The former [type of metaphor], however, is pure because it is unmixed with figurative usage (*upacāra*).
For what is called "figurative usage" is merely the concealment of the perception of difference between two words that are utterly distinct, by virtue of the power of an excellence of similarity—
just as, for example, in the case of a firebrand and a boy.
However, in the case of two white cloths, there is no perception of absolute difference;

therefore, in such instances, the indication (lakṣaṇā) is purely "pure" (śuddhā). Indications based on results (phalalakṣaṇā) are of two kinds, according to whether the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is hidden (gūḍha) or unhidden (agūḍha). // VisSd_2.10 //

The eightfold *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) shown with respect to purpose (*prayojana*) becomes sixteenfold when each is divided into two types— obscure (*gūḍha*) and non-obscure (*agūḍha*)— according to whether the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of that purpose is hidden or not. Among these, the "obscure" is that which is perceivable only by those whose intellectual power has been ripened through the contemplation of the meaning of poetry.
For example:
"Much was done there...
This is the unhidden [suggestion], which is perceivable by everyone due to its extreme clarity.
As it is said:
"The very intoxication of youth teaches graceful charms to amorous women."

Here, by the term "teaches" (*upadiśati*), "manifests" (*āviṣkaroti*) is indicated; and the excellence of this manifestation is clearly perceived, just like the subject matter itself. Furthermore, these [qualities] are also twofold, categorized according to whether they pertain to the substratum (*dharmin*) or the property (*dharma*), as is the case with the fruit (*phala*).

These sixteen varieties of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) mentioned immediately above become thirty-two varieties by being divided into two each—according to whether they reside in the substratum (*dharmi*) or in the property (*dharma*). To provide a mere illustration:

"The sky is smeared with the glossy, dark luster of clouds; the clouds are streaked with darting cranes; the winds are laden with spray; and the sweet warbling of the cuckoos—the friends of the clouds—is full of joy."
Granted, let it be so; I am Rāma, firm and hard-hearted, and I shall endure everything. But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast.

In this case, when Rāma—the substratum (*dharmī*)—is the indicated object (*lakṣya*), characterized by his capacity to endure extreme suffering, the excellence (*atiśaya*) of that very quality is the result (*phala*).
In the expression “a hamlet on the Ganges,” the excellence of the qualities of coolness and purity in the riverbank is the result.
Thus, forty varieties of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) are recognized by the wise. (VisSd 2.11)
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there are eight [types], and in the case of the fruit (*phala*), there are thirty-two; thus, there are forty varieties of *lakṣaṇā*.
Furthermore—each of those is also twofold, according to whether it resides in a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*).
And those forty varieties just mentioned are as follows;
among them, an example occurring at the level of the word (*pada*) is:
"A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
As for its occurrence within a sentence, it is as in the example:
"Much was done there.
Thus, indication (lakṣaṇā) is of eighty types.
Now, regarding the phonemes (vyañjanā):
that by which the supreme meaning is understood when denotation and the other [functions] have ceased. (ViSd 2.12)
That function is called *vyañjanā* (suggestion), belonging to both word and meaning;

it is that by which another distinct meaning is communicated after the three functions— namely *abhidhā* (denotation), *lakṣaṇā* (indication), and *tātparya* (implication)— have ceased their operation and become exhausted after having conveyed each of their respective meanings, according to the principle that "there is no further activity of words, cognitions, or actions once they have come to rest."

That power of the word, its meaning, and [their components such as] the stem and suffix—which is the object of designations such as "suggestion" (*vyañjanā*), "resonance" (*dhvanana*), "communication" (*gamana*), and "representation" (*pratyāyana*)—is called *vyañjanā*.
In this regard:
*Suggestion of the word is twofold, being rooted in denotation (*abhidhā*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).* (VisSd 2.13)

He states [the function] based on denotation (*abhidhāmūlā*): "When a word with multiple meanings is restricted to a single meaning by means of *saṃyoga* (association) and other factors, that which causes the cognition of another [meaning] is *vyañjanā* (suggestion); it is based upon denotation. (VisSd 2.14)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), separation and so forth are included.
For it has been said:
"Conjunction, separation, association, and opposition..."
The meaning, the context, the indicative mark, and the proximity of another word.
“Capacity, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth,
are the causes for the recollection of a specific meaning when the word’s meaning is otherwise undetermined.”
Thus:

by the association with the conch and discus, the word *hari* denotes Viṣṇu alone—as in "Hari with the conch and discus"; and by the dissociation from them, it denotes that very same one—as in "Hari without the conch and discus."
In the phrase "Bhīma and Arjuna," Arjuna is Pārtha;
in "Karṇa and Arjuna," Karṇa is the son of a Sūta;
and in "I bow to Sthāṇu," Sthāṇu is Śiva.
“Your Majesty knows all,” [refers to] Your Majesty as the God;
“the dolphin-bannered one is angry,” [refers to] the dolphin-bannered one as Kāma; “the God, the enemy of the cities,” [refers to] the enemy of the cities as Śiva.
In the phrase “the cuckoo is intoxicated by honey,” *madhu* means spring;
in the phrase “may your beloved’s face come toward you,” *mukha* means being face-to-face (*sāṃmukhya*); [and] “the moon shines in the sky.”
Thus, *candra* means the moon (*śaśin*).
According to the rule "the fire (*citrabhānu*) at night," *citrabhānu* means the sun by day.
Because it is expressed in the neuter gender as "the chariot-part (*rathāṅga*) shines," *rathāṅga* refers to the wheel.
However, since it is only in the Veda that *svara* (accent) produces specific understanding and not in poetry (*kāvyam*), its scope has not been illustrated here.
Some, disagreeing with this, say: "Even *svara*, in the form of *kāku* (intonation) and so forth, certainly produces specific understanding in poetry."

"Even though it possesses forms such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, according to the method stated in the recitation of the Sage, it produces the perception of specific aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*)"; this [argument] is indeed an appropriate example regarding this matter—but that is not so.
For instance, accents such as the falsetto (*kāku*) or the acute (*udātta*) and others convey only a specific quality in the form of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Indeed, what has been stated previously is not the specific feature consisting of the restriction of a word with multiple meanings to a single meaning.

Furthermore, if it were to be asserted that even in cases where there is no restriction by context or other factors, words with multiple meanings are restricted to a single sense in one instance by the power of a corresponding tone (*svaravaśena*), then it would follow that *śleṣa* (paronomasia) could not be admitted in such instances; yet that is not the case.
Therefore, they have said in the context of defining *śleṣa*:
"In the path of poetry, accent (*svara*) is not taken into account. This is the established principle.
Thus, enough with casting mere glances at the commentaries of those venerable authorities upon whom we depend.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [we include cases] such as "having breasts of this very size," where through gestures of the hands and so forth, the breasts and other parts take on the form of lotus buds and the like.

Thus, when a single meaning has been restricted by the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*), that power of the word-meaning which causes the cognition of another meaning is *suggestion* (*vyañjanā*) rooted in denotation (*abhidhāmūlā*).

For example, from my father’s feet—the great minister, the master of fourteen languages, the lover of the courtesans of poetry, the great lord of poets, the illustrious Candraśekhara Saṃdhivigrahika: [The verse follows...]

“With a form difficult to overcome, causing the mind-born god of love to close his eyes by his splendor, possessing the majesty of a rising king, endowed with great dignity, surrounded on all sides by serpents,

having the lord of stars as his eye, maintaining a deep devotion for the mountain-dwelling preceptor, and having stepped upon the earth with a body adorned by prosperity— the beloved of Umā shines resplendent.”

In this instance, since the meaning of the word *umāvallabha*— namely, King Bhānudeva, the beloved of the great queen named Umā— is restricted by the primary function (*abhidhā*) due to the context, the meaning "beloved of Gaurī" is understood solely through suggestion (*vyañjanā*). The same applies to other cases.
He states [the definition] based on indication (lakṣaṇāmūla): "That for whose sake indication is employed is the purpose;
that by which it is made known would be suggestion (vyañjanā) based on indication. (VisSd 2.15)

In expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges," once the primary function (*abhidhā*) has ceased because it conveys meanings such as "consisting of water" and the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) has ceased because it conveys the meaning of the "bank," that [function] by which an excellence such as coolness or purity is conveyed is suggestion based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūlā vyañjanā*).
Having thus explained verbal suggestion (*śabdī vyañjanā*), he states the fourfold nature of objective suggestion (*arthī*):

[The meaning is determined] from the speaker, the person to be addressed, and the sentence; from the proximity of others, the expressed meaning, the context, the place, and the time; and from tone of voice, gestures, and so forth. (VisSd 2.16)
The term "vyañjana" (suggestive expression) is understood here as the governing factor.
In that regard, when there is a distinction of the speaker, the statement, the context, the place, and the time—as in my own verse:
"The season is spring, and this flower-bowed god of love is enraged; the winds blow steadily, removing the fatigue of passion."
"Tell me, what should be done today, when even the pleasure-grove with its lovely thickets of *vañjula* trees is far away from her husband?"
"Let a secret lover be sent quickly to this place"—thus is indicated by a certain woman to her friend.
Regarding the distinction of the person to be understood (*boddhavya-vaiśiṣṭye*), as for example:

"The surface of your breast is completely stripped of sandal-paste; your lower lip has its redness rubbed away; your eyes are entirely devoid of collyrium; and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation."
"O false speaker!
O messenger! You have gone from here to the pond to bathe, not to the presence of that base man—[you] whose arrival with suffering was unknown to your kinsmen!"

In this case, by means of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (indication through the opposite), what is indicated (*lakṣya*) is: "You have gone precisely to his presence to sport. And its suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), namely "in order to sport," is understood through the specific character (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the female messenger.
An example [of suggestion] due to the specific character of the presence of another is as follows:
“Behold, motionless and still,
the crane shines upon the lotus leaf, as if resting within a vessel of pure emerald.”
"Like a conch-shell cord."
Here, by the stillness of the crane, its confidence is indicated;
by that, the solitude of this place is shown;
therefore, "this is the meeting-place"—thus does someone speak to a hidden lover standing nearby.
In this very context, the purpose is the excellence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), consisting of the solitude of the location.
The term *kāku* is defined by the learned as "a variation in the tone of the voice.
The various types of such *kāku*, as described in that manner, are to be understood from the authoritative sources (*ākaras*).
Regarding this specific quality,
as it is said: "Alas, intent on going to a very distant land because he is dependent upon his guru,
O friend, he will not return to this place made lovely by swarms of bees and cuckoos."
"At the time of the fragrant [season], he..."
In this case, it is suggested by means of intonation (*kāku*) that "he will not come here, but rather he will certainly come"—
as for example, in the case of a particularity of gesture (*ceṣṭāvaiśiṣṭya*).
“Having recognized that the lover was thinking of the time for their secret tryst, the clever woman closed her playful lotus-eye, its intent communicated through a glance from her smiling eyes.”
In this context, "twilight" is indicated by a certain woman through gestures such as the closing of her eyes, signifying that it is the time for a secret rendezvous.
In the same way, one should understand the specific significance of the speaker and other factors, whether taken individually or collectively.
These three types of meanings are each considered to be threefold. (VisSd 2.17)
"Since meanings possess three forms—as the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—all the types of suggestion mentioned immediately above are likewise threefold.
Among these, an example of the suggestion of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha-vyañjanā*) is: ‘The season is spring... and so forth.
An example of the suggestion of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha-vyañjanā*) is: ‘The sandalwood paste has been entirely washed away... and so forth."
As for the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), there is the example beginning with “ua ṇiccala-” and so forth.
The manner in which roots, suffixes, and the like function as suggestors (*vyañjaka*) will be elaborated upon later.
A word understood through its verbal form suggests a meaning, and a word also relies upon another meaning [to suggest].
If one [cause] possesses the capacity to manifest [an effect], then another acts as its auxiliary.
Since a word requires another entity even when acting as a manifestor, and an object likewise requires the word,
it must necessarily be admitted that when one is the manifestor, the other functions as its auxiliary cause.
Due to its association with the three limiting conditions (upādhi) such as denotation (abhidhā) and the rest, the word is also considered to be of three kinds:
expressive (vācaka), indicative (lakṣaka), and likewise suggestive (vyañjaka).
That which has the primary meaning (*abhidhā*) as its limiting condition is the denoter (*vācaka*);
that which has the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as its limiting condition is the indicator (*lakṣaka*);
and that which has the suggestion (*vyañjanā*) as its limiting condition is the suggester (*vyañjaka*).
Furthermore:
Others say that there is a function called *tātparya* (intentional import) for the purpose of understanding the connection between word-meanings;
they hold that this is the *tātparyārtha* (the intentional meaning), and that the sentence is the means of conveying it. (ViśSd 2.20)

The view of the proponents of the theory of "the connection of expressed meanings" (abhihitānvayavādins) is as follows: because the denotative function (*abhidhā*) ceases after conveying the meaning of each individual word, there exists a function called *tātparya* (intentional import) which conveys the connection of word-meanings that constitutes the sentence-meaning; the object of that [function] is the *tātparyārtha* (sentence-meaning), and the sentence is the conveyor of that [meaning].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Presentation of Literature" and "The Definition of the Nature of the Sentence.
Now begins the third chapter:
"What, then, is this *rasa*? It is said—

Through the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and likewise the transitory states (*saṃcārī*), the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love attains the state of rasa for those possessed of sensitivity. (VisSd 3.1)
The transitory emotions (*vibhāva*) and so forth will be explained later.
The involuntary emotions (*sāttvika*) are not mentioned separately because they are of the nature of *anubhāvas* (consequents).

Rasa is manifested only when it has been transformed into another form—according to the analogy of curd and the like—and thus made manifest; it is not manifested as something already established beforehand, like a jar by means of a lamp.
This has been stated by the authors of the *Locana*:
"The expression 'the rasas are perceived' is a figurative usage, like saying 'he cooks the rice'.

And here, although the status of being a *sthāyin* (permanent emotion) is already established by the very mention of the terms *rati* (love) and so forth, the term *sthāyin* is mentioned again for the purpose of demonstrating that even *rati* and the others serve as *sthāyins* within other rasas.
Consequently, laughter, anger, and the like are merely transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) within the erotic, heroic, and other [rasas].
As it has been said:
"A fundamental emotion (*bhāva*), when it reaches the state of rasa, attains the status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyin*)."
The manner of its aesthetic relish (*āsvādana*), which contains within it a description of its essential nature, is now described:
"Due to the predominance of *sattva*, it consists of consciousness that is undivided, self-luminous bliss;
it is devoid of contact with any other object of knowledge and is a twin brother to the tasting of Brahman. (Viṣṇu-samhitā 3.2)
This aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose life-breath is the wondrousness of the supramundane, is tasted by certain subjects as non-different from their own mental forms.

"Sattva is said here to be the mind untouched by rajas and tamas"—according to this stated definition, *sattva* is a certain internal quality that brings about an orientation away from external objects of cognition.
Its "predominance" (*udreka*) is its manifestation after having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*.
And the cause for this is the cultivation of such extraordinary, supramundane objects.

It is "indivisible" (akhaṇḍa), meaning this [experience] is indeed one, consisting of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of bliss arising from the manifestation of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and permanent moods (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love (*rati*). We shall state the reason for this below.
Its "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*) and so forth will also be explained according to the method to be presented later.
In the term *cinmaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
*Camatkāra* (wonder) consists of the expansion of the heart and is synonymous with astonishment (*vismaya*).

Its status as the vital essence [of poetry] was stated by the venerable Nārāyaṇa-pāda, the foremost among poets and scholars and the most eminent member of the circle of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) of our great-great-grandfather.
Thus Dharmadatta says in his own work:
"In every [aesthetic] flavor (rasa), the essence is the *camatkāra* (the sense of wonder);
since that *camatkāra* is the essence [of all flavors], the marvelous (*adbhuta*) is the flavor in every case.
Therefore, the wise Nārāyaṇa declared that the marvelous alone is the flavor."
Thus;
"by some" means by those endowed with past merit.
As it has been said:
"The meritorious, like yogins, perceive the continuous flow of rasa.

Although it has been stated according to the direction of the verse, "The relish [of rasa] arises from the fusion with the meaning of the poem; it is the emergence of self-bliss," such that rasa is not distinct from its relishing, [the following is said:]...
Nevertheless, the usage [of the term] as either an object or an agent—expressed as "rasaḥ svādyate" (the aesthetic flavor is tasted)—is based on accepting a conceptual distinction.
As it has been said: "For rasa is indeed not other than the very body of manifestation, because its essence consists solely in the state of being relished.
This same kind of figurative usage should be understood in other similar instances as well.
But surely, by this much, it has been stated that rasa is unknowable; and since suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is a specific kind of cognition, the two would result in being identical.
Consequently—“That which, through its own cognition, is the cause of another's understanding regarding an established object is considered a suggester (*vyañjaka*).”
Just as with a lamp, if there were no change, what distinction would there be between it and its creator?

If it is argued that, according to the direction stated above, there is indeed a distinction between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), just as in the case of a jar and a lamp, then how can rasa be something manifested?
This is well said.
For this very reason, they say:
“This activity called *āsvādana* (tasting) is indeed distinct from the differences between *kṛti* (action) and *jñapti* (cognition);
for this very reason, designations such as *rasanā*, *āsvādana*, and *camatkaraṇa* are themselves distinct.
Thus, by us—who are intent on establishing merely that there is an activity distinct from denotation (*abhidhā*) and so forth—it follows that *rasa* and the rest are *vyaṅgya* (suggested).

Now, it might be objected that since sentiments such as compassion (*karuṇa*) are of the nature of suffering, they could not possess the status of a *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) because they lack [the quality of] being directed toward that [bliss]. To this it is replied:
even in a sentiment such as compassion, there arises a supreme bliss.
In that regard, the experience of those possessed of consciousness is the sole authority.
By the word "etcetera," the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), and so forth are included.
Nevertheless, another position is stated to seal the mouths of those who lack aesthetic sensitivity (*asahṛdaya*):
moreover, when there is suffering within those [rasas], no one would ever be intent upon them.
For no conscious being engages in action for the sake of their own suffering;
and since everyone is seen to engage in compassion and other such virtues with great devotion, they consist of nothing but happiness.
He states another argument against this:
In the same way, works such as the Rāmāyaṇa will become causes of suffering.

If the aesthetic flavor of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) were a cause of suffering, it would follow that literary compositions such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which are dominated by the flavor of compassion, would also be causes of suffering.
[The opponent asks: "But how can pleasure arise from things that are causes of suffering? [The author] replies:

Let worldly things such as sorrow, joy, and the like indeed arise in the world.

Since they have attained the state of being extraordinary aesthetic excitants (*vibhāva*) by virtue of their reliance on poetry, what harm is there in the fact that pleasure arises from all of them? 3.7.

Indeed, those very things such as Rāma’s exile to the forest, which are called "pains" (duḥkha) in the world, when presented in poetry and drama, abandon their status as being denotable by the term "cause" due to possessing an extraordinary function of aesthetic manifestation (vibhāvana), and instead come to be denoted by the term "extraordinary excitants" (alaukika-vibhāva).
And from these, just as pleasure arises from the biting of teeth and so forth during sexual union, only pleasure is produced.

Therefore, the restriction that "worldly sorrow, joy, and so forth arise from worldly causes such as sorrow and joy" applies only to the world. In poetry, however, there is no fault whatsoever, because of the rule that "from all excitants (vibhāvas), etc., only pleasure arises. If this is so, how is it that tears and other such reactions arise even from seeing or hearing the life stories of Hariścandra and others in poetry and drama? It is said in response:
In the same way, the shedding of tears and so forth are considered to arise from the rapidity of the mind.
If this is so, why is such a manifestation of rasa not produced for everyone through poetry? To this he says:
"That savoring [of rasa] does not arise without the latent impressions (vāsanā) of love and other emotions. (VisSd 3.8)

If both present and past latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the cause for the relishing of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), then if the former did not exist, such relishing would occur even for those such as elderly Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) or ancient Mīmāṃsakas who lack them; and if the latter did not exist, then the arousal of *rasa* that is observed in some sensitive individuals (*sahr̥daya*) despite their lack of present impressions would not occur.
And it was said by Dharmadatta: "The appreciation of aesthetic flavor (rasa) belongs to those members of the assembly who possess latent impressions (vāsanā);
but those devoid of such impressions are, within the theater, like wood, walls, or stone."

Some say it is identical, while others say it is different. Those who say it is different argue that the stable emotion is the cause, and the manifestation is the effect; the former is the internal state, while the latter is the externalized experience. In this context, although only the excitant (vibhāva) consisting of Mālavikā’s form is described for Agnimitra, who desires Mālavikā, the attendant emotions (sañcāribhāvas) such as eagerness (autsukya) and the consequent states (anubhāvas) such as the dilation of the eyes are implied by the very propriety (aucitya) of the situation; this same principle should be inferred even when one thing implies another. This is an example of what is called *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter). However, it is not appropriate to say that rasa is merely an implication (*ākṣepa*) of something else. For if that were the case, then since the opening and closing of the lotuses are themselves the excitants (*vibhāvas*) for the rasa of wonder (*adbhuta*), the rasa would be nothing more than an implication of those excitants. But this is incorrect, because rasa is never an implication of anything else. Furthermore, if the moon had not actually risen, how could the night-lotuses open? And if the sun had not actually set, how could the day-lotuses close? Therefore, the rising of the moon and the setting of the sun must be understood as being directly expressed (*vācya*). Thus, the statement that "rasa resides in the object of imitation" is refuted. Because it is limited, because it is mundane, and likewise because it is subject to obstacles.
The mere arousal of the emotion of love or the like belonging to the character being portrayed would not constitute rasa.

For the arousal of love and other emotions in Rāma and others, arising from the sight of Sītā and so forth, is limited, worldly, and subject to interruption due to the viewing of drama or poetry; therefore, how could it attain the nature of rasa?
This is because rasa possesses characteristics that are distinct from these three attributes.
And he rejects the notion that this [imitation] resides in the imitator:
"By means of mere practice of the training and so forth, one attains the essential nature of Rāghava and others. (VisSd 3.18)
A dancer who merely demonstrates [the performance] cannot be a relisher of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Furthermore:
through the contemplation of the meaning of the poem, even this person becomes a fit recipient for the status of a connoisseur (*sabhyapada*). (Viśvavidyā 3.19)

If, however, even an actor were to manifest his own identity as that of Rāma and others through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of the poetic work, then he too would be counted among the members of the assembly. This [Self] is not something to be made known (*jñāpya*), because its existence is never subject to non-apprehension; for whereas things like a jar, which are objects to be made known, may sometimes remain unknown despite being present.
For this [self] is not like that,
because it does not exist apart from cognition;
since it consists of a collective mental apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the various manifestations (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is not an effect—
for if rasa were an effect, it would necessarily have the cognition of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth as its cause;
consequently, at the time of the apprehension of rasa, the excitants and other factors would not be apprehended.
Because the cognition of the cause and the cognition of the effect are not observed simultaneously—
for instance, the cognition of the touch of sandalwood and the cognition of the pleasure produced by it cannot occur at one and the same time—

and because rasa is perceived precisely as having the nature of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, it follows that the cognition of the determinants and others is not its cause; such is the intended meaning.
It is not eternal, for it is devoid of prior cognition;
indeed, at the time when there is no cognition, its existence is not found. (VisSd 3.21)
Indeed, it is not the case that an eternal entity is non-existent during the time it is not being perceived;

nor is it something yet to come, because its nature is directly blissful and self-luminous. Furthermore, it is not even merely present, because its state is not distinct from that of an effect [already produced].

Because it is the object of the reflective awareness of those who are discerning regarding its manifestation and so forth, and because it is clearly experienced by the wise as consisting of supreme bliss. (VisSd 3.23)
Non-conceptual cognition is not accepted as its apprehender, because it lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression. (VisSd 3.24)
It is to be experienced through conceptual cognition— for it is objects cognizable by conceptual knowledge that possess the fitness for the employment of words,
but rasa is not like that.
Nor is it [known] by way of direct perception;
its manifestation is not indirect, yet it is not immediate because it arises from words. (VisSd 3.25)
"Therefore, tell me: what is the nature of this [reality], whose mode of definition has never before been heard or seen?
To this he says: "Truly, this must be known by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) as something transcendent (*alaukika*).
What then is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence? To this he says:
In this matter, the wise maintain that the only means of valid cognition is aesthetic relish (carvaṇā), which is non-different from itself.
Carvaṇā means relishing.
And that [relishing] is of the kind described as: "Relish arises from the fusion with the meaning of the poem, resulting in the emergence of self-bliss.

Although savoring itself has no status as an effect because it is non-different from rasa, nevertheless, because it occurs only occasionally, its status as an effect is metaphorically attributed to it by means of this figurative "effect-ness."

This is the intended meaning.

By these [means], the excitants (*vibhāva*) are described. As it was said by Bhartṛhari:

One regards Kaṃsa and others as if they were directly present, taking them as the means [to an end].
Thus it is said.

Among these, the hero (*nāyaka*)—

A leader is one who is generous, skillful, of noble birth, prosperous, endowed with beauty, youth, and energy, capable, beloved by the people, and possessed of splendor, cleverness, and good character. (VisSd 3.30)
Dakṣa means one who acts with speed;

This is clear.

For example—Mādhava and others in works such as the *Mālatīmādhava*.

though his faults have been seen, he speaks falsely—such is the audacious leader.
As it was said by me:
"When I went near her to kiss her face, seeing that it was red, she immediately struck me with her foot;
then, as I laughed while holding her, [she bit my lip]."
O friend, even the anger of that fair-browed woman, as she sheds tears because she is unable to do anything there,
produces curiosity when meditated upon in the mind.
The *anukūla* (favourable) hero who is devoted to one alone— the *anukūlanāyaka* is one who is attached to only a single heroine.
For example:
"O friend, our two garments are not beautiful, nor is our necklace radiant."
There is no crooked gait, no haughty laughter, and indeed, there is no pride whatsoever.

As it is said:
“O rogue! When you suddenly heard the tinkling of another’s girdle-jewels, even as you were embracing me, the knot of your arms became instantly loosened.”
Where shall I tell this? My friend, reeling from the poison of your many words—which are like ghee and honey—does not attend to anything at all.
And because these are of three kinds— namely, superior, middling, and inferior—
it has been stated that there are forty-eight varieties of heroes.
Regarding these sixteen varieties that have been mentioned,
he now states their associates as a related digression: "But in the case of a *prāsaṅgika* (incidental) plot that follows at a distance, it should be [associated with] that."
His companion, known as the *pīṭhamarda*, is one who is slightly inferior in those qualities.
In the extensive narrative connected to the context of that hero, there is an assistant named *pīṭhamarda* who is slightly inferior to the general qualities of the hero just mentioned;
for example, Sugrīva and others for Rāmacandra and others.
Now, the assistants of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)—
In the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), his companions should be the *viṭa*, the *ceṭa*, the *vidūṣaka*, and others;
they are devoted, skilled in jesting, capable of dispelling the anger of their wives, and pure.
By the word "etcetera," flower-sellers, dyers, betel-vendors, perfumers, and so forth are included.
