Skilled in dress and social etiquette, eloquent, sweet-spoken, and highly esteemed in the assembly.

The *ceṭa* (servant) is well known; the *vidūṣaka* is one whose name is Kusuma, Vasantaka, or the like, who causes laughter through his actions, body, dress, speech, and so forth, who delights in quarrels, and who is skilled in his own duties. (VisSd 3.42)
One's own activity consists of laughter and so forth.
He states the assistant for the contemplation of matters: "The minister should be [the assistant] in the contemplation of matters."
The "objects" (arthas) are the tantrāvāpa and so forth.

Regarding this, however, in the context of describing the assistants, a certain author has provided the following definition: "The minister, himself, or both together are his friends in the deliberation of affairs."
That too should be characterized as the section concerning the means for a king’s reflection on state affairs (*arthacintana*), and not as the section concerning the mention of assistants;
for even if it were stated that "the minister is the assistant of the hero (*nāyaka*) in his reflection on state affairs," the hero would already be established by implication alone.
As for what was also stated— "The *dhīralalita* [hero] belongs to ministers; the others have their successes dependent upon ministers"—

that too is redundant, since it has already been established by the description of the specific characteristics of the *dhīralalita*, who alone is characterized as having his deliberations on affairs dependent solely upon ministers.
Furthermore, in the contemplation of the meaning, the minister is not his assistant,
but rather he is the accomplisher himself,
because the minister lacks the capacity for such contemplation of the meaning and so forth.
Now, those who accompany [the king] in the inner apartments—
likewise in the harem—
are dwarfs, eunuchs, Kirātas, Mlecchas, Ābhīras, Śakas, hunchbacks, and so forth. (VisSd 3.43)
Proud of his own foolishness, born of a base family yet endowed with power,
he is this king’s brother-in-law, the unmarried brother known as Śakāra.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the mute and others are included.
Among them, the eunuchs, dwarfs, Kirātas, hunchbacks, and so on are described in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"The dwarf, casting aside shame out of fear, enters this inner chamber-robe because the attendants have lost their sense of human dignity; thus, the counting of men has ceased."
The Kirātas have given their own name to the border-dwellers who resemble them; thus, the hunchbacked women walk slowly, solely out of humility, fearing that they might be mistaken for them.
The word *śaka* is well known from works such as the *Mṛcchakaṭikā*.
Others should also be understood according to what is observed [in the sources].
Now, the assistants of the staff (*daṇḍasahāya*):
Regarding the staff (daṇḍa): friends, princes, forest-dwellers, vassals, soldiers, and so forth [are its components].
Punishment is the restraint of the wicked;
this is clear.
The officiating priests and domestic chaplains should be knowers of Brahman, as should the ascetics, in accordance with dharma.
Those who know Brahman, those who know the Vedas,
or those who know the Self; and in this regard—
The superior ones are the *pīṭhamarda* and so forth— the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including the minister, the domestic priest, and others; the middling ones are the *viṭa* and the *vidūṣaka*.
Likewise, the Śakas, Cētas, and others are proclaimed to be the lowest.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādya*), betel-sellers, perfumers, and others are included.
Now, as an incidental topic, he states the definition of messengers according to their classification:
"The one with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*), the one with limited authority (*mitārtha*), and likewise the bearer of a message (*saṃdeśahāraka*)."
The messenger for a task is of three kinds, as are the female messengers.
In this context, the definition of a messenger (*dūta*) is one who is sent on a specific task;
therein,
having ascertained the intentions of both parties, he himself provides the reply.
He who carries out a task perfectly well is known as one to whom full authority has been delegated.
"Of both" refers to the one by whom he was sent and the one in whose presence he was sent.
One who speaks measured words and accomplishes the task is a "measured-word bearer";
one who conveys the message exactly as it was spoken is a "messenger. (VisSd 3.49)
Now, the qualities of the *sāttvika* hero:
grace, charm, sweetness, profundity, fortitude, brilliance, elegance, and nobility—these eight are the human qualities born of *sattva*. (Viśvavidyā 3.50)
In that regard— valor, skill, truthfulness, great energy, amiability,
and compassion in conduct, as well as rivalry [in excellence]— from these they know what is called "splendor" (śobhā). (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.51)
In that regard, his popularity was as follows:
"I alone am esteemed by the lord of the earth"—thus every subject thought among themselves;
like [the flow] of hundreds of rivers toward a low-lying place, there was never any disregard for him from anyone.
The same applies to other [emotions] as well.
Now, regarding *vilāsa* (grace):
in *vilāsa*, the gaze is steady, the gait is varied, and the speech is accompanied by a smile.
For instance:

"His gaze treats the essence of all beings in the three worlds as mere straw; his firm and haughty gait seems to bend the very earth. Even in his youth, he possesses a gravity like a mountain—is this the Heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa) that has arrived, or is it Pride itself?"
Lack of agitation even amidst disturbances is proclaimed as sweetness (mādhurya).
The example is to be inferred.
Profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) is the state of being free from transformation (*nirvikāratā*) despite [the presence of] fear, grief, anger, joy, and so forth.
For example:
Whether summoned for his consecration or dismissed to the forest,
I did not perceive even the slightest change in his outward appearance.
Fortitude is the lack of wavering from one's resolve even in the face of great obstacles.
Just as Hara became intent on profound meditation, losing a moment's attention to the songs of the Apsarases as he heard them,
so it is that for those who are masters of themselves, obstacles never have the power to break their concentration.
The inability to endure insults, contempt, and the like, even when inflicted by another at the risk of one's life, is declared to be "splendor" (tejas).
Sweetness of speech and dress, as well as graceful amorous gestures, constitute *lalita* (gracefulness).
Generosity accompanied by affectionate speech is *audārya* (magnanimity), which consists in equanimity toward both enemies and friends.
Examples of these should be inferred.
Now, the heroine (nāyikā) is of three types: one's own (svā), another's (anyā), and a common woman (sādhāraṇā).
She is endowed with the general qualities of a hero (nāyaka) as far as possible. (VisSd 3.56)
Furthermore, the heroine (nāyikā) is endowed with the general qualities of the hero (nāyaka), such as generosity and so forth, as far as possible.
She is of three types: one's own wife (svastrī), another's wife (anyastrī), and a common woman (sādhāraṇastrī).
Among these, the "one's own wife" is—
One's own wife is endowed with discipline, straightforwardness, and other virtues, devoted to her domestic duties, and faithful to her husband—
such as:
"She possesses shame as her sufficient ornament, and is insatiable in her devotion to others."
Wives who are undisciplined and lacking in intelligence are found in the houses of the fortunate.
She too, when classified, is said to be of three types: the innocent, the intermediate, and the mature.

In that regard—the *mugdha* (the innocent) is described as one whose youthful amorous transformations have first descended; she is resistant in sexual union, gentle in her indignation, and possessed of excessive modesty. (VisSd 3.58)
In that regard, the first stage of entered youth is as described by my venerable father:
"The hips attain fullness; the breasts grow heavy; the belly recedes far away; and the line of body hair hastens toward the straightness of the eyes.
Beholding the newly consecrated kingdom of Kandarpa, the limbs of the fair-browed woman instantly begin to plunder one another."

Just as in my *Pariṇaya* of Prabhāvatī, regarding one whose transformation by love has first descended: "She places her foot upon the ground with languid slowness and does not emerge from the inner apartments;
she does not laugh loudly, but for a moment assumes some kind of restraint born of shame."
She speaks somewhat with a depth of feeling, her face slightly touched by a trace of bashfulness; she gazes with a knitting of the brows at her friend as she exults in the tale of her beloved.
Regarding her behavior during lovemaking, as it is said: "When looked at, she casts her gaze downward; when addressed, she does not speak."
She remains tossing about on her bed;
embraced by a young man, she trembles.
As her friends depart from the bedchamber, she strives only to go out after them.
"Or rather, my newly-wedded beloved has now become a source of joy to me precisely because of her perversity."

An example of softness in pride (*māna*) is as follows: "At the time of her husband's first offense, the young woman—without the instruction of her friends—does not know how to indicate her resentment through the turning of her graceful limbs or through indirect speech;
with her lotus-eyes cast down and clear tears falling from the base of her translucent cheeks, she simply weeps, her long locks dangling and rolling about."
An example of one who possesses excessive modesty is found in the verse beginning with "she gave [the garland] slowly and hesitantly" (p.
113). Here, although her resistance to love has already been established by her being excessively modest, it is mentioned again because it possesses a particular strikingness (*vichitti-viśeṣa*).
Now, the middle [woman]:

the middle woman is one who possesses diverse amorous arts, whose passion and youth have fully blossomed, whose speech is slightly bold, and who is considered to possess moderate shyness. (VisSd 3.59)
Regarding her diverse amorous dalliances, as it is said:
"In such a manner was skill displayed by that deer-eyed woman, whose passion was aroused during their lovemaking,
that hundreds of domestic pigeons acted as her pupils, imitating her cooing many times over."
An example of one whose passion has fully blossomed is found right here [in this very work].
An example of one whose youth has fully blossomed is my own: "In her eyes, which outshine the *khañjana* bird..."
Her two hands are rivals to the lotus; her breasts attain a height that mocks the beauty of the *kārī* fruit;
her luster is a match for the golden *campaka* flower; and her speech distills nectar.
The mass of her sidelong glances was like a garland of blooming blue lotuses.
The same applies elsewhere as well.
Now, regarding the bold woman (*pragalbhā*): she is blinded by passion (*smarāndhā*), possesses intense youth (*gāḍhatāruṇyā*), and is skilled in all sexual arts (*samastaratakovidā*).
Her passion is elevated, her modesty slight, and she overcomes the hero with her boldness. VisSd 3.60.
As it is said regarding those blinded by passion: "Blessed are you, who can utter hundreds of confident and playful endearments even during the intervals of love-making when meeting your beloved;
but as for me, O friends, I swear that I do not recall anything at all once my lover has placed his hand upon the knot of my lower garment."
An example of one in the full bloom of youth: "Her chest has exceedingly high breasts, her eyes are very long,
and her eyebrows are exceedingly curved."
"Her speech is even more so; her waist is slender, yet her hips are not diminished in their weight, and the gait of this girl, possessed of some truly wondrous youth, is slow."

As those skilled in all matters of love have said: “Sometimes stained with betel juice, sometimes soiled by the marks of vermilion paste, sometimes smeared with fragrant powder, and sometimes bearing the imprint of feet dyed with lac; with the folds of its creases, with locks of hair fallen upon it, and with withered flowers—the bedsheet tells the story of a woman’s lovemaking in every stage.”
An example of *bhāvonnatā* (the heightening of emotion) is as follows:
"With sweet words, with the knitting of eyebrows and the pointing of fingers, with sudden placements of limbs that are like kinsmen to a great festival, and with repeated, wide, sidelong glances—
that woman acts as an ally to the five-arrowed god in his conquest of the three worlds."
An example of slight shame (*svalpavrīḍā*) is as follows: "You are blessed, you who speak thus"—
as in [the passage on] page 116.
An example of one whose lover has been overcome: "O playful Lord,
adorn your brow with curling locks and a tilaka."
"O Lord of my life, join back the necklace broken upon the slope of your breast!

Having spoken thus at the conclusion of their lovemaking, she whose face was like the full moon was touched by him; and though she had already regained consciousness, she fell once more into a state of swoon.
He states the other distinctions between the *madhyā* (moderate) and *pragalbhā* (bold) types:
"They are both *dhīrā* (composed) and *adhīrā* (uncomposed); thus, among the sixfold [types], there is the *dhīrādhīrā*.
These refer to the *madhyā* and *pragalbhā*.
In that regard:
"A steadfast *madhyā* heroine should burn her lover with words that are sarcastic and crooked. (Viśvavidyā 3.61)
The steadfast (dhīrā) and the unsteadfast (adhīrā) are distinguished by their weeping; the unsteadfast, by harsh words.

Among them, the steadfast heroine of the middle type (madhyā-dhīrā) is as follows: “‘That you called me your beloved was no falsehood,’ [she thinks], seeing him wearing the silk garment that had been worn by her lover.”
Come to my dwelling; for the beauty of adornment of lovers attains its fruitfulness through the sight of their beloved.”
The heroine who is both firm and unfirm is as follows:
"O young girl! O Lord! O proud woman, abandon your anger; what have I done out of wrath?"
"I am weary of you; it is not you who has offended me, but all offenses rest upon me. Why then do you weep with such faltering words?"
Before whom are you weeping? Is this not mine? And who am I to you?
"I am not your beloved"— it is for this reason that you weep.
This very same woman is the "restless" (adhīrā), as for example: "O rogue, she who was so charming with her artificial ornaments remains in your heart along with hundreds of your desires."
"There is no room for us here at all; therefore, enough with this mockery of bowing at your feet."
If she is bold yet steadfast, then her outward form conceals her anger.
O beloved, they remain indifferent during sexual union, though they display great affection outwardly;
as for example:
“Sitting together on one seat was avoided by rising from afar; even an impulsive embrace was thwarted under the pretext of fetching betel;
not even a conversation was mingled as she busied her attendants nearby—thus, by her clever treatment toward her lover, the anger of the artful woman was brought to its fulfillment.”
But the steadfast-unsteadfast woman torments him with sarcastic speech.
This hero;
as in my [verse]:
"O handsome one, even though unadorned..."

how much more so now that you are adorned with the nail-marks of her?"
One should threaten or strike another—
another who is lacking in fortitude—
as in the verse beginning, "Seeing her face red... and so forth.

These are the six types of heroines mentioned immediately above.
For example:

With his neck slightly bent and his hair standing on end, the rogue, his heart overflowing with love, kisses another woman whose cheeks glisten with an inner smile.

however, the *mugdhā* (innocent) is only one. Thus, there are thirteen varieties of the *svīyā* (one's own woman).
The woman belonging to another is said to be of two kinds: one who is already married and likewise a maiden.
Among them—she who is devoted to festivals and the like, who has married another [man], is unchaste and devoid of shame. (VisSd 3.66)
For example:
"The master grows indignant even at a sigh;
the co-wives are eager to catch every scent."
Your mother-in-law is the deity invoked by the lute-like movements of your eyes, and your sisters-in-law are the bees hovering over those eyes;
therefore, O connoisseur of the sweet compositions of wit, why now this salutation with folded hands from afar through the mere play of your glances?
"This effort here is in vain."
For in this case, because he is merely the provider of food, clothing, and so forth, he is her master (*svāmī*) and not her beloved (*vallabha*);

whereas you, through your delight in compositions sweet with wit, are my beloved—by virtue of such suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*), her love for a paramour is perceived. A maiden (*kanyā*), however, is one who has not yet been married, and is characterized by modesty and the onset of youth.
And because she is dependent on her father and others, she is "belonging to another," such as Mālatī and others in the *Mālatīmādhava* and similar works.
A courtesan is a "common heroine" who is steadfast and skilled in the arts. (VisSd 3.67)
She feels no aversion toward those devoid of virtues, nor does she feel attachment even toward those possessed of virtues;
having perceived merely his wealth, she displays passion outwardly.
Even if she has accepted him, she may expel a man whose wealth is exhausted,
even his mother, out of a desire for him to reunite with her once more.

Thieves, eunuchs, fools, those who have acquired wealth through easy means, and those who merely wear the outward marks [of asceticism] while secretly harboring desire and other passions— these are generally her favorites.
She too is subject to passion; whether she is truly devoted or merely attached—or even if she is detached—sexual union with her is extremely difficult to obtain.
A *paṇḍaka* is one afflicted by wind-disorders such as jaundice (*pāṇḍu*) and the like.
Those who desire what is concealed or hidden are "those whose desires are concealed" (*channakāmāḥ*).
Among them, those devoid of passion are exemplified by characters such as Madanamañjarī in the *Laṭakamelaka* and other works.
The passionate woman (*raktā*) is exemplified by Vasantasenā and others in works such as the *Mṛcchakaṭika*.
Furthermore:
"These eight [types of heroines] become sixteenfold through their various conditions (*avasthā*)."
Likewise, there are the woman whose husband is under her own control, the woman who has been slighted, and the woman going to meet her lover.
The woman separated by a quarrel, the deceived woman, the woman whose husband is away, the woman who has arrived at the trysting-place, and likewise the woman longing in separation. (VisSd 3.73)
In that regard:
she whose lover, drawn by the quality of sexual passion, does not leave her side, and who is intent on various amorous dalliances, is one whose husband is under her own control. (VisSd 3.74)
For example:
"O friend, our two garments... and so forth;
[or] when her beloved approaches her side marked by union with another.
The wise have declared her to be "the violated woman" when she is embittered by jealousy.
For example:

she who, being subject to the power of Love, causes her beloved to come to her is [an *abhisārikā*].
Or when she goes out herself, she is called an *abhisārikā* by the wise.

He gave this instruction: "O messenger, approach him skillfully and say something such as: 'Does he not perceive my lightness, and does he not likewise show compassion toward me? Thus he directed her.
"This pair of bracelets has been cast off,
the girdle is fastened firmly,
and with great effort, silence has been imposed upon the two noisy anklets."
"O dear friend, just as I have begun with impetuosity this festival of a secret tryst,
the moon— a Chandala— casts off its veil of darkness."

But if a courtesan should approach him, she would have variegated and radiant attire, her anklets and bracelets tinkling, and her face smiling with joy.
If a female servant approaches, her speech faltering with intoxication, her eyes wide with amorous confusion, and her movements and gait agitated; VisSd_3.79.
In that regard, the first [type] begins with "that which has been lifted," and so forth;
for the other two, examples should be inferred.
Incidentally, the locations for secret trysts (abhisāra) are now described:
A field, a garden, a ruined temple, a messenger’s house, a forest,
a garland-maker’s shop, a cremation ground, and likewise the banks of rivers and so forth.
Thus, for the diversion of unchaste women who have made their rendezvous,
there are eight locations, as well as any place whatsoever shrouded in darkness.
But she who, having driven away even her beloved husband with harsh words despite his flattering advances,
subsequently experiences remorse, is one separated by a quarrel.
As it was said by my venerable father:
"Neither was any flattering word heard, nor was the necklace even glanced at with a sidelong look."
For the sake of my beloved, even the words of my own friends were cast aside;
as he was departing that very moment after falling at my feet, alas, why did I, in my folly, not suddenly seize him by the neck with both hands?
She who, having made an appointment with her lover, does not come into his presence,
should be known as a "deceived" woman (vipralabdhā), utterly humiliated.
For example:
"Arise, messenger! Let us go; watch after watch has passed, yet he has not come."
Even if he were to live beyond this point, he would become the lord of her life."
Her husband has gone to a distant land due to various business matters.
Afflicted by the suffering born of love, she would become like a woman whose husband is away on a journey.
As it is said:
"You should know her to be one of few words, my second life, like a solitary female ruddy goose when I, her mate, have gone far away;
as these heavy days pass by, I think that young woman, filled with intense longing, has changed her very appearance, like a lotus-pond withered by the frost."
She who adorns herself when the chamber of her lover is prepared, having learned of his arrival, is known as *vāsakasajjā*. (VisSd 3.85)
As it says in the play of Rāghavānanda: “Keep your armlets far away; enough with jeweled bracelets on your pair of hands.”
"O Teacher, what is the use of this creeper-like necklace around your neck?
O Mother, for me, you should fashion a single new string of pearls; for in the rites of the festival of Love, there is no need for excessive ornamentation."
Even though her beloved has resolved to come, when he does not arrive due to fate,
she suffers from the pain of his non-arrival and is tormented by the longing of separation.
For example:
"Has he been stopped by some beloved woman, or has he been startled by my friend?"
"Or is there some weightiness of cause for which my beloved has not come today?"—
having reflected thus, the deer-eyed woman placed her lotus-face upon the palm of her hand and sighed deeply.
And they wept for a long time, and garlands of flowers were cast down."
Thus, there are one hundred and twenty-eight [types] according to their superior, middling, and inferior natures;
these constitute three hundred and eighty-four varieties of heroines.
And here, the two wives of others— the maiden and the remarried woman— are *abhisārikās* who, having previously felt longing in separation due to a rendezvous,
subsequently set out for it with a jester or similar companion; they are *vipralabdhās* (deceived) when the hero fails to reach the place of appointment from some cause.
"Thus, there are only these three states for these two [types of lovers] who lack control over their beloveds, because no other state is possible," says someone.
However, in some instances, a mutual intermingling of these states is observed among the objects of description (*lakṣya*).
For example:
"Indeed, we are not worthy of this gift; for she drinks from and protects you in secret.
O rake! Give this branch to her, so that there may be a long-lasting union between those who are well-matched."
O gambler, what is the use of these ear-ornaments of tree-sprouts and flowers placed upon us in vain? Indeed, our pair of ears has long been filled with those deceits of yours known to all people.
"Why do you offer us this flower-stalk, as if repeatedly deceived by the humming of bees?
O rogue, having entered her abode,
you have today bestowed upon her a great calamity!"
Having spoken thus in anger, another woman struck her lover simultaneously with a blue lotus fastened to her ear— its beautiful filaments of bristles quivering— and with her eye.

For this [type of heroine] is a mixture of the *dhīramadhyā*, *adhīramadhyā*, and *dhīrapragalbhā* types, characterized by indirect speech (*vakrokti*), harsh words, and the striking of the ear with a lotus;
one [of these traits] may be inferred even in other cases.
The others are also innumerable, but they have not been mentioned here for fear of prolixity.
These are the heroines.
Now, their ornaments—
those born of their innate nature (sattva) in youth are twenty-eight in number.
Among those, the three ornaments arising from the body are *bhāva*, *hāva*, and *helā*.
Splendor, loveliness, brilliance, sweetness, eloquence, nobility, and fortitude—these seven alone are produced without effort. (VisSd 3.90)

Līlā (playfulness), vilāsa (sportiveness), vicchitti (elegance), vivvoka (affected indifference), kilakiñcita (mixed emotion), moṭṭāyita (coquettishness), kuṭṭamita (feigned anger), vibhrama (bewilderment), lalita (gracefulness), and mada (intoxication). VisSd 3.91.
Sporting, scorching, innocence, distraction, curiosity, laughter, alarm, and play—these are the eighteen [types of amorous gestures]. (VisSd 3.92)
The ten states beginning with *bhāva* (feeling) arise in men by their very nature;
however, these same ten states, beginning with *bhāva* and ending with *dhairya* (fortitude), also occur in the heroines (*nāyikā*).
Nevertheless, all of these, when resting solely upon the heroine, nourish a particular kind of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).
In that regard, "state" (bhāva) refers to the first modification occurring within the mind, which is by nature free from change.
In a mind that has been changeless since birth, even a mere awakening of a modification is an emotional state (*bhāva*).
For example:
"That very same fragrant season; that very same Malaya breeze..."
"This is indeed that same woman, yet her mind appears as if it were another."
Now, regarding *hāva*:
"That which reveals a desire for sexual union through distortions of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth, yet with very slight perceptible distortions, is called *hāva*. (VisSd 3.94)
As it is said:
"Though she was the daughter of the Mountain, she revealed her inner emotion through limbs resembling blossoming young kadamba flowers;
she stood with her face beautifully turned aside, her eyes cast down."
Now, *helā*:
it is that very same [emotion] when its transformation is perceived as being entirely subtle;
it is indeed *bhāva* itself.
For example:
"Thus all the graceful movements of her limbs were employed by her toward her lover;
yet she remained for a long time suspicious even of her friends, as her true feelings were not yet manifest."
Now, regarding splendor (*śobhā*):
it is the adornment of the limbs by means of beauty, youth, grace, and the enjoyment of wealth and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.95)
Beauty has been described; among those, the beauty of youth is as follows:
"The unadorned ornament of her slender body, the intoxicant called no-wine, the cause of passion—"
Then she reached that age beyond childhood which is Cupid’s weapon, other than his flowery arrows.
The same applies elsewhere as well.
Now, as for *kānti* (splendor): that very splendor is the radiance intensified by another [quality].
Beauty that has become exceedingly expansive through the intoxication of love is called *kānti* (loveliness), as in the verse beginning:
"Her eyes surpass the *khañjana* bird... and so forth.
Now, regarding *dīpti*: luster (*kānti*) itself, when it is exceedingly expansive, is designated as *dīpti*.
For example, the description of Candrakalā in my play *Candrakalā*:
"The playfulness of youth, the smile of exceeding beauty,
an ornament for the surface of the earth, and the subjugator of the minds of young men."
Now, regarding sweetness (*mādhurya*): sweetness is loveliness in all particular states.
For example:
“A lotus, even when entwined with moss, is beautiful; the dark spot on the moon, though soiled, spreads its splendor.
This slender woman is exceedingly lovely even in her bark garment; for what indeed is not an ornament to those who possess beauty?”
Now, regarding boldness— boldness is the state of being free from timidity— as for example:
“Embraced with embraces, kissed with kisses,
and even bitten with bites, women reduce their beloved to the state of a slave.”
Now, regarding magnanimity: magnanimity is constant humility. (VisSd 3.97)
For example:
"She does not utter harsh words, nor does she knit her pair of eyebrows;
she does not cast her ear-ornament to the ground even when my offense is manifest."
In the inner chamber, the beloved woman, her eyes directed through the opening of a window, offers her face outward to her friend, yet her eyes are filled with tears.
Now, regarding fortitude (*dhairya*): Fortitude is a state of mind free from self-praise and unshakable.
As it is said: "Let the moon with its full orb blaze in the sky night after night,"
"Let Madana burn me;
what else can he do beyond death?
To me, my beloved father is praiseworthy, and my mother is of stainless lineage; but neither this man nor life itself is so."
Now, [the Lord is worshipped] through playful gestures, costumes, ornaments, beloveds, and even words. (VisSd 3.98)
They know that the imitation of a beloved, performed out of affection, is characterized by restlessness;
for example: "May Pārvatī protect the world with her playful grace—she who wears a coil of lotus-stalks as a serpent-bracelet, whose hair is bound in a topknot, and who resembles a string of pearls."
Now, as for *vilāsa* (graceful play):
it consists of the movements of the carriage, standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as the actions of the face, eyes, and other parts. (Viṣṇudharmaśāstra 3.99)
*Vilāsa* (sportiveness), however, arises from the sight of a beloved and so forth;
for example:
"In the meantime, there appeared something of indescribable variety, surpassing the power of words, possessing the playful grace of the long-eyed one."
Then there appeared the victorious power of Love, acting as a master that overcomes steadfastness by producing an abundance of involuntary emotional transformations.
Now, *vicchitti* (graceful distinction): even a slight arrangement of ornaments (*ākalpa*) constitutes *vicchitti*, which nourishes beauty.
For example:

“If the limbs of the playful women are washed by bathing in clear water, their lips brightened by the luster of betel, and their garments thin and pure— then this much alone would be sufficient adornment, provided they are not devoid of the flower-arrowed god.”
Now, as for *vivvoka* (coquettish disdain):
*Vivvoka* is a lack of regard even for a desired object due to excessive pride. (Viśvanātha’s Śāradātilaka 3.100)
For example:
"Those women who, despite following after excellent virtues, are primarily devoted to faults; those who would rather offer up their very lives..."

But let those Vāmās, whose nature is contrary to the three worlds, be ever victorious for you— those for whom even regarding an object that is most beloved and desired, the rule is one of negation rather than full vision.
Now, as for *kilakiñcita*:

the mingling of smiles, dry weeping, laughter, fear, anger, fatigue, and so forth, arising from the joy produced by union with a beloved and other such causes, is indeed called *kilakiñcita*. (VisSd 3.101)
For example:

"The woman with thighs like a young elephant’s trunk caused her lover to restrain his hands despite his unopposed desire, to utter reproaches laced with sweet smiles, and to break into charming, dry weeping even in the midst of pleasure."
Now, regarding *moṭṭāyita*:
when the mind is permeated by the feelings for her beloved during conversations and the like, scratching the ear and so forth are called *moṭṭāyita*. (VisSd 3.102)
For example:
"O fortunate one! At the commencement of your story, that woman—eager for the scratching of her ears and with the lotuses of her face blooming—pierces through [the restraint of] her limbs."
Now, regarding *kuṭṭamita*:
when the hair, breasts, lips, and so forth are grasped, even in the presence of joy, the shaking of the head and hands out of agitation is called *kuṭṭamita*. (VisSd 3.103)
For example:
"When her beloved bit her bimba-like lower lip, which rivaled a sprout in its likeness,
the young woman let out a shrill cry with her hand, its trembling bangles jingling as if in pain."

Now, regarding *vibhrama* (bewilderment): "Due to haste arising from joy, passion, and so forth, the misplaced arrangement of gestures such as *vibhrama* in relation to the arrival of a beloved and the like is considered *vibhrama*. (VisSd 3.104)
For example:
"Hearing that her lover was approaching from outside, she, with her ornaments still incomplete,
applied collyrium to her eyes and drew a tilaka-mark with red lac upon her cheek."
Now, *lalita* (the graceful): "The graceful (*lalita*) is the arrangement of the limbs through their delicacy. For example:
With the resonant sound of her heavy anklets and her left lotus-foot gracefully dancing, she then moved with her other foot, which was exceedingly tremulous and slow with passion.
Now, intoxication (mada):
intoxication is a transformation born from the arrogance of good fortune, youth, and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.105)
For example:
"Do not harbor pride, thinking, 'This cluster of blossoms was written by my beloved's own hand upon the surface of my cheek.
Is not another woman also surely a fit vessel for such things, provided that trembling does not become an obstacle within?"
Now, regarding *vihṛta*: silence out of shame even at the time for speaking is considered *vihṛta*.
For example:
“Though asked by me about her welfare as she had come from afar, she said nothing at all;
yet her tearful eyes told everything.”
Now, regarding *tapanam* (torment):
*Tapanam* is the behavior arising from the impulse of love (*smaravega*) upon the separation from a beloved. (Viśvāmitrasiddhānta 3.106)
As it says in my own work:
"She exhales sighs upon the ground, rolls about,
and gazes toward your path."
She weeps longingly,
stretching her creeper-like arms from here toward the earth;
moreover, O you who are as dear to her as her own life!
She has longed for union with you even in her dreams;
she desires sleep,
yet cursed fate does not grant it to her, not even that.

Now, regarding innocence (*maugdhyam*): "That inquiry concerning even a well-known object which is conducted as if out of ignorance in the presence of one's beloved is called 'innocence' by those who know its true nature. (VisSd 3.107)
For example: "What trees are they, in what village do they stand, and by whom were they planted? None [knows], for their fruit is the pearl placed upon my wrist."
Now, regarding diversion (vikṣepa):
"The partial arrangement of ornaments, feigned glances in all directions, and the slight disclosure of secrets—this is diversion in the presence of the beloved. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.108)
For example:
"The slender maiden arranges her braid so that half is released, and likewise applies the forehead mark incompletely; she speaks but little of the secret, and looks about startled."
Now, curiosity (*kutūhala*): curiosity is the longing to behold a beautiful object. For example:

“Another woman, having cast aside her foot— which was being massaged by her attendant and was still dripping with red lac— abandoned her graceful gait and extended a path marked by red dye from the window.”
Now, regarding laughter:
laughter (*hasita*) is a frivolous smile arising from the onset of youth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.109)
For example:
"Since this slender-limbed woman has laughed all of a sudden,
surely the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) reigns supreme over her."
Then, "startled" (cakitam)—
a state of fear and agitation arising before her beloved from some cause;
as for example:
“Trembling, her beautiful thighs struck by the darting minnows, she reached the height of amorous agitation;
oh, young women are violently disturbed even without cause—how much more so when a cause is present?”
Now, as for *keli*:
playing together with a beloved in a pleasure garden (*vihāra*) is called *keli*. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.110)
For example:

"A certain woman, her mind agitated and her breasts high and full, struck her lover on the chest with her bosom, for she was unable to dispel the pollen born of flowers from his eyes with the breath of her mouth."
Now, the gestures of affection of the innocent girl:

Having seen [her beloved], she shows bashfulness; she does not look him directly in the face; or she looks at her dear one when he is hidden, or when he is wandering about, or when he has passed by. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.111)
Even when questioned in many ways, with her face cast down very slowly, she generally speaks only a little of what is pleasing, in a faltering voice. (VisSd 3.112)
The young woman, full of passion for her beloved, listens with constant attentiveness to the stories told by others about him, directing her gaze elsewhere.
Now, the gestures indicative of passion in all types of heroines:
she highly prizes staying near her beloved for a long time,
yet she does not come into his line of sight unless she is adorned.
In some places, under the pretext of binding her hair or adjusting her garment,
she should clearly reveal the base of her arms, her breasts, and the lotus of her navel.
He provides clothing and other necessities for the attendants of his beloved;
he places trust in his friends and shows them great respect. (VisSd 3.116)
In the midst of her friends, she speaks of his virtues; she bestows her own wealth upon him;
she sleeps when he sleeps; and she bears sorrow in his sorrow and joy in his joy.
Standing constantly within the range of his vision, she gazes at him from afar; yet, as if overcome by the transformation of love, she addresses her attendants in his presence.
Whatever she perceives, she laughs pointlessly;
likewise, she scratches her ears and loosens or binds her braid of hair.
She yawns, stretches her limbs, embraces and kisses the child,
and likewise applies the tilaka mark upon the forehead of her female companion.
She draws with the tip of her big toe, gazes askance, bites her own lower lip, and speaks sweet words with her face cast downward. (VisSd 3.121)
The Leader does not leave that place where he is seen;
he comes to his home under some pretext of business.
Whatever has been given by her beloved, she gazes upon it repeatedly while holding it to her body;
she is constantly joyful in his company, but in his absence, she becomes dejected and emaciated.
She considers that conduct to be great; she considers what is dear to him to be dear;
she desires things of little value, and when asleep, she does not turn over. VisSd_3.124.
A beautiful woman, affectionately attached to him, does not encounter any sattvic transformations in his presence; she speaks words that are pleasant and true. (VisSd 3.125)

The gestures of a young woman (navastrī) in these situations are characterized by excessive modesty; those of a middle-aged woman (madhyā) possess moderate shame; while those of an older woman (prauḍhā) involve the shedding of bashfulness.
These same [behaviors] may also belong to a bold woman other than one's own wife, as well as to courtesans.
To give a mere illustration:
"Alas! Even though she is standing right next to me, she seems to look at me; even having seen me..."
He reveals the base of his arm, marked by fresh nail-scratches.
Likewise—by means of sending letters, affectionate glances, and gentle words; // VisSd_3.127 //
The manifestation of a woman’s inner disposition is sought through the dispatching of female messengers.
And these messengers are:
a female friend, an actress, a maidservant, a nurse’s daughter, and a neighbor. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.128)

"Women who have gone forth as artisans, craftsmen, and so forth, or likewise those who are themselves [such]; 'artisan' refers to washerwomen and the like; 'craftswoman' refers to women such as painters."
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [are included] betel-sellers, perfumers, women, and others. Among these, an example of a female friend (sakhī) is as follows:
"She releases sighs," and so on.
An example of the self-messenger (*svayaṃdūtī*) is as follows in my [work]: “O traveler, you appear thirsty; as you go, why not turn elsewhere?
There is not even a slight obstacle here for those who drink the essence of the clouds.”
And these women also serve as female messengers for heroes regarding heroines.
He states the qualities of a messenger:
"Skill in the arts, enthusiasm, devotion, knowledge of the mind, and memory. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.129)
Sweetness, knowledge of humor, and eloquence are their qualities;
these too are classified as superior, inferior, or middling according to their appropriateness.
These are the female messengers (dūtīs).
Now, regarding the antagonist (pratināyaka):
the antagonist is one who is haughty and resolute, a doer of evil, and addicted to vices.
Just as Rāvaṇa was to Rāma; now, as for the excitant determinants (uddīpana-vibhāvas): "The excitant determinants are those which intensify the rasa. (Viśvavidyā 3.131)
And those [factors]— the movements and so forth of the object, as well as place, time, and so on;
by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "movements and so forth," forms, speech, and the like are intended.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "time and so forth," [are meant] the rising of the moon, sandalwood, the warbling of the cuckoo, the humming of bees, and so on.
Among these, the rising of the moon is as in my own verse: "Placing his hand—[which has cast off the garment of the mass of darkness]—upon the breast-peak of the mountain of sunrise..."
"The moon kisses the face of the eastern quarter, whose eyes are blossoming night-lotuses."
That which is the excitant (*uddīpanavibhāva*) for a particular rasa will be described in the description of that rasa's own nature.
Now, as for the ensuants (*anubhāvas*):
"Manifesting outwardly the emotion awakened by its own causes... (VisSd 3.132).

In the world, that which is of the nature of an effect (*kārya*) is called an *anubhāva* in poetry and drama. Indeed, in the world, that which—by means of its respective objective (*ālambana*) and excitant (*uddīpana*) causes, such as Sītā or the moon—manifests externally the love and other emotions awakened within Rāma and others, is called an "effect"; however, in poetry and drama, that same thing is termed an *anubhāva*.
To the question "What, then, is this? he says:
"The ornaments of women have been described, as well as those born of the body and those born of their own nature. (VisSd 3.133)
Sāttvika states and other such gestures are of that same nature;
they are of the nature of *anubhāvas*.
In this regard, whichever [state] is the *anubhāva* of a particular rasa will be described in the description of its specific nature.
Among those,
the *sāttvika* transformations— those arising from *sattva*— are proclaimed to be *sāttvika*.
*Sattva* is a certain internal quality that causes illumination and repose within one's own self.

Although they are distinct from the perspective of their experiential manifestations, because they arise solely from *sattva*, [the distinction is made] "by way of the maxim of the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāyena*). This is the implied sense.
What are these? He says:
paralysis, perspiration, then horripilation, breaking of the voice, and trembling. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.135)
Change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions].
Among them:
paralysis (*stambha*) is the obstruction of movement caused by fear, joy, disease, and so forth.
Perspiration is the outflow of water from the body caused by sexual intercourse, the heat of passion, fatigue, and so forth;
horripilation is the transformation of the body hair caused by joy, wonder, fear, and the like. (VisSd 3.137)
They know *vaisvarya* to be a hoarse or faltering voice caused by intoxication, exhilaration, affliction, and the like;
*vepathu* is the trembling of the limbs resulting from passion, hatred, hunger, and so forth.
Change of complexion due to dejection, intoxication, anger, and so forth is discoloration (*vivarṇatā*).
Tears (*aśru*) are the liquid that flows from the eyes, produced by anger, sorrow, or intense joy. (ViṣSd 3.139)

Dissolution (pralaya) consists in the cessation of movement and cognition due to pleasure and pain. As it is said by me: "Alas! From the touch of her body, her eyes have slightly closed like buds; horripilation rises, and her entire frame falls into a state of numbness."
Surely his cheeks are moist with perspiration; his mind, having certainly ceased from all sensory objects, touches the supreme Brahman, which is intense bliss, instantaneously.
The same applies to the others.
Now, as for the transitory (vyabhicārin) [emotions]: they are called transitory because they move (caraṇāt) toward a particular [permanent emotion] with intensity (abhimukhyena).
In the stable [state], there are thirty-three varieties consisting of those that are emergent and submerged.

For when love and other [permanent moods] persist with stability, those such as despondency (nirveda) are called transitory states (vyabhicārin) because they move toward them by appearing and disappearing.
What are they? He says:
despondency, agitation, dejection, fatigue, stupor born of intoxication, ferocity, delusion, awakening, sleep, epilepsy, pride, death, lassitude, indignation, drowsiness, and dissimulation.

Longing, madness, and apprehension; memory and intelligence; disease, terror, and shame; joy, envy, and despondency; along with the fickleness of a companion, exhaustion, anxiety, and discursive thought.
In that context, *nirveda* (disgust/disillusionment) is as follows:
"Disgust arises from the knowledge of reality, from calamity, from envy, and so forth;
it consists of self-contempt and produces wretchedness, anxiety, tears, sighing, paleness, heaving of the breath, and the like. (Viṣṇu-saṃhitā 3.142)
Disgust arising from the knowledge of reality is as follows:
"Alas! This right-spiraling conch shell has been reduced by one who desired to fashion a stopper for a hole in a jar of clay, using sand!"
"I have reduced it to powder."
Now, agitation (āvega): agitation is a state of flurry; therein, that born of rain consists of the contraction of the limbs, while that born of portents consists of the trembling of the limbs.
Confusion caused by smoke and so forth arises from fire.
From the agitation caused by kings and the like, there arises the appearance of weapons, serpents, and so forth;
from wind filled with dust and the like, there arises the paralysis or trembling of elephants and other such beings. (VisSd 3.144)
From the desirable [objects] arise joys, and from the undesirable, sorrows; others should be understood accordingly as the case may be.
Among these, that which arises from an enemy is as follows:

Disregarding the king who was crying out, "The water of honor! The water of honor!", the elder brother of Bharata fixed upon him a gaze with its pupils wide open, like a flame from the fire of his wrath against the kshatriyas.
In this manner, other [emotions] are to be inferred.
Now, dejection (*dainya*):
Dejection is a lack of splendor caused by poverty and the like; it produces impurity and so forth. (VisSd 3.145)
For example:
"This husband of mine is old and blind, lying upon a couch; the house has nothing left but its pillars."
"The time for the arrival of the rains has come near, yet there is no news of my child's well-being;
the oil-flask, so carefully filled with drops of oil, is broken"—seeing her daughter-in-law thus distressed and languid from the weight of her pregnancy, the mother-in-law weeps for a long time.
Now, fatigue (*śrama*): fatigue is the exhaustion resulting from sexual passion, travel, and so forth, which causes labored breathing, sleep, and the like.
For example:

“Though she was as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, Sītā, having walked only three or four steps with haste even within the vicinity of the city, repeatedly asked, ‘How much further must we go? and thus brought about the first descent of Rāma’s tears.”
Now, intoxication (mada): intoxication is a mixture of delusion and bliss, born from the consumption of liquor. (VisSd 3.146)
By this [wind], the best person lies down; the middling one laughs and sings; and even the base-natured one speaks harshly and weeps. (VisSd 3.147)
For example:

"Amidst the threefold intoxication, there ensued the playful jesting of the fair-browed women— a jewel-like composition of enigmatic speech, accompanied by laughter and the disclosure of hidden secrets."

Now, regarding insensibility (*jaḍatā*): Insensibility is the lack of comprehension resulting from seeing or hearing what is desired or undesired; in that state, there are such signs as the unblinking gaze of the eyes and remaining silent. (VisSd 3.148)

As it says in my Prakrit poem, *Kuvalayāśvacarita*: "Only that pair of youths remained there for a mere moment near the funeral pyre, their eyes fixed upon one another, heavy with tears, as if they were painted in a picture."
Now, regarding ferocity (*ugratā*): Ferocity is a state of violence arising from [the perception of] an offense against one's valor and so forth.
In that state, there are perspiration, shaking of the head, threatening gestures, striking, and the like. (VisSd 3.149)
For example:

"This arm of mine, which grows weary even at being struck by playful blows from lovely *śirīṣa* flowers— blows obtained through the sweet humor of affectionate friends— shall fall upon the head of anyone who raises a weapon against your body to kill you, like the sudden staff of Yama’s rod."
Now, delusion (*moha*):
Delusion is a state of mental confusion caused by fear, the onset of suffering, and brooding; it produces fainting, ignorance, falling, whirling, blindness, and so forth. (VisSd 3.150)
For example:
"When her senses were paralyzed by a delusion arising from an intense shock, Rati—for a moment—seemed as if she had received a favor, since she remained unaware of her husband’s calamity."
Now, awakening: Awakening is the arrival of consciousness resulting from causes for the departure of sleep;
it produces yawning, stretching of the limbs, closing of the eyes, and looking about with the body. (VisSd 3.151)
For example:

"Young women, having attained the bliss of sleep from the exhaustion of long lovemaking, wake first even though they slept last; yet, with their limbs still unmoving, they do not break the firm embrace of their lovers' circling arms."
Now, as for dream:
a dream is the experience of objects by one who has fallen into sleep, which brings about anger, agitation, fear, exhaustion, pleasure, pain, and so forth. (VisSd 3.152)
For example:
"When you were somehow obtained by me through a vision in a dream, as I held my arms outstretched toward the sky for the sake of a merciless embrace,
surely many teardrops, as large as pearls, did not fall upon the sprouts of the trees from the local deities who were watching?"
Now, regarding epilepsy (apasmāra): Epilepsy is a derangement of the mind caused by possession by spirits and the like;
it brings about trembling of the body, perspiration, frothing at the mouth, salivation, and so forth. (VisSd 3.153)
“He suspected that lord of rivers to be epileptic— clinging to the ground, roaring loudly, with great waves in the form of tossing arms, and frothing at the mouth.”
Now, regarding pride (*garva*): Pride is intoxication arising from power, prosperity, learning, noble birth, and so forth;
it produces contempt, playful gestures, the display of one's limbs, lack of decorum, and the like. (VisSd 3.154)
In that regard, pride in heroism is as follows:
"As long as I am armed, what is the use of other weapons?
Or rather, what could possibly be accomplished by others with a weapon that has not been mastered by me?"
Now, regarding death:
death by means of weapons and the like is the relinquishing of life through acts such as prostrating one's limbs.
For example:
“Struck in her heart by Rāma’s unbearable arrow of love, that night-stalker,
anointed with fragrant blood-sandalwood, departed for the abode of the Lord of Life.”
Now, regarding indolence:
"Indolence is a state of dullness caused by fatigue, pregnancy, and so forth; it brings about yawning, smiling, and other such symptoms. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.155)
For example:
"The young woman, languid from the weight of her pregnancy, does not adorn her limbs in that way, nor does she speak to her friend in that way; she yawns again and again while sitting."
Now, indignation (amarṣa): Indignation toward censure, insult, humiliation, and the like is a state of intense fixation;
it manifests through redness of the eyes, shaking of the head, knitting of the brows, threatening gestures, and so forth. (VisSd 3.156)
As it is said: "I shall perform penance for my transgression against you, who are worthy of honor;
but I will never defile the great vow of wielding the sword."
Now, regarding sleep:
Sleep is the closing of the mind, born of fatigue, intoxication, and so forth;
it is the cause of yawning, the closing of the eyes, labored breathing, the stretching of the limbs, and other such effects. (VisSd 3.157)
As it is said:
"She, speaking words both meaningful and meaningless with slow syllables,
her eyes half-closed in sleep— she remains, as if painted, within my heart."
Now, regarding *avahitthā* (concealment): *Avahitthā* is the concealment of outward signs such as joy and the like, caused by fear, respect, shame, and so forth;
it manifests through engagement in other activities, speaking otherwise than one feels, looking away, and the like. (VisSd 3.158)
For example:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing by her father's side with her face cast down, began counting the petals of her play-lotus."
Now, longing (autsukya): Longing is the inability to endure the passage of time due to the non-attainment of a desired object;
it causes mental distress, haste, perspiration, long sighs, and so forth. (VisSd 3.159)
For example,
regarding the verse beginning with "He alone is the bridegroom who took away my maidenhood" (p.

15), that which was stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* concerning the primacy of rasa (*rasa-prādhānya*) should be understood as already implied by the fact that even a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), by virtue of its connection to the nature of aesthetic relish (*rasana*), is denotable by the term *rasa*.
Now, insanity (*unmāda*):
Insanity is a delusion of the mind caused by desire, grief, fear, and so forth; it consists of laughing, weeping, singing, and prattling at inappropriate times. (VisSd 3.160)
As it is said by me:
"O brother bee!
While wandering all around, have you seen my beloved, who is dearer to me than life?"
(Having experienced the sound *bhaktaṃkāra*, with joy:
"I say, my friend, what is this *om*?
Tell me quickly: what does it intend, from where does it come, and of what nature is it?"
Now, regarding doubt (śaṅkā):
Doubt is the conjecture of misfortune arising from the cruelty of others, one's own faults, and so forth;
it causes changes in complexion, trembling, loss of voice, looking to the side, and dryness of the mouth. (Viṣṇusiddhānta 3.161)
As it says in my own work:
“At the end of the night, her limbs tormented by nails pressed down by her lover’s breath, this slender-limbed woman applies sandalwood paste for a long time;
she repeatedly applies lac-dye to her lower lip where tooth-marks have been inflicted, casting her eyes anxiously all around.”
Now, regarding memory (smṛti):

"Memory is said to be the cognition whose object is a thing previously experienced, produced by similar cognitions, reflection, and so forth, and characterized by the raising of the eyebrows and other such signs. (VisSd 3.162)
As it says in my own work: “When her eyes were cast somewhere with feigned artifice, and she had turned away slightly with pupils rolling askance;
when she saw her friend approaching and looked down bashfully—then I remember that smiling face of the lotus-eyed one, grinning again and again.”
Now, as for *mati*: the determination of meaning through following the path of ethics and so forth is *mati*.
A smiling countenance, fortitude, contentment, and great respect arise from it. (VisSd 3.163)
For example:
"Without doubt, my mind desires her, for she is capable of accepting a husband;
for the inclinations of the inner sense are the authority of the virtuous regarding matters that are subjects of doubt."
Now, regarding disease:
disease consists of fever and the like, caused by the humors such as wind (vāta) and so forth, which produce trembling of the earth and other symptoms.
In that context, when it is characterized by a state of burning, there is the desire for the earth and so on.
In the case of being composed of coldness, trembling and so forth [occur];
this is a clear illustration.
Now, as for fear—
Terror caused by thunderclaps, lightning, meteors, and the like, which produces trembling and other such effects.
For example:
"With their thighs struck by darting fish, their gazes unsteady with alarm,
and their sprout-like hands trembling, the celestial nymphs became an object of sight even for their own female companions."
Now, regarding *vrīḍā* (shame): shame is the absence of audacity (*dhārṣṭya*), caused by misconduct, which brings about such things as the lowering of the face.
For example:
“‘With deceit toward me’—and so forth” (p. 173).
Now, joy (*harṣa*): Joy is the clarity of mind resulting from the attainment of what is desired, which causes tears, a faltering voice, and so on. (Viṣṇu-siddhānta 3.165)
For example:
"Just as a poor man, after a long time, beholding the face of his son as if it were a jar of buried treasure,
was unable to contain his joy within his own body, so too was the ocean unable to contain itself when surging at the rising of the moon."
Now, envy (asūyā): Envy is the intolerance of another's excellence in virtue due to arrogance;
it manifests through the proclamation of faults, the knitting of eyebrows, contempt, anger, and gestures. (VisSd 3.166)
For example:
"Then, the Lord of Cedi could not endure the honor bestowed upon the enemy of Madhu (Kṛṣṇa) by the son of Pāṇḍu in that assembly; for the minds of the proud are envious of the prosperity of others."
Now, dejection (*viṣāda*):

Dejection arises from the absence of means; it is a depletion of the vital essence (*sattva*), and it brings about sighing, gasping, mental anguish, and the searching for allies, and so forth. (VisSd 3.167)
As it was said by me: "This braid of yours, bound with this mass of curly hair, O friend, when it falls upon my breast, it crushes my heart like a black cobra that has been provoked."

Now, regarding fortitude (dhṛti): Fortitude is the state of having one's desires completely fulfilled through the attainment of knowledge, desired objects, and so forth; it is characterized by expressions of contentment, joy, laughter, eloquence, and the like. (VisSd 3.168)
As it is said by me:
"Having oppressed the wretched among my own kin, having engaged in verbal strife, and without considering even the most grievous torments of the hereafter for a long time,
I have indeed accumulated heaps of wealth for whose sake this very body— alas!— is now fulfilled merely by a handful of wild rice."
Now, regarding fickleness (*cāpalatā*):
Fickleness is instability arising from envy, hatred, passion, and so forth;
in that state, there are such things as reviling, harshness, and acting according to one's own whims. (VisSd 3.169)
For example:
"O bee, for now, divert your restless mind toward other flowering creepers that can endure being crushed."
"Why do you pointlessly torment this innocent jasmine bud, which has not yet reached its season, out of time?"
Now, regarding exhaustion (*glāni*):

arising from sexual passion, physical fatigue, mental distress, hunger, thirst, and so forth, exhaustion produces a state of being breathless, emaciation, lack of enthusiasm, and the like. (VisSd 3.170)
For example:

"Like a tender sprout severed from its bond, her body— pale and emaciated— is withered by a harsh and long-lasting grief that dries up the flower of her heart, just as the autumnal heat withers the inner petal of a *ketakī* flower."
Then there is reflection (cintā)—meditation (dhyāna). Reflection is the failure to attain what is beneficial; it causes distress and a sense of emptiness.
As it has been said of me:
“O fair-faced one, with your face resting in your palms, what are you thinking within yourself, as you join the blooming lotus with the moon’s orb, though they are natural adversaries?”
Now, as for reasoning (tarka): reasoning is investigation; it is the dancer of the eyebrows, the head, and the fingers arising from doubt.
For example:
"Is he detained by his beloved? and so forth.
Regarding the statement that these are the thirty-three varieties of transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), he says that this is merely an illustration:
Even *rati* (love) and the other emotions may become transitory (*vyabhicārin*) when they occur within an indefinite rasa.

For instance, in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa, it is *rati* alone that is designated by the term "permanent" (*sthāyin*) because it persists without being interrupted; whereas *hasa* (laughter), arising again and again, is merely transitory, as it lacks the defining characteristics of a permanent emotion.
As it has been said:
"The supreme emotion (bhāva), existing as rasa, attains the state of being the permanent mood (sthāyin)."
To the question, "For which stable emotion (*sthāyin*) and in which rasa does [which transitory emotion] function as a transitory state (*sañcārin*)," he says:
"Laughter is considered to belong to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the heroic (*vīra*), and likewise anger is held to belong to the heroic. (ViśSd 3.172)
"Disgust is said to be a transitory state even in the context of the peaceful [rasa];
thus other [transitory states] should likewise be inferred by those whose intellects have been cultivated. (VisSd 3.173)

Now, regarding the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*): That emotion which, whether consistent or inconsistent [with other emotions], is incapable of being suppressed by them, and which is the bulbous root for the sprout of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), is recognized as the "permanent" (*sthāyin*). (VisSd 3.174)
As it has been said:
"Like a thread running through a string of beads, the permanent emotion (sthāyī) follows after other emotions; it is not concealed by them, but rather is nourished by them to the highest degree."
Thus [it was said].
He states their subdivisions:
"Love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, and likewise fear,"
In this way, disgust, wonder, and tranquility are also said to be eight. (VisSd 3.175)
In this context:

*Rati* (love) is the inclination of the mind toward an object that is agreeable to it; *hāsa* (laughter) is intended as the expansion of the heart through transformations of speech and other faculties. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.176)

The mental despondency resulting from the loss of what is desired and so forth is designated by the term "sorrow" (śoka). The perception of harshness toward disagreeable objects is held to be "anger" (krodha).
The firm enthusiasm at the commencement of tasks is called *utsāha* (perseverance). Distraction of the mind produced by the power of *raudra* (the fierce sentiment) is *bhaya* (fear). *VisSd* 3.178.
Censure arises from the observation of faults and so forth; loathing arises from wonder regarding various objects that transcend the boundaries of worldly experience. (VisSd 3.179)
That expansion of the mind which occurs is declared to be wonder (*vismaya*);
tranquility (*śama*) is the bliss born of resting in one's own self within a state free from effort.
As, for example, love (*rati*) in the *Mālatīmādhava*,
laughter (*hāsa*) in the *Laṭakamelaka*,
and sorrow (*śoka*) in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
In the *Mahābhārata*, there is tranquility (*śama*);
likewise in other places as well.

For these [emotions] are not interrupted by the various states—both contradictory and non-contradictory—that arise within them; on the contrary, they are fully nourished, as established by the experience of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
Furthermore:
Since they bring forth aesthetic flavors (rasas) through their connection with various modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya),
these are therefore called "emotions" (bhāvas)— namely, the permanent (sthāyin), the transitory (saṃcārin), and the involuntary (sāttvika).
As it has been said:
"The state [of the self] through states such as pleasure and pain is the cultivation of that state. Now, he states the divisions of *rasa*:
"The erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the comic (*hāsya*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the furious (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*)."
The loathsome, the marvelous—thus eight flavors are recognized, as well as the peaceful.

Among these, the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*): "For *śṛṅga* is the arousal of love; that which has its cause in the arrival of this [arousal] is the erotic sentiment (*rasa*), which is primarily characterized by persons of superior nature. (VisSd 3.183)
Excluding one who has already been married and a courtesan who lacks affection,
the heroines shall be the supporting characters, as shall the heroes such as the *dakṣiṇa* and others.
The moon, sandalwood, the *narolamba* bird, and the like are considered the excitants (*uddīpana*);
the movement of the eyebrows, side-long glances, and so forth are proclaimed to be the ensuants (*anubhāva*). (VisSd 3.185)
Having abandoned ferocity, death, indolence, disgust, and infidelity, its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is love; it is dark-complexioned and has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
For example:
“An empty dwelling,” and so forth.
Here, the hero whose nature has been described and the young woman whose nature has been described are the objective determinants (ālambana-vibhāva).
The empty bedchamber is the excitant (uddīpana-vibhāva);
the kiss is the ensuant (anubhāva);
and shame and laughter are the transitory states (vyabhicārin).

The aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) of love (*śṛṅgāra*), when manifested by these [factors] and experienced by those with refined sensibilities (*sahṛdaya*), assumes the form of the erotic sentiment. He states its divisions:
"It is considered to be of two kinds: the love-in-separation (*vipralambha*) and the love-in-enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*). (VisSd 3.186)
In this context:
"But where there is intense passion, yet the desired object is not attained, that is *vipralambha* (love-in-separation);
[the desired object being] either the hero or the heroine."
And that [love] is fourfold, consisting of longing, pride, separation, and sorrow. (VisSd 3.187)
In that regard—
when two people have developed mutual passion through either hearing of or seeing one another,
that particular state which exists before their union is called *pūrvarāga* (preliminary passion). (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.188)

In that regard, hearing [the mantra] may occur through the mouths of messengers, captive women, or female friends; while seeing it occurs in a magical illusion, in a painting, or directly in a dream. (VisSd 3.189)
Longing, reflection, remembrance, recounting of qualities, agitation, lamentation,
madness, disease, stupor, and death— these are the ten stages of love in this world.
Longing is desire; anxiety is the thinking about means for attainment and so forth;
and madness is the lack of discernment even regarding what is sentient and what is insentient. (VisSd 3.191)
Due to the intense wandering of the mind, there may be incoherent speech;
as for the disease, it consists of long sighing, paleness, emaciation, and so forth.
Inertness is the lack of movement in the limbs as well as in the mind;
the rest is clear.
The examples follow in order:
“May those various gestures of the lovely-eyed one—moist with love, touching with affection, arising from familiarity and the dawning of intense passion, and naturally sweet—be directed toward me;
for even when merely imagined through longing, they bring about in an instant a dense absorption of bliss that obstructs the functioning of the external senses within the inner heart.”
Herein lies the longing of Mādhava, whose passion has taken root from the direct sight of Mālatī:
“How may I behold the fawn-eyed one, the very personification of the God of Love’s fortune?
Thus, overwhelmed by anxious thought, my beloved does not find sleep throughout the night.”
Here, there is the reflection of a hero whose passion has grown intense from witnessing a magical illusion (indrajāla) regarding a certain heroine.
"This is mine"—
in such passages as "toward me with feignedness," there is the recollection of the hero.
In passages such as "eyes that outshine the *khañjana* bird," there is the description of qualities (*guṇa*). In "she releases sighs," there is agitation (*udvega*).
And: "When three parts of the night remained, she closed her eyes and suddenly woke up."
"O Blue-throated One, where are you going?"— thus she spoke with an unperceived voice, her arms entwined around his neck in a false embrace.
In this context, there is *pralāpa* (incoherent speech);
for instance, in the verse beginning with "O brother, O *dvirepha*," there is *unmāda* (madness). [And as in:
"Your face is pale and wasted, your heart is full of passion, and your body is languid..."
"O friend, it announces a deeply seated disease within the heart."
In this case, there is illness:
"Her entire body is placed upon a terrifyingly hard bed and is completely motionless;
only this long-drawn breath tells [us] that she is merely living."
In this context, there is insentience;
"this is mine.
Death is never described [as a poetic theme] because it causes the interruption of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
If that which is almost born, which is to be expressed, and which is thus desired by the mind,
were even described, it would be like reviving [the dead] before one's very eyes.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Having seen the *śephālikā* flower in full bloom, the slender maiden was somehow able to sustain her life;
but now, having heard the cry of the cockerels, what will become of that poor girl? I do not know."
The second example is as follows:
"Let the bees fill the quarters with the clamor of their humming;
let the breeze born from the sandalwood groves also approach very gently."
"Let the playful cuckoos on the tips of the mango trees sing their fifth note in intoxication; let these vital breaths, as hard as stone, depart—depart quickly!"
These two belong to me.
As for the third, it is as found in the account of Mahāśvetā and Puṇḍarīka in the *Kādambarī*.
We shall explain later that this variety pertains to the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) within the scope of the love-in-separation (*vipralambha*).
But some [say]:
"First is the delight of the eyes, then the attachment of the mind, then the mental resolve;
the breaking of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, and the loss of shame."
"It is said that there are exactly ten stages of love: longing, thought, recollection, dreaming, loss of shame, intoxication, fainting, and death.
And therein—first, the passion of the woman is to be expressed, and subsequently that of the man through her gestures.
The gestures have been described,
as in the *Ratnāvalī* regarding Sāgarikā and King Vatsarāja;
even when a man's passion occurs at first, it becomes thus more deeply moving to the heart.
Indigo, safflower, and madder; and the "first passion" is also threefold.
In that regard:
"That love which does not depart from the mind, yet does not shine excessively, is called the indigo-dye attachment (*nīlī-rāga*), as in the case of Śrī Rāma and Sītā. (Viṣṇu-saṃhitā 3.196)
They call that the safflower-dye which fades yet remains beautiful;
they call that the madder-dye which does not fade and shines exceedingly.
Now, regarding pride (*māna*): Pride is anger, and it is of two kinds, arising from affection or from jealousy.
Pride of affection occurs between two people even when there is great joy. (VisSd 3.198)
Because love follows a crooked course, there is anger without cause;
this [anger] belongs to both—the hero and the heroine—and thus the mutual affection of both should be described.
An example:
In that regard, as for the hero, it is said:
“O handsome one, with your limbs bristling from the touch of my cheek, you who are half-asleep with eyes closed, grant me an opening.”
"I shall not delay any longer."
As in the case of the heroine, for example, in the *Kumārasambhava* during the description of the twilight;
as in the case of both [the hero and the heroine], for example:
"Of the two, who are angry with each other, who have cast aside their garments, and who are full of pride..."
Who is the wrestler against those who have bestowed their command by means of steady, restrained, and silent breaths?
However, if it cannot endure the culmination of affection (*anunaya*), it does not constitute a variety of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation),
but rather possesses the status of a transitory emotion (*sañcārī-bhāva*) known as *sambhoga* (enjoyment).
For example—
“Even when a frown is fashioned, her gaze looks up with even greater longing; even when her speech is restrained, this scorched face breaks into a smile.
Even when her heart is made to reach hardness, her body takes on a thrill of horripilation. When that person is seen, how can there be a conclusion to my pride?”
Or as it is said:

“On a single bed, turning their faces away from one another and suffering in silence, the husband and wife maintained their dignity even though the plea for reconciliation lay in each other’s hearts; yet, as their eyes gradually mingled through the power of sidelong glances, the quarrel of pride was broken, and they were suddenly locked in an embrace with laughter.”
When the union with another's beloved is seen, inferred, or heard; ||| VisSd_3.199 ||

Envy and pride may arise in women; in that regard, there are three types of inference based on the occurrence of snoring during sleep, marks of sexual enjoyment, and the slippage of one's family name.
Regarding that which is seen, for example:
"O beloved, as she removes the pollen from her eyes with the breath of her face,
the two eyes of her rival, who is unfriendly toward her, are repeatedly filled with the dust of anger."
An example of inference through the sign of enjoyment is as follows:
“You hide your body with its fresh nail-marks beneath your garment, and you cover your lip, bitten by teeth, with your hand;
yet how can this pervasive, foul odor, spreading in every direction and proclaiming your union with another woman, be concealed?”
In the same way,
the husband should employ other means as well— conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, flattery, and indifference— as alternative methods in sequence to break her [resistance]. (VisSd 3.201)
In that regard, conciliation consists of pleasant speech; sowing dissension is the winning over of their friends;
bribery is the giving of ornaments and such under the guise of a gift; and prostration is falling at their feet. (Viśuddhimagga 3.202)
But when the *sāma* (conciliation) and other [means] have been exhausted, there may be disregard through indifference;
or, from impetuosity, fear, joy, and so forth, there may be a lapse of anger into another aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (VisSd 3.203)
For example: "And no flattery was heard," and so forth (p. 129).
Here, the five [means], beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), are indicated.
The other flavors are to be inferred.
Now, regarding exile: exile consists of being in a different country, whether due to a task, a curse, or agitation.
In that state, there is dirtiness of the limbs and clothing, and the head bears a single braid of hair.
Sighing, gasping, weeping, falling to the ground, and so forth occur.
Furthermore:
there is a lack of physical grace in the limbs, fever, pallor, emaciation, and loss of appetite. (Viṣṇusamhitā 3.205)
Lack of fortitude, lack of support, delusion, intoxication, fainting, and death—these ten stages of love (smaradaśā) are to be known here in their proper order. (VisSd 3.206)

Lack of physical vigor, the occurrence of impurities, and fever are the heat of the fever of separation; lack of relish is detachment from objects, and lack of composure is a state of dissatisfaction toward everything.
Moreover, emptiness is said to be the mind's state of being without an object;
for that [mind] consists of that [emptiness], and its manifestation is likewise both externally and internally.
The rest is clear.
As in a single verse from my father’s works:
"The mind is motionless with anxieties; the surface of the cheek is pressed against the palm."
Her face is pale as the moment of dawn, her lower lip is withered by constant sighing;
the fever does not subside even with water-sprays or lotus leaves.
What is so difficult for her to obtain that she endures such a miserable state? Who is it she seeks?
It may be threefold—as future, present, or past; therein, that which arises from an effect [is the future].
Because an action is preceded by intention, it is threefold.
Among these, that which is about to happen is as in my [verse]:
"Let us go, O beautiful one..."
"O traveler,
O beloved, do not grieve in vain;
for what grief could I have at your departure, and why then do you shed tears?"
"Why is there this haste of yours to make me go when you yourself do not depart quickly?
My own agitation is even greater than yours, as I wish to go along with you."
As you have said:
"The departure was made by words;
it went continuously by means of weapons, dear friends."
Not for a moment did she remain steadfast;
her mind resolved to go ahead.
When the beloved had made up her mind to depart, O life-breath, all set out together when it was time to go.
Why indeed is this caravan of dear friends being abandoned?
As for the *bhūta* [sentiment], it is as follows:
"Stilled by anxieties," and so forth (page 200).
As for the *śāpa* [sentiment]: [it is as follows:]
"One should recognize that [as described] in the passage beginning with 'ityādi' (page 130):
agitation arising from celestial or human portents, thunderbolts, calamities, and so forth;
as, for example, in the *Vikramorvaśī* between Urvaśī and Purūravas."

In this context, although both sets—the ten states such as longing (*abhilāṣa*) and so forth mentioned under "love at first sight" (*pūrvarāga*), and the ten such as the beauty of the limbs (*aṅgasauṣṭhava*) and so forth mentioned here—are possible in both [types of love-in-separation], they are presented separately according to ancient convention.
Now, regarding "love-in-separation due to death" (*karuṇavipralambha*):
