when one of the two lovers has gone to the other world and is not to be recovered again...
When one person becomes despondent, then it is called the "deception through compassion."
For example, in the *Kādambarī*, within the narrative of Tuṇḍarīka and Mahāśvetā,
when [the goal] is unattainable, the sentiment (rasa) is indeed that called Karuṇa (Pathos), even though it is attainable through another body;
furthermore, in this case, the Śṛṅgāra (Eros) occurs immediately after the speech of the celestial Sarasvatī.
Because delight arises from the hope of union,
the learned authorities maintain that at the very beginning, there is only compassion.
Regarding this, some say that even after the expectation of union, it is merely a variety of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) called "prolonged absence" (*pravāsa*);
others, however, consider it to be distinct from that because of the occurrence of the specific element of death.
Now, as for *saṃbhoga* (union):
Where two lovers, mutually enamored, engage in looking, touching, and so forth, this is declared to be *saṃbhoga*.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), mutual drinking from the lower lip, kissing, and so forth are included, as in the verse beginning with "The bedchamber was empty... (p. 22).
Because it is impossible to enumerate due to its many varieties such as kissing, embracing, and so forth,
this alone is declared by the wise to be the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*).

Therein, there shall be the six seasons, the moon and the sun, as well as their rising and setting; [there shall be] water-sports, strolls in the forest, dawn, drinking honey-wine, the night, and so forth.
Ointments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as other things that are pure and fit for sacrifice, should be mentioned;
and thus Bharata says:
"Whatever in the world is pure, fit for sacrifice, radiant, or beautiful—all that is compared to (and employed in) the erotic sentiment."
Furthermore:
This [love] is said to be fourfold, according to its sequence starting from "prior passion" (pūrvarāga) and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.213)
As it has been said:
"Without separation, union does not attain fullness;
for when cloth and such are dyed with astringent, the color increases greatly."
Thus it is said.
Among these, enjoyment following prior passion is as in the *Kumārasambhava* in the case of Pārvatī and Parameśvara. Enjoyment following separation due to travel is as in my father’s [work]:
“Is all well with you, O long-lashed one? “How can there be great security for me?
For how could such emaciation belong to you, whose body was once so full?”
"By what means, O fair-browed one, have I become so broad?
"By the union with the body of a doe, from you, O lady of beautiful eyebrows."
"I am not a monkey; if this were a matter of safety, why would you ask?"
In this way, it should be inferred in other cases as well.
Now, laughter arises from a deceiver through distorted appearance, speech, dress, gestures, and so forth.
The comic [rasa] has laughter as its dominant emotion; it is white in color and has the Moon as its presiding deity.

When people laugh upon seeing someone whose form, speech, and gestures are distorted, they say that person is the objective support (ālambana) here; that [distortion] is considered the excitant (uddīpana). VisSd 3.215.
The external manifestations (anubhāvas) are the contraction of the eyes, a smile on the face, and so forth;
while sleepiness, lassitude, dissimulation, and the like would be the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) in this context.
For the superior there is the smile and the laugh; for the middling, the derisive laugh and the mocking laugh;
and for the inferior, the loud laughter and the excessive laughter—thus this [laughter] has six varieties.
A smile is characterized by slightly opening eyes and the quivering of the lips; when the teeth are slightly visible therein, it is called "laughter" by the wise. (VisSd 3.218)
A smile is characterized by a sweet voice; a laugh involves a shaking of the shoulders and head;
a derisive laugh has tearful eyes; and a loud laugh is accompanied by the tossing of the limbs. (VisSd 3.219)
For example:
"Having studied the words of the Guru for five days and the Vedānta scriptures for three days, and having inhaled the arguments of logic, here have arrived the venerable Kukkuṭamiśra."
The full development of this [comic sentiment] is to be seen in works such as the *Laṭakamelaka*.
And in this regard:
"If the laughter of someone is not directly portrayed anywhere at all..."
In the same way, this [emptiness] is perceived through the power of the [three] aspects, such as the object of negation (vibhāva) and so forth.
Because it is perceived without distinction due to the commonality of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors,
this comic sentiment (*hāsyarasa*) is experienced by the members of the audience.

In this same way, it should be understood regarding the other rasas as well. Now, concerning the pathetic (karuṇa): from the loss of what is desired and the attainment of what is undesired, the rasa called the pathetic arises.
This pigeon-colored [stone] is declared by the wise to have Yama as its presiding deity.

In this [sentiment], sorrow is the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva); that which is to be mourned is considered the objective basis (ālambana); furthermore, its states such as burning with grief constitute the excitant (uddīpana).

The manifestations [of the afflictions] include reviling fate, weeping at the king’s transgressions, and so forth, as well as changes in complexion, gasping for breath, holding the breath, and incoherent prattling. (VisSd 3.224)
Despair, delusion, epilepsy, intoxication, languor, forgetfulness, fatigue, despondency, numbness, madness, anxiety, and so forth are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). (VisSd 3.225)
That which is pitiable consists of the loss of kinsmen and the like;
as in my *Rāghavavilāsa*:
"Where is this binding of matted locks in the forest, and where is this charming body of yours?"
The union of these two is clearly like cutting a *śirīṣa* flower with a sword—indeed, it is so by the decree of fate.
For here, there is the lamentation against fate by Daśaratha, who is afflicted by the grief born of Rāma’s exile to the forest;
in the same way, examples may be cited for the loss of kinsmen, the destruction of wealth, and so forth.
Its full development, however, is to be seen in the Strīparvan of the Mahābhārata.
He states the distinction [of this rasa] from *vipralambha* (separation) due to its nature as sorrow:
"This rasa is distinct from *vipralambha* because its dominant emotion (*sthāyin*) is sorrow;
in *vipralambha*, however, the dominant emotion is love (*rati*), which is caused by union (*saṃbhoga*). (VisSd 3.226)
Now, the Furious [sentiment]: The Furious has anger as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*); it is red, and Rudra is its presiding deity (*adhidaivata*).
In this case, the enemy is considered the objective basis (*ālambana*), and his actions are considered the excitant (*uddīpana*). (VisSd 3.227)
Through the striking with fists, throwing down, mutilating, cutting, and tearing apart,
as well as through the tumult of battle and the like, its intense radiance becomes fully developed.
Frowning, pointing with the lips, slapping the arms, threatening gestures, recounting one's own heroic deeds, and brandishing weapons.
The manifestations (anubhāvas) are likewise the casting of glances, cruel looks, and so forth;
as well as ferocity, agitation, horripilation, perspiration, trembling, and intoxication.
In that [state], delusion, indignation, and other such emotions may function as transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
For example:
"By you, who are like beasts among men, devoid of all restraint and with weapons raised, this heinous crime has been committed, approved, or witnessed."
"Together with Naraka’s enemy, Bhīma, and Kirīṭin, I shall now offer this oblation of blood, fat, and flesh to the quarters."
He states the distinction of this [hero] from the warrior-hero (yuddhavīra):
"In this case, having red faces and eyes is what distinguishes it from the warrior-hero. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.231)
Now, the Heroic [sentiment]: the Heroic is of the highest nature (*uttamaprakṛti*), having energy (*utsāha*) as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*);
its presiding deity is Mahendra, and it is declared to be golden in color. (Viśvavidyā 3.232)
The objects of focus (ālambana) are considered to be those who are to be conquered and so forth;
the excitants (uddīpana) of that [state] consist of their gestures and the like;
and the consequents (anubhāva) therein would be the seeking of allies and so forth. (VisSd 3.233)
The transitory [emotions], however, are fortitude, intelligence, pride, memory, reasoning, and horripilation.
And that [heroism] is fourfold, being endowed with generosity, righteousness, battle, and compassion. (VisSd 3.234)
And that hero is of four kinds: the hero of generosity (*dānavīra*), the hero of righteousness (*dharmavīra*), the hero of battle (*yuddhavīra*), and the hero of compassion (*dayāvīra*).
Among these, the hero of generosity is exemplified by Paraśurāma: "His renunciation culminated in the unfeigned gift of the earth sealed by the seven oceans."
In this [passage], the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is the enthusiasm for renunciation on the part of Paraśurāma;
it is manifested by the *ālambana-vibhāvas*, namely the Brahmins who are the recipients of the gift, and by the *uddīpana-vibhāvas*, such as his resolve rooted in goodness (*sattva*);
and it is further made manifest through the *anubhāvas*, such as the renunciation of all his possessions.
When nourished by transitory emotions such as joy and fortitude, it attains the state of the heroic sentiment of generosity (*dānavīra*).
An example of the heroic sentiment of righteousness (*dharmavīra*) is Yudhiṣṭhira:
"The kingdom, wealth, my body, my wife, and my brothers and sons—"
And whatever in the world is under my control, that is ever dedicated to the Dharma.”
The hero of war is exemplified by Śrī Rāmacandra:
"O Lord of Laṅkā!
Let Janakajā be given; Rāma himself begs for her. What is this delusion of your mind? Remember the law of conduct; has not enough already been endured?"
If it were not so, this bird, made crimson by the binding of my bowstring and stained with the blood from the throats of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras, would not have survived.
As for the hero of compassion, Jīmūtavāhana:
"Blood still flows from the openings of my veins, and there is yet flesh remaining in my body;
I do not see that you have reached satiety even now—why then, O Garuḍa, have you desisted from devouring me?"
In these [rasas] as well, the determinants (vibhāvas) and so forth are to be inferred as in the previous examples.
Now, the *bhayānaka* (the terrible):
"The *bhayānaka* has fear as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), and its presiding deity is Bhūta."
Kṛṣṇa is considered by those expert in the principles to be of a feminine and inferior nature.
That from which fear arises is considered here to be the objective support (*ālambana*);
furthermore, his most terrible activity constitutes the excitant (*uddīpana*).

In this context, the external manifestation (*anubhāva*) consists of changes in complexion, speaking with a choked voice, fainting, perspiration, horripilation, trembling, looking toward the directions, and so forth. (Viṣṇu-sādhanā 3.237)
Disgust, agitation, delusion, terror, exhaustion, dejection, apprehension, epilepsy, confusion, death, and so forth are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). (Viśuddhimārga 3.238)
For example:
"The eunuchs [saw] that which was destroyed... and so forth (page 105).
Now, the loathsome (bībhatsa):
The aesthetic flavor (rasa) based on the stable emotion of disgust is called the loathsome (bībhatsa);
it is declared to be blue in color and to have Mahākāla as its presiding deity.
The foul-smelling flesh, blood, and fat are considered the objective support (ālambana);
therein, the falling of worms and so forth is declared to be the excitant (uddīpana).

Spitting, distorting the mouth, and the contraction of the eyes and so forth are considered the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*) therein; likewise, there may be transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*).
Fainting, epilepsy, agitation, disease, death, and so forth [are examples].
As it is said:

“Having first cut off and repeatedly hacked away the skin, and then having devoured the flesh—abundant with massive swellings, easily obtained from parts such as the shoulders, buttocks, and the mass of the back, and intensely putrid—”
With eyes rolling back and fangs bared, the wretched ghost greedily devours the raw flesh—be it from the lap of a corpse or even that which remains within the hollows of the bones.
Now, the marvelous:
the marvelous has wonder as its dominant emotion (sthāyibhāva) and the Gandharvas as its presiding deity.
The yellow-colored object is considered the support for the one who has transcended the world;
furthermore, the greatness of its qualities serves as the excitant.

Stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, faltering voice, agitation, as well as the dilation of the eyes and so forth, are proclaimed to be the secondary emotional manifestations (*anubhāvas*). (VisSd 3.244)
The transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) include agitation caused by the force of thought, confusion, joy, and so forth;
for example:
“[He] who was intent on breaking the staff-like bow of Candraśekhara, which had been bent by his staff-like arms...”
"How is it that this sound of 'ṣṭaṃ', the drum heralding the adventures of the noble Bāla,
whose fierce intensity swirls within the belly of the vessel of the universe as its two halves are suddenly cast together, does not even now come to rest?"
Now, regarding tranquility (śānta):
Tranquility is considered to be a state of being established in peace, characterized by the highest nature.

Having a luster as beautiful as a jasmine flower or the moon, with Śrī Nārāyaṇa as its presiding deity, it is that which consists of the worthlessness of all things through their impermanence and so forth. (VisSd 3.246)
Alternatively, the nature of the supreme self is held to be its object of focus;
so too are sacred hermitages, the holy fields of Hari, pilgrimage sites, and delightful forests.
Association with great beings and the like are its excitants (*uddīpana*);
horripilation and the like are the consequents (*anubhāva*); and likewise, there may be transitory states (*vyabhicārin*). (VisSd 3.248)
Disgust, joy, recollection, thought, fear, compassion,
and so forth— as for example:
"As he wandered through the middle of the street, clad in a worn-out ragged garment, he was looked upon by those city-dwellers with both terror and curiosity, and with compassion."
"When shall the fearless crow, without hesitation, plunder the alms-offering from my cupped hands as I sleep within the ocean of the nectar-essence of the unfeigned consciousness?"
The nourishment [of this rasa] is to be seen in the *Mahābhārata* and other such works. He states the distinction of this [rasa], such as the heroic sentiment of compassion (*dayāvīra*), from others:
"Because its nature is free from egoism, this [rasa], such as the heroic sentiment of compassion, is not [identical to] that [ordinary heroism]. (VisSd 3.249)

For in works such as the *Nāgānanda*, where Dayāśiva and others are the heroes, we observe that while there is the attainment of sovereignty over the Vidyādharas at the conclusion—following the passion for Malayavatī and other events in the interval of Jīmūtavāhana and his companions—the subsiding of egoism (*ahaṅkāropaśama*) is not seen;
however, the Quietistic Sentiment (*śānta-rasa*), because its sole nature consists in the complete pacification of egoism in every respect, does not deserve to be included therein.
Consequently, the claim that the *Nāgānanda* and similar works have the Quietistic Sentiment as their primary aesthetic flavor is refuted.
Now, it is said: "That state wherein there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither anxiety, nor hatred and passion, nor any desire whatsoever—
that is declared by the lords of sages to be the 'Peaceful' (śānta) aesthetic flavor (rasa), which maintains an equal measure toward all objects."

It may be asked: since such a state of tranquility, characterized by the attainment of the true nature of the self, manifests only in the state of liberation (mokṣa), and since the transitory emotions (*sañcārībhāva*) and so forth are absent there, how can it be called "rasa" (flavor)? It is said in reply:

because that very tranquility which exists in the states of both union and separation attains the status of *rasa*, therefore the presence of the transitory emotions and so forth within this [state] is not contradictory.
As for the absence of happiness mentioned in this context, there is no contradiction, because that refers specifically to sensual pleasure;

for it has been said: "Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the destruction of craving."
“If those such as the ‘heroic compassionate’ (dayāvīra) and others likewise attain a state of being permeated by egoity in every respect, then they too deserve to be included herein.”
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [are included] dharma-vīra, dāna-vīra, and those such as attachment (*rati*) directed toward deities.
Among these, attachment directed toward a deity is as follows:
"When shall I dwell here in Vārāṇasī on the bank of the celestial river, wearing a loincloth and placing my joined palms upon my head?"
O Lord of Gaurī!
O Destroyer of Tripura!
O Śambhu!
"O Three-eyed One!
Be gracious!"—crying thus, I shall pass my days as if they were but a single moment.
Then, the one esteemed by the lords of sages spoke of *vatsala*: "The wise know *vatsala* as a rasa clearly characterized by wonder;
its stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is the affection of parental fondness (*vatsalatā-sneha*), and its objective basis (*ālambana*) is considered to be one's son and so forth. (VisSd 3.251)
The excitants (uddīpanas) are his activities, such as skill, heroism, compassion, and so forth;
[the ensuants (anubhāvas) are] embracing, contact with the limbs, kissing the head, and gazing. (VisSd 3.252)
Thrills, joy, tears, and so forth are proclaimed as the consequent emotions (anubhāvas);
apprehension of the undesirable, joy, pride, and so forth are considered the transitory emotions (sañcārin).
The complexion of his skin is like the interior of a lotus, and the deities are the Mothers of the World.
As it is said:
"When he uttered the first words taught by his nurse, he took hold of her finger."
And that young boy became humble through his training in prostration, and thereby spread joy for his father.
And he states the mutual incompatibility of these sentiments (rasas): "The first [sentiment] is incompatible with the pathetic, the loathsome, the furious, the heroic, and the terrible."

The pathetic sentiment (karuṇa) is opposed by the terrible (bhayānaka), yet it is also opposed by the comic (hāsya). Similarly, the pathetic sentiment is also opposed by the comic and the erotic (śṛṅgāra) sentiments.
The Furious sentiment is [conjoined] with the Comic, Erotic, and Terrible sentiments;
likewise, the Heroic sentiment is said to be [conjoined] with the Terrible and the Peaceful.
The heroic rasa is [suppressed] by the erotic, furious, compassionate, comic, and peaceful rasas;
the peaceful rasa is [suppressed] by the heroic, erotic, furious, comic, and fearful rasas.
The opposition between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) has thus been explained;
the first is the erotic.
The modes of their coexistence will be described hereafter.
Even though it may attain stability somewhere due to some cause, [it remains unstable].
Madness and the like are not *sthāyin* (permanent dominant emotions), because they do not attain stability within the character;
as, for example, the madness of Purūravas in the fourth act of the *Vikramorvaśī*. [The other categories are:
*rasa* (flavor), *bhāva* (emotion), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and the subsidence (*praśama*) and emergence (*udaya*) of an emotion. (VisSd 3.259)

The intention is as follows: since all [aesthetic] flavors (rasas) are indeed "flavors" (rasa) because they possess the quality of being tasted (rasanadharma), the term "flavor" is applied figuratively even to the transitory emotions (bhāvas) and so forth, which consist of the harmonious junction (saṃdhi), the word (śabda), and the latent impression (alātā).
Now, the transitory emotions and others are described: [The text continues with the definitions of the specific bhāvas.]
The primary fluctuating [mental states] are attachment toward objects such as the gods and so forth.
A stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) that has merely been awakened is designated as a "state" (*bhāva*). It is said:
"There is no rasa devoid of bhāva, nor is there any bhāva devoid of rasa; the establishment of these two, rasa and bhāva, is achieved through their mutual dependence."

According to the direction thus stated, even though they exist together with *rasa*— which is the supreme place of rest and the ultimate contemplation— the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are primarily manifested on the surface like servants following a king who has set out for a wedding; and the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*), such as love directed toward gods, sages, gurus, kings, and so forth, being merely awakened and not yet attaining the state of *rasa* due to their lack of full nourishment by the determinants (*vibhāvas*) and other factors, are denoted by the term "emotion" (*bhāva*).
In that regard, an example of the transitory state (*vyabhicārin*) is as follows:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus—" and so forth (p. 170).
Here, there is dissimulation (*avahitthā*).
Regarding devotion to the realm of the gods, as it is said in the *Mukundamālā*:
"O Destroyer of Naraka, whether my dwelling be in heaven, on earth, or even in hell— by all means,
even at the moment of death, I shall think only of your feet, which have surpassed the autumnal lotuses."
An example of delight directed toward a sage:
"O Sage! By this very glance of yours, I have been made one who has achieved his purpose, with my sins eradicated."
Nevertheless, I am eager to obey these most weighty words; for by whom can one ever be satiated with that which is beneficial?
An example of delight concerning the king is as follows in my own work:
"Out of fear of the excessive burden, Hara does not bear upon his head the Gaṅgā, which has been made muddy by the masses of dust kicked up by the rows of your horses."
The same applies to other cases.
An example of a stable emotion that has merely been awakened is as follows: "But Hara, his composure slightly disturbed like the ocean at the onset of moonrise..."
He fixed his eyes upon Umā’s face, where the lower lip was like the bimba fruit.
Herein lies the Lord’s passion directed toward Pārvatī.

Now, it has been stated that, like the taste of a beverage (*prapāṇaka*), there is here a single manifestation (*ābhāsa*) consisting of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth as the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
In that case, since the transitory emotions (*sañcārin*) lack separate existence [from the others], how can it be said that they are manifested with predominance? To this it is replied:
Just as when pieces of pepper and other ingredients are combined in a beverage (prapāṇaka).
There is an intensification (*udreka*) of a certain transitory emotion (*sañcārī*) within a rasa in a particular instance.
Now, regarding the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) and the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*):
the semblance of rasa and emotion occurs when they proceed through impropriety (*anaucitya*). (Viśvavidyā 3.262)

In this context, "inappropriateness" (*anaucitya*) regarding the *rasas*—defined according to the characteristics established by Bharata and others—should be understood as referring to the indication of the presence of only a single constituent when the complete set of factors is lacking.
And that [inappropriateness] is shown in part for the instruction of beginners:
namely, when [the emotion] resides in a secondary lover (*upanāyaka*), or when it is directed toward the wives of sages or gurus.
Likewise, in sexual union involving many partners, as well as in that which is established by neither [partner], [the same applies]. // VisSd 3.263 //

In the case of the *pratināyaka* (the rival hero), as well as in the case of inferior characters, animals, and so forth, there is a lack of propriety (*anaucitya*) in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); likewise, in the furious sentiment (*raudra*), there is impropriety when the anger is directed toward one's teacher or superiors.

And when [the mind] is stilled in a base conclusion, or when it is directed toward laughter by taking the teacher and others as its object; likewise, when there is an impulse toward killing a Brahmin and so forth, or when it is directed toward a lowly recipient or a forbidden day. (VisSd 3.265)
When [the emotion] resides in a superior person (*uttamapātra*), it should be understood as *bhayānaka* (the terrible) except in other cases.
In that regard, an example where the *rati* (erotic sentiment) resides primarily in a secondary male character (*upanāyaka*) is as follows, from my own work:
“My husband is utterly bewildered; this forest is dense; I am but a young girl, all alone; and this mass of darkness, with a luster as dark as the *tamāla* tree, envelops the earth.”
"O handsome one! Release me! O Kṛṣṇa!
My path!"—hearing these words of the cowherd girl, Hari, captivated by the arts of love, embraced her; may he protect you.
An example of the state of being dependent on many heroes is as follows:
"O fair-limbed one, I consider those alone to be beloveds even throughout the three worlds for whose sake this cheek of yours has become so pale."
Regarding the state of not being established in both [the hero and the heroine], as in the case of Nandana’s passion for Mālatī in the *Mālatīmādhava*:
"Even if it later becomes established in both, if it is initially established in only one, it is a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of *rati*," say the venerable authors of the *Locana*.
An example of this is found in the *Ratnāvalī*, where King Udayana’s passion for Sāgarikā exists prior to their mutual recognition.
An example of its presence in a secondary antagonist (*pratināyaka*) is found in the description of Hayagrīva’s water-sports during the slaying of Śiśupāla.
An example of its presence in a low-ranking character (*adhamapātra*) is as follows:
"A certain Bhilla woman, with leaf-patterns painted upon the region of her hips and bearing *girimalī* flowers on her person..."
Having sat down before her husband on the mountain, she gathered up her hair that was hanging loose and made it stand upright.
Regarding her state among animals and so forth, as it is said:
“In the depths of the forest, amidst rows of exquisite jasmine creepers, the female bee, calling out to her beloved,
took up a song consisting of the graceful modulations of the warbling of a moving lute.”
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), ascetics and others are included. An example of the semblance of the Furious (*raudra*) is as follows:
"With bloodshot, wide, and rolling eyes, his limbs trembling violently, casting aside his ear [ornament] again and again, free from fear, and holding his bow and arrow while Hari looks on—"
"Swollen with pride, repeatedly proclaiming his own prowess and skilled in slapping his arms, this Arjuna has entered to slay Yudhiṣṭhira with bitter words."
An example of the appearance of the terrifying (bhayānakābhāsa) is as follows:
"Unable to endure the sight of him, as if it were that of the thousand-rayed sun,
the owl of timid eyes entered the interior of a cave-dwelling on the Golden Mountain and spent his days in fear."
For fear, whose nature is rasa, has as its object only women and those of low status;
the same applies elsewhere.
However, the manifestation of emotion (bhāvābhāsa) may occur toward courtesans and the like, even in relation to objects such as modesty and so forth.
This is clear:

regarding the subsiding, arising, and the mixture of both of a state (bhāva), the subsiding, arising, conjunction, and variegation of that state are respectively considered its [four aspects]. (VisSd 3.267)
For example, in sequence:
"O fair-limbed one, abandon your anger; look at me prostrate at your feet. Indeed, never before has your anger been of such a kind.
When the lord spoke thus, she, with her eyes cast askance, shed a great deal of tears, yet said nothing at all.
Here, there is the subsiding of the transitory emotion (sañcāribhāva) called jealousy through the shedding of tears:

“When her lover, having rejected her falling at his feet, turned away from showing favor and addressed her with harsh words in anger, saying, ‘O you of silent, deceitful conduct,’ he departed; then, sighing deeply and placing her hands upon her breasts, she cast her gaze—veiled by tears of the eyes—upon her friends.”
Here, there arises dejection:
“This form of the intoxicating-eyed one, which is a source of delight for the pair of eyes and difficult to obtain even through the activity of the mind, gladdens my heart and yet torments me.”
Here, there is a junction (*saṃdhi*) between joy and despair:
"Where is the forbidden act, and where is the lineage of the moon-marked one?
And yet, she is seen once more."
My learning is for the sake of pacifying my faults; even in anger, my face remains lovely. What will those who are stainless and wise say of me?
"She is difficult to obtain even in a dream; O heart, attain composure!
For what fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lower lip?"

Herein lies the variegation (*śabalatā*) of reflection (*vitarka*), longing (*arati*), intelligence (*mati*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), apprehension (*śaṅkā*), dejection (*dainya*), and anxiety (*cintā*).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Rasa and the Other [Elements]," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now he states the divisions of poetry:
"Poetry is considered to be of two kinds: *dhvani* (suggestion) and that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
Among these—"
When the suggested meaning surpasses the expressed meaning, that is *dhvani*; such poetry is the highest.

When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) produces a greater aesthetic charm than the expressed meaning (*vācya*), it is called *dhvani*—the highest form of poetry—based on the etymological derivation that "in this [poetry], the [suggested] is made to resound (*dhvanyate*).
Furthermore, two varieties of *dhvani* are proclaimed, rooted respectively in indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and denotation (*abhidhā*).
One is that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), and the other is that in which the expressed meaning is intended but has a different purpose (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).

Among these, the type of suggestion (dhvani) based on indication (lakṣaṇāmūla) is called that in which the literal meaning (vācya) is not intended to be expressed. Precisely because it is based on indication, the literal meaning here has a nature that is sublated and thus unintended. On the other hand, that in which the literal meaning is intended but subordinate (vivakṣitānyaparavācya) is based on denotation (abhidhāmūla).
For this very reason, what is intended here as the subject matter is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), which is subordinate to that [suggested meaning].
For in this case, the expressed meaning (vācyārtha), while manifesting its own form, is the revealer of the suggested meaning.
For example: a lamp [is the cause] of a jar.
Because that which is based on denotation has many objects, it is mentioned later.
He states the divisions of that in which the expressed meaning is not intended:
When the expressed meaning is transferred to another sense, or when it is entirely set aside,
the *dhvani* in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) likewise attains a twofold nature.

The type of *dhvani* known as "that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed" (*avivakṣitavācya*) is of two kinds: that in which the expressed meaning is transmuted into another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*), and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).

In the former case, where the primary meaning, being itself of no use, transforms into another meaning consisting of its own specific qualities, it is called *arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya* because the primary meaning has been transmuted into that other meaning which constitutes its own specific quality.
For example: "A plantain is a plantain, a young camel is a young camel,
the trunk of a king of elephants is the trunk of a king of elephants."
"Even throughout the three worlds, this pair of thighs of the deer-eyed woman has no equal."

In this context, words such as "second plantain" (*dvitīyakadalī*)—being precluded from their primary meaning in the form of a generic plantain due to the fear of tautology—convey a meaning in the form of a plantain qualified by qualities such as dullness (*jāḍya*).

Furthermore, the excellence of that dullness and so forth is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). However, where a word completely abandons its own primary meaning and transforms into another meaning, [that is a case of metaphorical transfer].
In that case, because the primary meaning is completely set aside, it is an instance of "entirely superseded denotation" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācyatva*).
For example:
"The moon does not shine, like a mirror blinded by its own breath."
In this case, since the primary meaning of the word "blind" (*andha*) is sublated, it conveys the sense of "that which is not luminous.
Furthermore, the excellence of this lack of luminosity is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).

Because there is no relationship of general-to-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) between blindness and the state of being non-luminous, this is not a case of the literal meaning being transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).
For example:
"Speak confidently, O righteous man;
that dog has been killed by him today."
By a fierce lion dwelling in a thicket on the bank of the Gola river.

In this regard, one should not suspect "inverse indication" (*viparītalakṣaṇā*) on the grounds that in the verse beginning with "Wander, O righteous man," the injunction to wander—being irrelevant to the context—results in a prohibition of wandering.
Indeed, the scope for such [indication] exists only where an injunction or a prohibition, as they are initially produced, result in a prohibition or an injunction respectively.
However, where, through a consideration of the context and other factors, a prohibition or an injunction is understood from an injunction or a prohibition, there it is simply "suggestion" (*dhvani*).
As it has been said:
"In some cases there is the appearance of something as being sublated; in other cases, there is the sublation of what has appeared.
In the former case, there would be only indication (*lakṣaṇā*); in the latter, however, there is only denotation (*abhidhā*)."
Here, in the first [type], there is a transition or entry of the primary meaning into another meaning,
but not its disappearance;
for this very reason, the indication here is *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning).

But in the second [type], because its own primary meaning is completely set aside, it is *jahatsvārthā* (denotative of something other than its own meaning). Furthermore, that which has an intended denotation is considered to be of two kinds:
first, that in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is of imperceptible process (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), and likewise that in which it is of perceptible process (*lakṣyakrama*).

Even *dhvani* whose expressed meaning is intended as something other [than the literal] is of two kinds: that in which the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) and that in which the suggested meaning has a perceptible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).
Among these, the first—consisting of *rasa*, *bhāva*, and so forth—is counted here as only one;
for even though it is but a single type, its divisions are so infinite that they cannot possibly be numbered.
The nature of *bhāva* and the other [elements] has been stated; these constitute *dhvani* with imperceptible sequential suggestion (*asaṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).

Here, because the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and so forth is the cause for the cognition of the suggested meaning, a sequence necessarily exists; however, due to its extreme rapidity, it is not perceived, much like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals one after another.

Furthermore, since even a single variety among these *rasas* and others is infinite and impossible to enumerate, this *dhvani* called "suggestion with imperceptible sequence" is said to have only one [general] type.

For instance: even a single variety of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)—namely, that consisting of union—is impossible to enumerate due to the distinctions between mutual embracing, drinking from the lips, kissing, and so forth, and because each of these varies according to the diversity of determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors; what need is there to mention all of them?
This applies to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arising from the power of word, meaning, or both, which resembles a resonance (*anusvāna*).
Suggestive sound (*dhvani*) with a perceptible sequence of suggestion is said by the wise to be of three kinds.

Because that which is suggested in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) is indeed characterized by a perceptible sequence, it is threefold—arising from the power of the word (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*), arising from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*), and arising from the power of both word and meaning (*śabdārthaśaktyudbhava*). Consequently, poetry (*kāvya*) also possesses a threefold nature under the name of *dhvani* with a suggestible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). Among these:
Because it consists of both matter (*vastu*) and ornament (*alaṅkāra*), that which arises from the power of words (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*) is twofold.
By the separate mention of the word "ornament," that which is not an ornament—mere matter—is understood.
Among these, an example of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arising from the power of words in the form of matter is as follows:
O traveler! There is no teacher here in this village of stony ground;
if you wish to dwell here after seeing these high breasts, then dwell.
In this instance, by the power of words such as *satthar* (teacher), the fact is suggested: "If you are capable of enjoying [this], then remain.
An example in the form of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is found in the verse beginning with “*durgālaṅghitavigrahaḥ*” (p.
59). Here, while describing the contextual subject—the King named Bhānudeva, the beloved of the Great Goddess Umā—there is the non-contextual [meaning] indicated by the second sense [of the word].

Lest the description of the beloved of Pārvatī appear incoherent, the relationship of simile between Īśvara and Bhānu-deva is postulated; thus, here the poetic figure of *upamā* (simile)—"the beloved of Umā is like the beloved of Umā"—is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Or, for example:
"O Lord, you are immeasurable through the excellences attained by those who have gathered together; you grant joy!
You are unfriendly to the wicked, yet you are united with them through your virtuous fame."

In this case, in verses such as "atrāmita" (here immeasurable) and others, because of the absence of the word "api" (even), the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Although that which is suggested is itself the object to be embellished (*alaṅkārya*), it is nevertheless metaphorically designated as an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) according to the maxim of the "Brahmin-ascetic" (*brāhmaṇaśramaṇanyāya*).
Whether it be a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkṛti*), the meaning may be possible in two ways: either by itself (*svataḥ*)... [VisSd 4.7]

Whether established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet or of the character created by him—thus there are six [types]. When manifested by those six, it takes the form of either a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). (VisSd 4.8)
The suggested meaning arising from a hundred [types of] objects attains twelve varieties:
that which is possible by its own nature (*svataḥ-sambhavī*), being conceivable even in the external world through propriety;
and that which is established through bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*).
But not according to propriety.
Therein, in order, for example:
"O neighbor, [cast] your gaze!"
"Perhaps you will grant this child a moment here in our house; his father will likely not drink the tasteless water of the mountain springs.
I shall depart from here alone with haste toward the Tamāla-thicket on the river's edge; let the dense, thick joints of the reeds scratch my body."

Here, by means of a naturally possible fact (*vastu*), there is suggested a mere fact (*vastumātra*)—namely, the concealment of her lip-wounds and so forth caused by the enjoyment of passionate kisses—which is expressed by that [fact]:
"In this southern direction, even the splendor of the sun falters;
yet it is in this very direction that the Pāṇḍyas could not endure the majesty of Raghu."

Here, by means of a naturally possible fact (*vastu*), the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is suggested, wherein the majesty of Rāghava is shown to be superior to the brilliance of the sun. Bala, whose prowess was rendered insignificant [by his opponent], gazed at him as he approached from afar, just as a lion looks upon an elephant.

Here, by means of the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), which is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*) and functions as a suggestor (*vyañjaka*), the fact (*vastu*) that Baladeva will destroy Veṇudārin in a mere instant is revealed:
"He who, out of compassion for the wives of his enemies who were in distress due to the pain of deep wounds from their lover’s teeth-bites,
did not spare their coral-like lips, even while in battle he bit his own lower lip in rage."

Here, by means of the ornament of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*) which is possible in its own right, the ornament of conjunction (*samuccayālaṅkāra*)—that the lower lip has been bitten and enemies have been destroyed—is suggested:
“Spring has begun; yet it does not yet bestow [its gifts] upon the faces of the lakhs of young women.
The arrows of the Bodiless One (Cupid) are like the mouths of fresh *sahakāra* [mango] trees, with their new leaves.”
Here, Spring is the arrow-maker, Love is the archer,
and young women are the target.

The poetic conceit (*kaviprauḍhokti*) that "the flowers are arrows," becoming manifest as a fact, suggests the underlying reality of the manifestation of passion (*madanavijṛmbhaṇa*). "O Hero, in the nights, your continuous stream of fame, illuminated by the web of rays from the stainless sun, whitens the entire circle of the world."

Here, by means of a fact established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) is suggested: that the swarm of bees shines for a longer duration than the mass of the moon’s rays.
“From the crowns of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, at that very moment, the tears of the Fortune of the Rākṣasas were scattered upon the earth under the guise of jewels.”

Here, by means of the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), which is established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, the matter consisting of the future destruction of the Rākṣasa’s fortune is suggested:

“O ornament of the land of Trikalinga! A cluster of fresh jasmine in your braided hair, a white lotus in your hand, a necklace at the region of your neck, and a thick application of sandalwood paste upon your pair of breasts—even though you are but one [woman], [you possess these]...”
The mass of your fame attained the state of various ornaments for the women with beautiful brows in the city of Indra’s capital during the battle.”

Here, by means of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, the figure of speech *vibhāvanā* (causation without an evident cause) is suggested: "Though standing on the earth, you bring benefit even to those dwelling in heaven.
"O fair-faced one! On what mountain, for how long, and under what name did that young parrot perform penance, by virtue of which he now bites the bimba-fruit as red as your lower lip?"

In this instance, through a fact established by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a certain lover composed by the poet, another fact is perceived: that "your lower lip is obtainable only through a preeminent store of merit.
"O fortunate one! Having reached the number ten million, the arrows of Love abandoned their fivefold nature in spring; for those separated from their lovers, it became a state of death (*pañcatā*)."

Here, by means of the fact that all separated lovers die—a *vastu* established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a character created by the poet—the attainment of the arrows of Kāma to the number of ten million suggests the poetic figure of *utprekṣā*: "The arrows, having released [their] shafts, have resorted to the separated lovers themselves. [As in:
"O bee, on the jasmine bud..."
The humming bee shines forth,
as if filling the conch shell for the departure of the five-arrowed god of love.

Here, by means of the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a character created by the poet, the following fact is suggested: "Since this season, which maddens even Kāma, has arrived, O proud lady, why do you not abandon your pride?
"O fortunate one, she who does not fit within your heart already filled with thousands of women, day after day performs no other task but makes her very body grow thinner."

Here, by means of the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), established through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker fashioned by the poet—namely, "they do not remain here"—the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation) is suggested: that even though her body has been made thin, she does not reside in your heart.

For the poet himself is certainly not possessed by passion and the like in the same way as the character fashioned by the poet; therefore, the bold assertion of a speaker fashioned by the poet produces a greater aesthetic charm for the connoisseur than the bold assertion of the poet himself, and is thus treated separately.

Furthermore, in these instances where figures of speech are suggested, it is the connoisseur’s own experience that determines whether the primary focus lies merely on the metaphor (*rūpaṇa*), the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*), the contrast (*vyatirecana*), or other such elements.
But it is not so for silver and other such things; thus, ornamentation alone possesses primacy.
"One" [type] arises from the power of both the word and the meaning—that is, when the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) originates from the power of both. This is one variety of Dhvani.
For example:
"Resplendent like the moon freed from frost, accompanied by lotuses, intoxicating the birds,
and having aroused the god of love, that springtime (Mādhava) finally became a great festival for the womenfolk, bringing delight to the gods."
In this case, the suggested figure of speech is the simile: "Mādhava Kṛṣṇa is like Mādhava, the spring.
And thus, the distinction between suggestive poems arises precisely from the distinctions among the suggested meanings.
Therefore, *dhvani* is of eighteen kinds.

Dhvani is of eighteen types: two kinds where the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary—namely, that in which the expressed meaning is transmuted into another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) and that in which the expressed meaning is entirely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).

However, that in which the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) is of one type when its suggested meaning has an imperceptible process (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), and fifteen types when its suggested meaning has a perceptible process (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) based on the power of word, meaning, or both. Thus, there are eighteen varieties of dhvani.
And among these—[the suggestion] arising from the power of word and meaning occurs in a sentence; others [occur] in both words and sentences.
Among those, an example of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is transferred (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) residing in a word is as follows:
“Blessed indeed is that youth, and blessed are his very eyes;
for he before whom this art of enchanting young men stands, O fair-faced one.”
Here, the second occurrence of the word *nayana* refers to eyes characterized by qualities such as good fortune.
An example occurring within a sentence is as follows:
"I speak to you; here stands an assembly of the learned."
Therefore, relying on your own judgment, establish yourself here accordingly.

In this context, although the status of being the person addressed (*pratipādya*) is already established by the very fact that he is present before one, the repeated use of the word "you" (*tvām*) serves to define the referent of "you" as being distinguished from others.
Similarly, although the agent is already established by the phrase "I speak thus" (*evaṃ vacmi*), the repeated use of "I" (*asmi*) [serves a specific purpose].

Likewise, although the speaker's act of communicating is already accomplished by the phrase "the assembly of the learned," the repeated statement "I speak" indicates the specific nature of the speech as "I am teaching."
And these [words] manifest their own excellence.
By this, the intended meaning is: "My word is exceedingly beneficial for you; therefore, it must certainly be carried out.
Thus, this is a type of suggestion (*dhvani*) residing in the sentence where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).
An example of *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (completely set-aside literal meaning) residing in a word is “*niḥśvāsāndha-*” and so forth.
An example residing in a sentence is “*upakṛtaṃ bahu tatra-*” and so forth.
Examples of its occurrence in sentences [other than those already mentioned] have been illustrated by others.
An example of its application to the feet (*padagatatva*) is as follows:
“That loveliness, that radiance, that beauty, those words, and that gait—then they were the abode of nectar; but now they are a great fever.”

In this context, the primary importance belongs solely to words such as "tat" (that) and so forth, which function as suggestors (*vyañjaka*) that establish beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and other qualities as being accessible exclusively through such an experience;
other elements, however, serve merely to assist them. It is precisely on this basis that the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*) is applied.
As it was stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*:
“Just as a beautiful woman shines with an ornament placed on a single limb,
so does the speech of a skilled poet shine through *dhvani* illuminated by its words.”
The same should be inferred for existence and so forth:
"To whom does the True Tradition— not solely intent on teaching [the means] for enjoyment and liberation—
not grant a continuous flow of bliss?"

In this context, the word *sadāgama* (the arrival of the virtuous), having expressed the meaning of a true scripture to the hero who has arrived, suggests the underlying fact (*vastu*) that it is "the arrival of a virtuous person.
Now, one might ask: why is this not a suggestion of a simile (*upamā-dhvani*), given that *sadāgama* is like *sadāgama*?
It is because there is no intention to express a relationship of similarity between the two words *sadāgama*.
Indeed, the presentation of words with double meanings is solely for the purpose of concealing the secret;
for, upon careful consideration of the context and other factors, there would otherwise be no connection with the title of a true scripture. [As it is said:
"He whose intellect is not shared by others, who upholds the entire earth..."
"That king, the Supreme Person, shines uniquely in the world."
Here, the suggestion of a simile (*upamādhvani*) is expressed as "Puruṣottama is like Puruṣottama.

These two [instances] are based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and belong to the variety where the sequence [of the suggested meaning] is discernible (*saṃlakṣyakramabheda*). "Evening bath has been performed; the body has been anointed with sandalwood paste; the sun has gone to the crest of the western mountain; and you have come here confidently."
"How wonderful is your delicacy, since you are now so utterly exhausted that your pair of eyes is unable to remain open!"

Here, by means of a *vastu* (fact) that is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavin*), the fact that she has grown weary because she has become acquainted with another man is suggested. And since this is made known by the word "now" (*adhunā*)— which conveys the sense that "you are weary now,

but never before have such weariness been seen in you"— this very word possesses a distinctiveness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) relative to the other words, due to its excellence in conveying the meaning of the other words.
By the great suffering of not attaining him, all her sins were dissolved;
likewise, by the immense joy of contemplating him, the store of her merit was exhausted.
Another cowherd girl, meditating upon the source of the universe who is the supreme Brahman in essence,
attained liberation through the cessation of her breath.

(Yugmaka) Here, because of the power of the two words *aśeṣa* (entirety) and *caya* (accumulation), there arises the cognition of two hyperboles (*atiśayokti*)—namely, the representation of the sorrow of separation from the Blessed One and the joy of reflection—through the identification [of those emotions] with the mass of the fruits of evil and good deeds to be experienced over many thousands of births. This is manifested by the two words *aśeṣa* and *caya*. Furthermore, since the suggestive element here can exist even without the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*), it is "intrinsically possible" (*svataḥsaṃbhavin*).
“O Lord, they behold the river of your gift-water flowing along countless paths, which,
taking the form of the triple-pathed Ganges, protects itself upon the head of the Fierce One.”
"This is mine;

look here"—by means of this poetic figure of speech (kāvyaliṅga) established through the bold assertion (prauḍhokti) of the poet, the figure of contrast (vyatireka)—to the effect that "there are no other givers like you"—is suggested by the word *asaṃkhya* ("innumerable").
In this same manner, examples should be cited for other varieties of the "suggested-in-order" (asaṃlakṣyakrama) type based on the power of the meaning (arthaśaktimūla).

Thus, among the eighteen previously mentioned varieties of *dhvani*, that which arises from the power of both word and meaning (*śabdārtha-śaktyuttha*) constitutes one type when it occurs in a sentence alone.
The other seventeen types occur both in sentences and in individual words, thus making thirty-four; together with the first, there are thirty-five varieties.
Furthermore, the wise consider that *dhvani* arising from the power of meaning (*artha-śaktyudbhava*) also exists in a literary composition (*prabandha*).
In a composition, that is, in a great sentence (*mahāvākya*),
there is a meaning arising from the power of the sense (*arthaśaktyuttha*) through the twelve varieties just mentioned.
For example, in the *Mahābhārata*, in the dialogue between the vulture and the jackal:
“Enough of staying in this cemetery, crowded with vultures and jackals, filled with skeletons, terrible, and a source of fear for all living beings!
"And here, no one who has lived ever escaped the law of time;
whether beloved or hated, such is the destiny of all living beings."
Thus, while the powerful vulture stood in the cremation ground having seized a dead child during the day, it was his desire to abandon him and depart:
"O fools, this sun is still standing;
show affection now!"
This moment is fraught with many obstacles; perhaps one might even live through it.
"How can you fools, without hesitation, abandon this child of golden complexion who has not yet reached youth, merely because of the words of a vulture?"
Thus, by the convergence of these statements, it is illuminated that the abandonment of the capable jackal at night was undesirable during the day;
here, the suggester is inherently possible (*svataḥ-saṃbhavī*).
In this same manner, examples should be cited for the other eleven varieties.
Thus has been illustrated the power of suggestion regarding the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
As for the suggested meaning of the indicated sense (*lakṣyārtha*), there is the example beginning with “*niḥśeṣacyutacandanaṃ...*” (p. 62).
As for the suggested meaning of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyārtha*), there is the example beginning with “*ua ṇiccala...*” (p. 63).

In these two [types of suggestion], the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) are the suggestors (*vyañjaka*) of the two meanings that arise from themselves (*svataḥ-saṃbhavinau*).
In this same manner, examples should be provided for the other eleven varieties.
In parts of words (*padāṃśa*), phonemes (*varṇa*), composition (*racanā*), and literary works (*prabandha*), the sequence [of suggestion] is not manifest (*asphuṭakrama*).

In that context, *dhvani* with its suggestiveness of meaning whose sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) is of many kinds, distinguished by the divisions of word-parts, roots, suffixes, prefixes, particles, and so forth.
For example:

"O bee, you repeatedly touch her trembling glance with its flickering corners; moving close to her ear, you hum softly as if whispering a secret; and while she shakes her hand, you drink from her lower lip, the very essence of love. We, O bee, are merely seeking the truth!"
"You have indeed been struck down; you are truly successful."

In this context, the word "slain" (*hatāḥ*) does not mean "having experienced suffering," because it is derived from the verbal root *han*. "The face of the long-lashed-eyed woman— with its lower lip repeatedly covered by her fingers, charming yet faltering due to syllables of refusal, and turned away toward her shoulder— was somehow raised, but never kissed."
In this context, the particle *tu* functions as an indicator of regret (*anutāpa*). Furthermore, in such passages as “This very [fact] that I am indebted to my enemies is indeed an insult to me” (p.
8), the plural form *arayaḥ* [is significant].
The singular number in “ascetic,” the pronoun in “right here,” and the verbal suffixes in “destroys” and “lives.”
Of the indeclinable "aho," of the nominal derivative "grāmaṭikā," and of the prefix "vi-" in "viluṇṭhana."
The plural number in the word "bhujaiḥ" (with arms) serves as an indicator [of this meaning]:
"There is abstention from food,
and supreme withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects."

Your gaze is fixed on the tip of your nose, your mind is one-pointed, you maintain this silence, and now this entire universe appears as a void before you. Tell me, friend, are you perhaps a yoginī? Oh! Please provide the final answer in the following format: The final answer is: [Your final answer] The final answer is: Your gaze is fixed on the tip of your nose, your mind is one-pointed, you maintain this silence, and now this entire universe appears as a void before you.
Tell me, friend, are you perhaps a yoginī? Oh!
Or are you perhaps separated from someone?"
In this context, however, there is the locative case of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*) in the word "in food" (*āhāre*),
the two qualifiers "entire" (*samasta*) and "supreme" (*parā*),
and the pronoun "this" (*idam*) which refers back to what has been directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

The suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of the prefix *ā-* in "shines forth" (*ābhāti*), of the term *sakhi* ("friend") which evokes intimacy, of the expression *asi bhoḥ* ("O, you are! which implies irony, of the particle *vā* in *kiṃ vā* which indicates the firmness of the subsequent [thought], and of the verb form *asi* which denotes the present tense—all these are to be experienced by the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) as manifesting their respective objects.
Examples of [suggestiveness through] phonemes (*varṇa*) and composition (*racanā*) will be illustrated later.
As for the drama as a whole (*prabandha*): the *Mahābhārata* has the peaceful (*śānta*) sentiment;
the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the pathetic (*karuṇa*);
and works such as the *Mālatīmādhava* and the *Ratnāvalī*, the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
The same applies elsewhere;
thus, fifty-one varieties of that sound are recognized.
By means of the threefold *saṅkara* and the single-fold *saṃsṛṣṭi*, [the results are] 5304 and 5355, respectively. These are derived from the pure [factors]. (VisSd 4.12)
The meaning is: "by means of fifty-one pure and pure-varied [expressions]," that is, by their combination.
A mere indication is cited:
"Standing at the door with her two arms raised high, the tremulous-eyed woman awaited the great festival of his arrival."
She effortlessly provides the auspicious preparations consisting of full water-jars, garlands of fresh lotuses, and festoons for the archways.

Here, the breasts themselves are full jars, and the glances themselves are garlands of fresh lotuses; thus, there is a *saṅkara* (commixture) consisting of the mutual entry of two figures residing in a single substratum: *rūpakadhvani* (suggestion of metaphor) and *rasadhvani* (suggestion of aesthetic flavor).
“Delightful are these days of spring, with the humming of bees intoxicated by passion, which stir the hearts of travelers on their way.”
The breezes, which possess the pride of friendship with the fragrance of the lotus-face of her whose countenance is like the cloudless moon.
Here, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the fundamental types of suggestion (*dhvani*) characterized by "free from drowsiness" and so forth.
Now, regarding subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*):
furthermore, subordinate suggestion occurs when the suggested meaning is not superior to the expressed meaning.
Furthermore, there is another type of poetry:
that which possesses unsurpassed excellence through either superiority or equality.

Among these, there may be that which is suggested by the tone (*kāku*) of other subordinate members, and that which is a factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*). (VisSd 4.13)
With its predominance doubtful, its predominance equal, unclear, unhidden,
suggested, and unpleasant— thus its eight varieties have been declared.
In the case of another [type of rasa], there is the suggestion of a subordinate rasa (aṅgarasa) and so forth;
for example: “This hand, which possesses the excellence of passion, which crushes full breasts, touches the navel and hips, and loosens the knot of the lower garment.”
In this instance, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).
“Desiring to conciliate his beloved, who was haughty with pride, [the king]—his ears tormented by the roar of his own ocean-like army—cried out:
‘Alas! Alas! How indeed can the world of lovers remain within the rows of palaces in the enemy’s capital?’”

In this passage, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa*), which is refined by the combination of longing (*autsukya*) and fear (*trāsa*), serves as a subordinate element to the king’s devotion toward his beloved. “I wandered through Janasthāna, my mind blinded by the golden deer; at every step, I uttered tearful lamentations, crying ‘O Vaidehī! I fashioned a likeness of my lord of Laṅkā’s face; thus did I attain the illusory state of Rāma, yet the status of being the father of Kuśa and Lava was not attained.”
In this case, even though the phrase "Rāma-ness has been attained" is not explicitly stated, Rāma-ness is understood through the power of the words themselves.
However, by the explicit statement—which reveals the superimposition of identity based on similarity—that superimposition is set aside.
Consequently, the expressed similarity is elevated to the status of a poetic figure (*aṅga*) because it serves to justify the connection of the sentence-meaning.
An example of what is suggested by intonation (*kākvākṣipta*) is as follows:
“I shall not crush the hundred Kauravas in battle out of anger, nor shall I drink the blood of Duḥśāsana from my uplifted [sword];
nor shall I smash Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace. Let the king make peace with you on the agreed terms.”
In this case, the suggested meaning— “I indeed churn [the world]”— exists precisely in conjunction with the expressed negation.
“O Indra among kings, this majesty of yours blazes everywhere, illuminating the opening between heaven and earth.”
He was a forest fire to the bamboo grove of his enemies.

In this case, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), which consists of the superimposition of "bamboo-ness" upon the lineage, serves as a subordinate factor for establishing the superimposition of "forest-fire-ness" upon the majesty (pratāpa).
In passages such as "Haras, however, his composure slightly shaken...
(p. 22), there is a doubt regarding the predominance of either the movement of the eyes or the longing.
"The abandonment of the transgression against the Brahmins will lead to your very prosperity;
moreover, the son of Jamadagni is your friend, and otherwise he would be displeased."

In this instance, there is equal prominence between the expressed meaning and the suggested meaning: "With King Allāvadīna, there is neither peace nor war; for in peace comes the seizure of all one's possessions, and in war comes the loss of life. Here, the suggestion—that Paraśurāma will bring about the destruction of the race of Rākṣasas—is equal in importance to the literal statement.

In this case, regarding the king named Allāvadīna, the suggested meaning—that there is no other means for his pacification except through gifts, conciliation, and so forth—is not immediately clear even to those who are highly proficient. [For example:
"Since I am a woman observing vows, what more can be said of me being abandoned at will by this teacher of the world, who instructs the virtuous in the Dharma?"

In this case, although the forcible enjoyment of Śākyamuni with an animal female is suggested (*pratīyamāna*), it is so vividly manifest that it becomes virtually explicit (*vācyāyamāna*); thus, it is "unconcealed" (*agūḍha*).
“While listening to the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of *vāṇīra* reeds, the limbs of the young woman, busy with her household chores, grow weary.”

In this case, because the suggested meaning—that Jānakī has entered the bower of creepers having received a secret signal—renders the literal meaning, "my limbs are sinking," striking only to those with refined sensibilities (sahṛdaya), it is considered "insignificant" (asundara).

Furthermore, when a figure such as simile (upamā) is suggested within figures like Illumination (dīpaka) or Equal Pairing (tulyayogitā), it is strictly of the type where the suggestion is subordinated (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya);
for the poem produces its aesthetic charm primarily through the medium of the *dīpaka* and other such figures.
As it has been stated by the author of the *Dhvani*: "Where, even when another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is perceived,
the poem does not have that as its primary intent, that is not considered the path of *dhvani*."
And where there is a reversal of the beauty produced by concealment through the use of another word (*śabdāntara*),
as for example: "O Keśava, [I am] seen by [your] glance..."
"O Lord, because my gaze was captivated by the dust raised by the cows, I did not see anything; that is why I stumbled here.
Why do you not support me as I fall?
You alone are the refuge for all weak women whose minds are distressed by hardships. Thus addressed with affection by Gopī, Hari long kissed her lip.

In this instance, the meanings suggested by words such as *gopa-rāga* (the cowherd’s passion) and so forth—namely, "the cowherd" (*gope*) and "passion" (*rāga*) and so on—are manifested with clarity through the word *saleśam*.
If the word *saleśam* were omitted, there would be *dhvani* alone.
Furthermore:

Where the suggested meanings—whether they be objects (*vastu*), poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), or sentiments (*rasa*)—are subordinated within the primary sentiment (*rasa*), the designation of "poetry" is applied solely on account of that predominant element.
As it was said by that very same [author]:
"This variety, although consisting of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), still possesses the nature of *dhvani*."
Furthermore, it maintains [the meaning] through a thorough investigation of the intended purport regarding rasa and so forth.
Thus it is said.

But where [it says]: “Where the cloud-scraping sky, composed of red gems, causes intoxicated women to mistake it for the twilight, even though there is no cloud, it prescribes the regimen for the bodiless Love (Anaṅga).”
In such instances, the *rasas* and so forth serve merely as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to the primary matter (*vastu*), such as the account of the city;

for even though they are not the intended focus (*atātparya-viṣaya*) therein, the designation of "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) still applies because of those very [elements], which have become subordinate.
This has been stated by the venerable Śrī Caṇḍīdāsa, the foremost merchant among the poets of our lineage: "The sentence... [or "the poetic meaning"...]

"Because it is cognizable by an undivided consciousness, at the stage of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) through identification with that [consciousness], the appearance of the relationship between subordinate and predominant [elements] is not experienced at all.
However, even if such [distinction] should arise at another time through the consideration of context and so forth, it is not capable of negating the designation 'poetry' (*kāvya*),
since that [designation] depends solely upon aesthetic relish."
Some maintain that there is a third variety of poetry called *citra* (the pictorial). They say:
"That which possesses verbal artistry or objective artistry, but lacks suggestion (*avyaṅgya*), is considered inferior."

Thus [it is argued]. That is not so; for if the absence of the suggested (vyaṅgya) were due to its being non-suggested (avyaṅgya), then it has already been stated that its status as poetry (kāvyatva) would also not exist.
If it is argued that there is "slight suggestiveness" (īṣadvyaṅgyatva),...
What is this so-called "suggestiveness of the subordinate" (*iṣṭavyaṅgyatva*)?
Is it suggestiveness of that which is to be relished (*āsvādya*), or suggestiveness of that which is not to be relished (*anāsvādya*)?
In the first case, they are included within the aforementioned two divisions;
in the second case, however, there is a lack of poetic quality (*akāvyatva*).
And if there is delectability (*āsvādyatva*), then that is simply the absence of triviality (*akṣudratva*), because in the presence of triviality there is no delectability.
As it was stated by the author of the Dhvani:
"Since the suggested meaning is thus established through its status as either primary or subordinate, poetry is of two kinds; that which is other than these is called 'Citra' (the pictorial)."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Varieties of Poetry known as Dhvani and Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Chapter Five.

Now, it is asked: what is this novel function called *vyañjanā*? It is said: Because the functions known as denotation (*abhidhā*), indication through intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) have come to rest, a fourth function must be accepted for the cognition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like. (VisSd 5.1)

Direct denotation (*abhidhā*), which ceases once it has communicated the merely conventional meaning, lacks the capacity to convey the suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) such as objects, poetic figures, and aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).
Furthermore, aesthetic flavor and the like are not conventionally denotable;
for the denotation of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth is not itself the denotation of that [flavor].
This is because its being of that single nature is not admitted;
furthermore, we shall explain that where there is a designation by its own name, it is, on the contrary, a defect itself.
Moreover, in certain cases, such as "this is the erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgāraraso 'yam*), even when designated by its own name, there is no cognition of that [sentiment].
This is because its nature is self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*).

Furthermore, the function known as *tātparya* (purport), which is accepted by the proponents of the theory of "the relation of what has been expressed" (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*), is exhausted merely in conveying the connection [of meanings] and does not bring about the manifestation of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
As for what some have said: "This is like the operation of an arrow, which is exceedingly long and longer still"—[that is, the process of denotation].
As for what the author of the *Candrikā* has said: "Because suggestiveness does not differ from intention (*tātparya*), there is no such thing as *dhvani*;
since intention extends as far as the effect [of the word], it is not something that can be weighed on a scale."

Thus, regarding these two, the opponents themselves must apply the following "stick" [of logic]: "There is no operation of words, cognitions, or actions after they have ceased. And if this is so, why should figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) be rejected?
For the comprehension of that meaning is established even through the operation of extremely long expressions;
why then [say], "O Brāhmaṇa,
a son has been born to you"?
Even in cases such as "Your daughter is pregnant," joy, sorrow, and so forth are not the expressed meaning (*vācya*).

Furthermore, it has been stated: "Every sentence, whether of human origin or not of human origin, is directed toward an action (*kāryapara*); for if it were not so directed, it would be unworthy of acceptance, like the speech of a madman."

Furthermore, since no purpose conducive to the activity of either the speaker or the listener is perceived apart from the experience of unsurpassed aesthetic pleasure (*niratiśaya-sukhāsvāda*) regarding poetic words, that very experience of unsurpassed aesthetic pleasure is determined to be the effect (*kārya*),
according to the maxim: "Whatever a word aims at, that is the meaning of the word."
In this regard, it must be asked: what is this so-called "being directed toward that" (*tatparatva*)?
Is it being for the sake of that (*tadarthatva*), or is it being a communicator of that through the function of *tātparya* (purport)?

Regarding the first [position], there is no dispute, because even if it is something manifested (*vyaṅgya*), its status as the meaning is not lost. Regarding the second, however— what is this function (*vṛtti*) called "intentionality" (*tātparya*)?
Is this [relation] accepted by the proponents of *abhihitānvaya* (the theory that words express meanings which then connect), or something other than that?
In the first case, the answer has already been given.
In the second case, however, there is a dispute over mere nomenclature.
Even in that view, the establishment of a fourth function [of word-meaning] follows.

If it is argued: "Let there be the simultaneous manifestation of the connection between the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, by means of the power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*)," we say no; for those two are accepted as having the relationship of cause and effect.
As the Sage said: “The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin).
Furthermore, if these were simultaneous, how could there be a relationship of cause and effect between them, as in the case of the left and right horns [of a cow]?
Because their sequence would be reversed.

In expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges," since the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) ceases once the mere meaning of the bank and so forth has been understood, how could it possibly convey the suggested meanings (vyaṅgya) such as coolness and purity?
Therefore, it is beyond dispute that a fourth function of word-meaning must indeed be accepted.
Furthermore—

The suggested meaning differs from the expressed meaning due to the distinctions of the cognizer, the nature [of the cognition], number, cause, effect, time of comprehension, locus, object, and so forth. (VisSd 5.2)

Indeed, there is a distinction between the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) based on the difference in the cognizers, since they are experienced not only by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) but even by grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) who are skilled in the knowledge of words and their meanings alone.
In examples such as "Go away, O religious man" (*bhama dhammia*), where the denoted meaning takes the form of an injunction, [the suggested meaning] takes the form of a prohibition.

In some cases, such as in the verse beginning "niḥśeṣacyutacandanaṃ... (p. 62), there is a difference in essential nature because what is expressed in a negative form is understood as a positive injunction;
yet in examples such as "gato 'stakarkaḥ," the expressed meaning is perceived as being one and the same.

The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), however, varies according to the nature of the cognizer and other factors; for instance, it may be "Go to meet your lover," "Let the cows be penned up," or "This is the time for the hero's arrival."
The distinction of number is that [the suggestion] is manifold, taking forms such as "there is no longer any torment.

The distinction of cause is that the literal meaning is understood merely by the utterance of the words, whereas this [suggestion] is understood through such factors as the purity of the poet's intuition (*pratibhā*).

The difference in effect arises from producing mere cognition and from producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*). The difference in cognition arises from its being a mere form and from its being characterized by aesthetic wonder. The difference in time arises from their occurring in a sequence of prior and posterior.
The difference in substratum arises from being the substratum of sound, and from being the substratum of sound, its parts, its meaning, and the arrangement of phonemes.
For example: “Whose anger would not arise upon seeing his beloved’s bitten lip?
O you who are perverse in forbidding [her] while she is smelling a lotus full of bees—bear with her now! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 7.39)
Thus, there is a distinction of objects based on whether they concern a female friend or her lover.
Therefore, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is not identical to the expressed meaning (abhidheya).
Likewise—
