Because taste and so forth do not exist prior [to the contact], the two—indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and naming (*abhidhā*)—are not cognizers;
furthermore, indication is also absent due to the lack of any sublation of the primary meaning.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "not denoters of *rasa*.

For there exists no entity established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— distinct from the operation consisting of the essence of *rasa* and denotable by words such as "rasa"— which these two [words], through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), might cause to be understood.

Furthermore, it is precisely in cases such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where the intended syntactic connection between the meanings of the words employed is sublated by its own impossibility, that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) enters.
As the teacher Udayana stated in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*:
"A sentence, having obtained the connection of what is heard, does not indeed seek another [connection], for it lacks further expectancy."
"Because of the absence of a connection between the word-meanings, there is a connection with that which is implied by them."
Furthermore, in cases such as "The dwelling-house is empty" (p. 22), there is no sublation of the primary meaning.
And if, in instances such as "A hamlet on the Ganges," the purpose were the indicated sense (*lakṣya*), [then the following would apply].
Otherwise, the primary meaning of "bank" would be sublated,

and since that [secondary meaning] would also be something to be indicated (*lakṣya*), there would be another purpose for it, and yet another purpose for that, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor, moreover, is there indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank as qualified by the purpose itself.
This is because it is not accepted that the object and the purpose are perceived simultaneously;
for it is only immediately after the cognition of blue and so forth that there can arise either the state of being known (*jñātatā*) or the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
Furthermore, inference is not capable of making known those suggested meanings such as taste and the like.
Because the causes are merely appearances, there is no memory [of them], nor is there cognition of taste and so forth.
For the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* states: “Even that cognition of rasa and the like which arises from the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth must be included within inference itself.
For the cognition of the excitants, ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) is held to be the means of establishing the cognition of rasa and the like.

Indeed, these [factors], being the causes, effects, and auxiliary conditions of the mental states such as love (*rati*) and the rest, produce the rasas precisely by making those [states] known through inference.”

"Those very [elements], when being perceived and having entered the path of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), are called *lasas*; thus, the sequence of their perception is inevitable, but it is not noticed solely because it occurs with such rapidity, which is why this process of manifestation remains unperceived even today. This is what was stated.

In this regard, it must be asked: do you intend by "rasa" (aesthetic flavor) the very cognition of passion and so forth residing in Rāma and others, which is inferred from the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and other factors presented through verbal expression and dramatic gesture;
or is it the self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*) being cultivated by the spectators (*bhāvakas*) through the cultivation of that [cognition]?
In the first case, there is no dispute.
However, the distinction is simply this: "We do not designate the cognition of passion and so forth residing in Rāma and others by the name 'rasa'.
As for the second [argument], it is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) because the reason is fallacious due to the absence of a grasped pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And as it was stated by that very same person:

"Wherever there is the mention or the representation of such excitants (vibhāva), ensuants (anubhāva), involuntary states (sāttvika), and transitory emotions (sañcārin), there the manifestation of the erotic and other rasas occurs"— thus, both the universal concomitance (vyāpti) and the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) are easily apprehended.
By means of these—
“That very collection of causes which you accept as the basis for the manifestation of another meaning is, in our view regarding inference, agreed upon as the means of cognition.”
Thus,
this too is not contradictory for us;
for we do not intend such a cognition to be an object of aesthetic relish (*āsvādya*), but rather— as resting solely in self-luminosity— it is filled with intense bliss (*sāndrānanda*).
Therefore, in this case, because a different matter is being established from the matter intended to be proven, the reason is fallacious (*hetvābhāsa*).
And as for the matter that is suggested in the verse beginning with "O observer of religious duty" (*mama dhammia*) on page 242:

“May Kṛṣṇa protect the world— he who, during their water-sports, repeatedly covers and uncovers Rādhikā’s face with his hand tremulous from play, and who delights in the parting and joining of the ruddy geese.”
In such cases, poetic figures like metaphor (*rūpaka*) and others are indeed only inferable (*anumeya*).

To explain: "Inference is the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*) from a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by its presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*), its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛttatva*).
Consequently, a meaning that is unrelated to the expressed sense is not cognized at all.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension;
therefore, there must indeed be some relationship between the two meanings—the signified and the signifier.
Consequently, the signifying meaning is the *liṅga* (probans).
The subject (*liṅgin*) is that which is to be understood, and the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*pakṣasattva*) of the object to be understood is indeed explicitly stated.

Although its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*) and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛttatva*) are not explicitly stated, they are to be understood through the force of the context.

"Therefore, in this case, since the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), which is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), arises from the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) as the mark (*liṅga*), it ultimately results in nothing other than inference (*anumāna*).

This is not so; for in cases such as "Go away, O [innocent] woman" (*bhama ammia*), where it must be stated that "the wandering prescribed by the cessation of barking dogs in the house leads to the inference of non-wandering on the banks of the Godāvarī due to the perception of a lion," the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Since it is possible for even a timid person to go [to meet a lover] by the command of a teacher or a master, or out of affection for their beloved, the word of a harlot may or may not be authoritative; thus, the reason is doubtful and unestablished (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).

Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "jalakeli," one should not claim that this is merely an inference (anumāna) to the effect that "he who causes the separation and reunion of the cakravāka birds through his appearance and disappearance is indeed the moon."
Because [the reason] is inconclusive due to the presence of things that cause terror and so forth;

even in the inference: "An object of such a kind is a communicator of an object of such a kind, because it is an object of such a kind; for what is not so is not so," the logical reason (hetu) shares the same status as a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).
“Because it has such a meaning”—by this very reason, even that which accomplishes such an undesirable [result] is established.
Likewise, in passages such as: “O neighbor, look here for a moment in our house,” and so forth (p. 250).
The thinning of the knots of the *nalas* and her traveling along the stream alone are said to be the signs of her enjoyment by a lover of another.
Moreover, since that [inference] can also occur here through her own affection for her beloved—as expressed right here—the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, as for the inference of the messenger girl's (*dūtī*) enjoyment by that lover in the passage beginning with "The sandalwood paste has completely fallen away" (p. 62), does that occur because she is the one being informed?
Or by others present at that time,
or by connoisseurs through their contemplation of the meaning of that poem;
there is no dispute regarding the first two cases.
But in the third case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in instances where such an intention is absent.
Now, it should not be argued that the reason (*hetu*) is qualified by being accompanied by the state of the speaker and so forth;
for there is an absence of any such consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, since such poetic works are born solely from the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) and do not necessarily require factual validity, the reason (*hetu*) is "doubtfully unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).
Moreover, the proponent of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) has stated that these word-meanings become suggestors only when accompanied by the term "lowly" (*adhama*);
therefore, how can there be an inference as to whether the lover's lowliness is actually established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) or not?
By this, the view that suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) are cognizable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also refuted;
for even presumptive testimony proceeds only by depending upon a previously established pervasion (*vyāpti*) and intention (*icchā*).
For example: "Whoever lives, he resides somewhere."
And [it is said]: "Caitra lives here in the assembly, yet he is not present," and so forth.

Furthermore, this [subject] is not even cognizable by an indicative cognition—such as the cognition of the number ten through the raising of the index finger during the sale of cloth and similar instances—because even indicative cognition is admitted to be a form of inference, as it depends upon worldly means of knowledge such as convention (*saṅketa*).
And as for the claim made by some that "the cognition of taste and so forth is memory because it is produced by mental formations (*saṃskāra*)," even there,
the reason is fallacious due to its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
as seen in the verse beginning with "durgālaṅghita-" (p. 59).

Furthermore, as for what Mahimabhaṭṭa stated—that there is no such thing as a second meaning—that is merely a "blindfolded gaze" (gajanimīlikā) on the part of one who denies what is established by experience.

Thus, it is proven that a fourth function (*vṛtti*) must indeed be accepted, because the meanings characterized as the various *rasas* and so forth are established by experience and cannot be denied; because they follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of their respective words and so forth; because they are not known through means of knowledge such as inference (*anumāna*); and because they are not cognized by the three functions beginning with denotation (*abhidhā*).
And since this occurs even without the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, it is entirely stainless.
What, then, is the name of this function?
It is said: "This function is called *vyañjanā* by the wise."
Furthermore, others understand the function called "tasting" (rasanā) to be the manifestation of flavor (rasa).
And this has been explained in detail in the section on the definition of *rasa* (aesthetic flavor); thus everything is clear.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "The Definition of the Function of Suggestion" (*vyañjanā-vyāpāra-nirūpaṇa*).
The Sixth Chapter.

Having thus stated the two divisions of poetry by way of the predominant expressed meaning (*dhvani*) and the subordinated suggested meaning (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), he further states another two divisions by way of being visible (*dṛśya*) or audible (*śravya*):
"Furthermore, poetry is considered to be of two kinds according to the distinction between the visible and the audible.
Among these, the visible is that which is to be enacted (*abhineya*)."
He states the reason for its designation as a "metaphor" (rūpaka): "It is a metaphor because of the superimposition of that form. (VisSd 6.1)

That visible poetry is called *rūpaka* (a "representation") because of the superimposition of the nature of Rāma and others upon the actor. He asks, "What is this *abhinaya* (representation)? and says:
"Representation (*abhinaya*) is the imitation of states; it is fourfold."
Likewise, there are the bodily, the vocal, the artificial, and the natural [abhinayas].
Acting (*abhinaya*) is the imitation of the conditions of characters such as Rāma and Yudhiṣṭhira by actors through means such as gestures (*aṅga*).
He states the divisions of drama (*rūpaka*):
"The drama (*nāṭaka*), then the play (*prakaraṇa*), the monologue (*bhāṇa*), the performance (*vyāyoga*), the mixed drama (*samavakāra*), and the farce (*ḍima*)."
The *īhāmṛga*, *aṅka*, *vīthī*, and *prahasana*—these are the ten types of dramatic compositions (*rūpaka*).
Furthermore:
the *nāṭikā*, the *troṭaka*, the *goṣṭhī*, the *saṭṭaka*, the *nāṭyarāsaka*, the *prasthāna*, the *ullāpyakāvya*, the *preṅkhaṇa*, and likewise the *rāsaka*. (Viśvavidyā 6.4)
Saṃlāpaka, Śrīgadita, Śilpaka, Vilāsikā, Durmallikā, Prakaraṇī, Hallīśa, and Bhāṇikā. (VisSd 6.5)
The wise have declared there to be eighteen minor dramatic forms (*uparūpaka*); apart from specific distinctions, the characteristics of all of them are considered to be like those of the *nāṭaka*.
Of all the major forms such as the *prakaraṇa* and others, as well as the minor forms (*uparūpaka*) such as the *nāṭikā* and others.
Among them:
a *nāṭaka* should have a well-known plot and be endowed with the five junctures (*saṃdhi*).
It is endowed with qualities such as grace and majesty, along with various manifestations of power.
The arising of pleasure and pain, uninterrupted by various flavors—
therein, the numbers beginning with five and ending with ten are proclaimed.

A hero (nāyaka) is considered one who belongs to a renowned lineage, who is a royal sage (rājarṣi), who is fierce and noble, and who is powerful; he may be divine, or both divine and non-divine, and is endowed with excellent qualities.
There should be only one predominant sentiment (aṅgin), whether it be the erotic (śṛṅgāra) or the heroic (vīra);
all other sentiments are its subordinates (aṅga), and the marvelous (adbhuta) should be employed in the conclusion (nirvahaṇa).
Four or five principal men engaged in the task [should perform it]; its binding is said to be like the tip of a cow's tail. VisSd 6.11.
"Renowned" (khyāta) refers to a narrative well-known from sources such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*,
for example, the life story of Rāma and so forth.
The junctures (*sandhi*) will be explained [later].
"Endowed with various manifestations" means possessing great companionship.
The arising of pleasure and pain is well-known from the accounts of Rāma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and others.
The royal sages (rājarṣis) include Duṣyanta and others.
The divine ones are Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others. "Divine" (divya) means one who, though divine, possesses the conceit of being a human being.
Just as with Śrī Rāmacandra;

some say that "the digits should be made subtle in sequence like the tip of a cow's tail," while others say: "just as in a cow's tail some hairs are short and some are long, so here some actions are completed in the *mukhasandhi* and some in the *pratimukha*."
"In this same way, there are some [elements] among others as well.

a *goṣṭhī* is adorned by nine or ten common men; it does not employ noble speech and is characterized by the *kauśikī* style of performance.

The mastery of words of world-weariness is known as *vinyāsa*;
the destruction of delusion is *vibodha*, while false proclamation is *sādhvasa*. (VisSd 6.311)
The offering here [of the self] with words of reproach and the affliction of anger, and the presentation of an illustrative example, is called "cessation" (nivṛtti). VisSd 6.312.
They call "conclusion" (saṃhāra) the completion of an action;
there are clear examples of this,
such as Kāmadattā.

Although all of these constitute the fundamental elements of drama (*nāṭaka-prakṛti*), they are to be adopted according to propriety and availability, following the specific requirements stated for the drama.
Furthermore, where even that which has already been mentioned in the drama is taken up again, there its presence is mandatory.
Now, as for the poetic works intended for recitation (*śravya-kāvya*):
That which is to be heard consists merely of what is audible; it is of two kinds: composed of verse and composed of prose.
Regarding that, he speaks of those consisting of verse: "Verse (padya) is that whose words are bound by meter; that which is free from such [binding] is the *muktaka* (isolated verse).
A pair (*yugmaka*) is formed by two [verses], while a *sandānitaka* is held to consist of three. (VisSd 6.314)
A *kalāpaka* is considered to consist of four [verses], and a *kulaka* of five. Among these, an example of a *muktaka* (isolated verse) is as follows, by me:
“That which yogis, intent upon meditation, repeatedly worship for even a moment—the supreme, infinite, imperishable, unborn state of intense bliss;”
"Blessed are those sweet and beautiful young women who, out of curiosity, embrace that Brahman, caress it in a hundred ways, pull at it, and kiss it."
An example of a pair (*yugmaka*) is as follows from my own work: "O beloved, what are you doing with this cheek near your ear?"
O beloved, when one is inclined toward affection, anger is not appropriate in a situation that is not private.
Even as we were thus desirous of speaking to the fawn-eyed one, the sweet humming of bees suddenly arose from the mango tree.
The same applies to other [types] as well.
A *mahākāvya* (great poem) is a composition concerning creation; in it, there is one hero who is a god.
Whether he be a Kṣatriya of noble lineage or one endowed with the qualities of a hero and magnanimous (dhīrodātta),
[the king] may be a monarch descended from a single dynasty or many born of a noble family.
Among the erotic, the heroic, and the peaceful sentiments, one is desired as the primary sentiment (aṅgin),
while all other sentiments serve as its subordinate members (aṅga), as do all the structural junctures (saṃdhi) of the drama.
Whether it be a narrative derived from history or another account centered on virtuous people,
it should consist of four sections, and there should be a single fruit for them all.
At the beginning, there may be a salutation, a benediction, or simply the statement of the subject matter;
in some cases, there is censure of the wicked and the like, as well as the praise of the virtues of the virtuous. (VisSd 6.319)
In this work, there are more than eight cantos, composed of verses in a single meter with other meters appearing at the conclusion; they are neither too short nor too long.
A certain creation consisting of various meters is seen somewhere;
at the end of a creation, there occurs a hint of the narrative of a future creation. (VisSd 6.321)
The twilights, the sun, the moon, night, the onset of darkness, and day;
morning, midday, hunting, mountains, seasons, forests, and oceans.
The sharing of wealth, separation, sages, heaven, purificatory rites, sacrifices,
battle, military expeditions, marriage, mantras, the afterlife, prosperity, and so forth.
These [elements], along with their primary and secondary limbs, should be described here as appropriate,
either by the name of the poet, the meter, the protagonist, or another.
Its name is "Sarga" (Creation) because it tells of the undertaking of creation;

however, the "limbs of the junctures" (*sandhyaṅga*) should be employed here as they may be found. In the rule "at the conclusion with other meters," the plural number is not intended to be restrictive.
"With all their limbs and sub-limbs" refers to such things as water-sports, wrestling, and so forth.

For example—the *Raghuvaṃśa*, *Śiśupālavadha*, *Naiṣadha*, and so forth; or likewise my own works such as the *Rāghavavilāsa* and others. In this [category of] *ārṣa* poetry, however, the sections are called *sargas* and are designated as *ākhyānas*. (VisSd 6.325)
In this great poem—
just like the Mahābhārata—
which was composed in the Prākṛta language, the cantos are designated as "restorations" (āśvāsas).
This may be done in verse, in prose, or in some cases even in mixed verse and prose.
For example—the *Setubandha*; or likewise my own—*Kuvalayāśvacarita*. In this work composed in Apabhraṃśa, the cantos are designated as *kuḍavakas*.
Likewise, there are various types of meters suitable for Apabhraṃśa.
For example—the *Karṇaparākrama*.
Because of the rules governing the primary and secondary forms of speech (*bhāṣā-vibhāṣā*), poetry is composed in cantos (*sarga*);
it consists of verses directed toward a single purpose, yet is devoid of the complete formal junctions (*saṃdhi*) [of epic narrative]. (Viśvadatta 6.328)
For example: *Bhikṣāṭana* and *Āryāvilāsa*.
A *khaṇḍakāvya* (fragmentary poem) follows a single portion of a [longer] poem.
For example—the *Meghadūta* and so forth.
A *kośa*, however, is a collection of verses that are independent of one another. (ViSd 6.329)
That very same [collection], when arranged according to a sequential order (vrajyākrama), becomes exceedingly beautiful;
the arrangement of similar things in one place is called a *vrajyā*,
such as the *Muktāvalī* and other works.
Now, prose compositions (*gadyakāvya*). Among them, prose (*gadya*) is:
"Prose is that which is devoid of the scent of meter (*vṛttagandha*), as well as the *muktaka* and that which has the scent of meter (*vṛttagandhin*). (VisSd 6.330)
There are four types of *cūrṇaka*:
primarily the *utkalikā* and the [other three]; the first is devoid of compounds, while the latter is endowed with metrical portions.
Another [type] is rich in long compounds, while the fourth has few compounds.
An example of the *muktaka* (isolated verse) is: “The teacher in speech, the broad one in chest,” and so forth. An example of the *vṛttagandhi* (verse-like prose) is as follows, by me:
“*Samarakaṇḍūlanibiḍabhuja-daṇḍakuṇḍalīkṛtakodaṇḍaśiñjinīṭaṅkārojjāgaritavairinagara*, etc.
In this passage, “*kuṇḍalīkṛtakodaṇḍa*” is a quarter-verse (*pāda*) of the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and “*samarakaṇḍūla*,” with its first two syllables removed, is also a quarter-verse of that same meter.

An example of *utkalikāprāya* (the state of longing) is from my own work: “O you who have shattered the enemy forces in battle with a shower of arrows discharged from a bow that has been drawn back... and so forth.
An example of *cūrṇaka* (the powder-like style) is as follows: “O ocean of the jewels of virtue! O sole connoisseur of the world!”
"O Madana of the passionate women! O Delighter of the people! and so forth.
In this narrative, the flavorful subject matter is composed entirely in prose.
In some places here there may be Āryās, and in others Vaktras or Apavaktras;
at the beginning, there is a salutation in verses and a description of the conduct of the wicked and so forth.
For example—the *Kādambarī* and others.

An *ākhyāyikā* (prose narrative) is like a *kathā*, but it includes a recitation of the poet's own lineage; furthermore, in this form, the deeds of other poets may also be included, and there are verses here and there. (VisSd 6.334)
The division of narrative sections is called an *āśvāsa*, composed in any meter such as *āryā*, *vaktra*, or *apavaktra*. (VisSd 6.335)
The indication of a future event under the guise of something else occurs at the beginning of a narrative,
as in the *Harṣacarita* and similar works.
However, it is observed that there is no fixed rule even in that case, because such indications are also uttered by others [in those works].
Based on the statement of Daṇḍin Ācārya, some say that "the narrative (ākhyāyikā) must be composed by the hero alone"; however, that is incorrect,
because stories such as the ākhyāna are not mentioned separately since they are included within the categories of *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*.
As Daṇḍin himself has stated: "The remaining types of narrative will be included within these very [categories].
An example of these is the *Pañcatantra* and similar works.
Now, regarding those consisting of both prose and verse:
"A poem (*kāvyam*) composed of both prose and verse is designated as *campū*. (VisSd 6.336)
For example—the *Deśarājacarita*.
A panegyric (*viruda*) consisting of both prose and verse is called a royal eulogy;
for example—the *Virudamaṇimālā*.
But the *karambhaka* [hell] is fashioned with various kinds of speech.
Just as my *Praśastiratnāvalī* consists of sixteen languages,
so too other varieties have not been defined separately, because they are well-known merely by their enumeration and do not exceed the varieties already mentioned.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "The Description of Dramatic and Lyric Poetry.
In this seventh chapter, first of all, the sequence of the presence of defects (*doṣa*), merits (*guṇa*), styles (*rīti*), and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) in poetry is demonstrated.
Now, in response to the inquiry "What are they?", he states the nature of the defects (doṣas) which follow the order of their enumeration:
"The defects are those things that detract from the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
The meaning of this has already been clarified previously.
He states their specific divisions:

"Furthermore, they are considered to be fivefold, as they occur in the word (*pada*), its constituent part (*tadaṃśa*), the sentence (*vākya*), the meaning (*artha*), and also in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (VisSd 7.1)
Harshness, the three kinds of vulgarity, the use of inappropriate meanings, vulgarity, unintelligibility, ambiguity, inelegance, and tautology; (VisDh 7.2)
Inexpressiveness, obscurity, the production of a contradictory cognition,
and the state of having an undiscerned predicate-part belong to words and sentences.
Certain defects may occur even within a word-part or in a subsequent word: namely, meaninglessness, lack of semantic connection, and corruption of grammatical form. (VisSd 7.4)
*Duḥśravatva* (unpleasantness to hear) consists in causing pain to the ears due to harsh phonemes, as for example:
“When will that slender-limbed woman come under the sway of the bodiless god [of love]? (*kārttarthyaṃ yātu tanvaṅgī kadānaṅgavaśaṃvadā*).
Inappropriateness (*aślīlatva*) is of three kinds, owing to its suggestive power of shame, disgust, or inauspiciousness.
The examples follow in order:
“O King, you who are satisfied with the conquest of your enemies...”
"Your means of accomplishment is very great";
"O slender one, the wind then slowly spread at your destruction.
In these instances, the words *sādhana*, *vāyu*, and *vināśa* are indecorous (*aślīla*).

"Heroes attain immortality in the sacrifice of battle, being like sacrificial animals. Here, the state of being a "sacrificial animal" (*paśutva*) reveals cowardice; thus, there is the fault of *anucitārthatva* (inappropriateness of meaning).
Similarly, *aprayuktatva* (unconventionality) is the state of not being employed by poets, even though it is well-known [in general usage].
For example: "The lotus shines in the lake."
In this context, the word *padma* is masculine. Vulgarity is illustrated as follows: "Your hip steals my mind."
In this context, the word *kaṭi* is vulgar (*grāmya*).
"Unconventionality" (*apratītatva*) refers to being known only in a restricted sense;
for example:
“With his latent tendencies shattered by yoga.”

In this context, within the Yogaśāstra itself, the word *āśaya* has the meaning of *vāsanā* (latent impression). Regarding the phrase, "Having placed the venerable lineage of teachers upon your ear, show compassion," there is a doubt as to whether the word *vandyām* means "one who has been made captive" (*bandībhūtāyām*) or "one who is to be revered" (*vandanīyām*).

Non-literalness (*anyarthatvam*) is the manifestation of a secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) caused by incapacity, due to the absence of either conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
For example:
"O fair-faced one, you have placed your foot upon the lotus; your face has been placed upon his eye."

In this instance, the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) is the state of being conquered by a kick of the foot. The fault of "meaninglessness" (*nihatārthatva*) occurs when a word with two meanings is employed in a sense that is not well-known;
for example:
“He spread the sky with the Yamunā as his *śambara*.
The word *śambara* is well known to mean a demon (*daitya*), but here it has its primary sense [of “water”] suppressed.
"In *gīteṣu karṇam ādatte*," here the root *dā*- preceded by the prefix *ā-* is not expressive of the sense of "giving. Or, for example:

"In the phrase, ‘When you, the Victor, have arrived, even the night shrouded in darkness [is as if it were day],’ the word *dinam* (day) is non-expressive (*avācaka*) with respect to the sense of ‘being full of light. Here, the difficulty (*kliṣṭatva*) consists in the delayed comprehension of the intended meaning, as for example:"
“Clear are the waters, the birthplace of the lotus, the abode of Lakṣmī, who is born from the ocean of milk.
Here, *kṣīrodajā* refers to Lakṣmī; her *vasatiḥ* is the lotus; and the *janmabhūḥ* (birthplace) of that [lotus] are the waters.
“[May the Lord of Bhavānī be for our prosperity].”
Here, the word *bhavānīśa* (Lord of Bhavānī) produces a contradictory cognition because it suggests another husband for Bhavānī.
The state of being subordinate (*guṇībhūtatva*) due to the absence of reflection upon the predicate is "the flaw of an unreflected predicate" (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśatva*).
For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"In these arms, which have grown vainly swollen for the sake of plundering the petty village of heaven—what [use are they]?
Here, "vainness" (*vṛthātva*) is the predicate (*vidheya*); however, because it is subordinated within the compound, it results in the perception of it as a mere restatement (*anuvādya*).
Or for example:
"Even the *rākṣasas* are unable to stand before my younger brother Rāma.
Here, it should have been stated as "Rāma's" (*rāmasya*).
Or as in:
"Of those who rule the earth unto the ocean.
Here, it should have been stated as "unto the ocean" (*āsamudram*).
Or for example:
“O fair-browed one, wherever your sidelong glance falls, it is like the sixth arrow of the five-arrowed god.”
In this context, it should be understood as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as if it were the sixth [instance].
Or, for example:
"O Lord, not being released by you..."

In the phrase "Even for a moment she was not released before," since the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), it is more appropriate that [the state of being unreleased] is indeed the predicate (*vidheya*).
As they say:
“That in which the injunction is subordinate and the negation is primary,
where the negative particle (nañ) is connected with the action, is called prasajya-pratiṣedha.”
For example:
"This is a fresh rain-cloud, not a haughty night-stalker.

However, in the aforementioned examples, when there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is subordinate, the negation is understood as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and thus it is not perceived as the primary thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
As they say:
"Where the injunction is primary and the negation is secondary,
that should be understood as a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation)."
Wherein there is a negative particle with the following word.
Therefore—“He protected himself without fear; he practiced dharma without being afflicted;
he acquired wealth without greed; and he experienced happiness without attachment.”

In this case, since the concealment of one's own self and so forth is to be enjoined by restating fearlessness and other qualities, it is appropriate that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), thereby becoming subordinate.

If it is argued: "But surely, just as in the cases of 'a Brāhmaṇa who does not eat at a funeral feast' (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*) and 'the king’s wives who do not look upon the sun' (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), here too in the phrase 'not liberated' (*amuktā*), there must be a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)," we reply:

No. Even here, only if the negative particle were connected with the verbal action in the form of eating and so forth could it be said that it constitutes a simple negation. [Since it is not so connected here, it is an exclusion.]

And it is not so; for the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected only with the agential portion (*kartṛ-aṃśa*), which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the primary element whose sense is that of eating.
As they say:
"Since the agent is understood as one who is habitually engaged in eating at a *śrāddha* feast..."
But that is not merely a matter of food, according to the injunctions of the Kartrī-nirvāṇa.
Thus,

in the case of "amuktā," however, because it is connected only with the verb, it is indeed a fault. Furthermore, these faults such as *kliṣṭatva* (obscuration) and so forth are word-faults occurring specifically within compounds.
An example of harshness in a sentence is as follows:
"Blinded by the agony of passion, when shall I attain fulfillment in separation from you?"
A poet who applies himself to one purpose for the sake of another swallows up what he has already vomited.
In this case, there is indecorousness (*aślīlatā*) characterized by disgust (*jugupsā*):
"The body is adorned with curved [limbs] possessing the redness of rising lotuses."
In this context, the redness of the *kalala* [embryonic stage] is the ruby (*padmarāga*),
and "crooked" refers to those who are perverse;
thus, there is an intentional meaning (*neyārthatā*).

“Upon beholding the beauty of Dhammilla’s hair, whose locks are as lovely as those of a young fawn, whose mind would not take pleasure, given his lack of prior experience with such a novel arrangement?”
In this case, the connection— “Whose mind does not become agitated upon seeing the beauty of Dhammilla?”— is *kliṣṭa* (defective).

In the verse, “This very fact that there are enemies is indeed an insult to me,” the intention is to present the insult (*nyakkāra*) as the predicate (*vidheya*), such that it is understood as “this [fact] is itself the insult.”
And that [meaning] is rendered subordinate by the inversion of the word-order;
since the order of the two words is reversed, it is a defect of the sentence:
"O fair-browed one, he who has arrived gladdens your eyes."

In such passages as these, according to the maxim "there is a constant connection between *yat* and *tat*," the words *idam*, *etad*, and so forth— which are presented as having the same referent as the word *tat* in order to provide the necessary completion for the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the word *yat* introduced at the beginning— are logically intended to be the predicate (*vidheya*).
However, in this particular case, because they stand in close proximity to the word *yat*, they produce the cognition of being the subject of reference (*anuvādya*).
Even the word *tat* (that), when situated in proximity to the word *yat* (which), possesses merely the function of referring to what is already well-known;
for example:
"O fair-browed one, he who brings joy to your eyes—he has arrived."
However, those [words] that stand separated by the word *yat* convey a state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*),
as in:
"He who has now arrived gladdens your eyes."

The same applies even when words such as "this" (*idam*) and so forth are employed. Furthermore, where it is possible for either of the two— *yad* or *tad*— to convey the intended meaning, there is no deficiency, because the cognition of a complete sense (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) arises even from the employment of only one of them.
For instance, when the word *yat* is employed as part of a subsequent clause, by virtue of its inherent capacity, the word *tat* functions as its correlative in the preceding clause;
for example:
"The self knows whatever is evil."

Likewise, in such passages as: “When all the mountains, having imagined themselves to be the calf, [milked] the radiant jewels and great medicinal herbs from Meru, which stood as the skilled milker”— in these cases as well,

when the word *tat* has as its referent that which is under discussion (*prakrānta*), that which is well-known (*prasiddha*), or that which has been previously experienced (*anubhūta*), it serves as the correlative for the meaning of the word *yat*.
For example, in sequence:
"Having slain Vālin, that hero installed Sugrīva in his long-desired position, just as a grammatical substitute (ādeśa) takes the place of a verbal root (dhātu)."
“May he whose crest is the digit of the moon grant you identity with him”; “I meditate upon her whose face is as beautiful as the moon in my heart.

Even in cases where pronouns such as *idam* (this) and others stand near a relative pronoun (*yat*) yet possess different genders and case-endings, there is still a state of complete syntactic expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvam*).
For example, in sequence:
"This deer-eyed woman shines, she who is the ornament of the world," and "The moon shines; by it, the wives of travelers are consumed."
In some cases, there is comprehension through implication even when both [the agent and the object] are not explicitly mentioned, as for example:
"Do not grieve, O Māyā; there is no one who can subdue my Māra."
"In the house of Nanda, there is a certain boy of wondrous prowess."
In this context, it is understood that "whoever exists here shall be the one to relieve your burden.
Regarding the statement, "Who indeed will take away whatever sorrow of separation I have?"— it should not be said that the single word *yat* (who/which) is syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).
For instance: by the phrase "whatever" (yadyat), it is intended that an object existing in some form is the universal essence;
there is a reference to such an object by means of the word "that" (tat).
In this way, the examples occurring within other sentences should also be understood.
An example of harshness (*duḥśravatva*) in a word-part (*padāṃśa*) is as follows:
"tadraccha siddhyai kuru devakāryam" and "dhātumattāṃ girirdhatte."

In this instance, the word *matta* is used in the sense of "intoxicated" (*kṣība*). In the phrase, “Is Mahāsena described as one whose [enemy] Tāraka is to be conquered (*vijeya*)?”, the suffix *-ya* (a *kṛtya* suffix) in the word *vijeya* is non-expressive (*avācaka*) in the sense of the suffix *-ta* (*ktapratyaya*).
“*pāṇiḥ pallavapelavaḥ*” (*a hand as delicate as a sprout*). The first syllable of the word *pelava* is indecorous (*aślīla*). “In battle, the heroes slain have become arrows in their speech.”

In this case, if the word *vacaḥ* (speech) were to signify the word *gīḥ* (song), it would constitute the fault of *neyārthatva* (forced interpretation). Likewise, in that same verse, if the reading *śara* (arrow) were substituted for *bāṇa* (arrow),
both words would be incapable of substitution (*aparivṛttisaha*).
In cases such as *jaladhi* (ocean), the latter member [of the compound] is defective;
in cases such as *vāḍavānala* (submarine fire), it is the former member.
In this way, other defects of word-parts should also be understood according to their respective occurrences.
Furthermore, the three defects beginning with meaninglessness (nirarthakatva) occur only in relation to individual words; their occurrence in the poetic illustration (lakṣya) is as follows, in order:
"O proud woman, abandon your pride! (muñca mānaṃ hi mānini).
For here, the word *hi* serves solely the purpose of completing the meter.

In the phrase "The slender-waisted one strikes the bower" (*kuñjaṃ hanti kṛśodarī*), although the verb *hanti* is listed as having the sense of "going," it is not capable of that meaning in this context.
“The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva struck the chest of the Three-eyed One with his two arms, which resembled a slab of gold.

By the force of the grammatical rules— “āṅo yamahanaḥ” and “svāṅgakarmakācca”— the middle voice (ātmanepada) is restricted to the verb *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* when its object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*).
But here, since that [rule] has been transgressed due to a deficiency in the grammatical definition, there is a lapse of refinement (*cyutasaṃskāratva*).
Now, one might object: "In this case, the word *ājaghne* is not defective in itself, but only in relation to another word; therefore, is this not a fault of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*)?"

Not so; for while it is established that merits, defects, and ornaments reside in both word and meaning—since their presence or absence follows the presence or absence of those two—the reason here is different.

In this case, the defect follows the presence or absence of the single word "ājaghne" alone, because it remains exactly as it is even when other words are substituted. Therefore, it is indeed a defect of the word.
Just as in this case there is no fault of the word even when the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is replaced,
so too there is no fault of a word-part (*padāṃśa*) regarding the verbal root *han*;
thus, in the example "padmaḥ," it should be understood that the ungrammatical usage resides in the word itself.

In this way, even when there is a loss of the characteristics of grammar such as those of the *prākṛta* dialects and so forth, one should infer the fault of "corrupted refinement" (*cyutasaṃskāratva*).
However, in this context, the total absence of usage for words constitutes "incapacity" (*asamarthatva*),
whereas infrequent usage constitutes "obscured meaning" (*nihatārthatva*).
*Nihatārthatva* (redundancy) pertains to words that have multiple meanings. *Apratītatva* (unintelligibility), however, is the absence of universal usage even for a word that has a single meaning.
*Aprayuktatva* (non-usage) pertains to words that have a single meaning.
Incapacity pertains to words that have multiple meanings.
For instance, even verbs such as *han* (to kill) are recorded as having the sense of "going" when they lack their primary capacity;
similarly, verbs such as *div* (to play) are used in the sense of "shining" and the like when they lack their primary capacity.
"Not so" constitutes a mutual contradiction.
Thus, the faults of sentences belonging to the same class as the faults of words have been stated; now, those belonging to a different class are being stated.
“Contrariety of syllables, the loss of the visarga that was intended, the presence of redundant or deficient words, and the violation of the meter; // VisSd_7.5 //"
The loss of excellence in the falling [of the word], harshness and indecorousness at the juncture,
the occurrence of a single word across two halves of a verse, and the resumption of what has already been concluded. (VisSd 7.6)
The absence of a perceived connection, lack of sequence, incomprehensibility, lack of purpose for another, non-expression of the literal meaning, and likewise broken uniformity; VisDh_7.7.
Abandonment, misplaced application, the dropping of words or compounds, confusion, and redundancy are defects that pertain solely to the sentence. (VisSd 7.8)
Incompatibility (*pratikūlatva*) refers to the discordance between colors and tastes.
As in my own verse:

The failure to maintain the focus on the principal subject (*aṅgin*) occurs, for example, in the fourth act of the *Ratnāvalī*, where Sāgarikā is forgotten upon the arrival of Bābhravya.

The mention of the irrelevant (*anaṅga*) occurs, for example, in the *Karpūramañjarī*, where the King and the Heroine disregard the description of spring composed by themselves and instead praise that described by the bard.
Excessive elaboration of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is as follows: for instance, the amorous dalliances of celestial nymphs and the like in the *Kirātārjunīya*.
Furthermore, there are characters (*prakṛti*) who are divine, non-divine, or both divine and non-divine;
and these possess the qualities of the "noble and firm" (*dhīrodātta*) and so forth.
These [characters] also possess superior, inferior, and middling qualities.
Among them, the defect known as *prakṛtiviparyaya* (contradiction of nature) occurs when one describes a character in a manner that does not correspond to his actual state.
For example, the slaying of Vālin by Rāma—who is *dhīrodātta* (noble and steadfast)—under the pretext of being *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty).

Or, for example, in the *Kumārasambhava*, there is the description of the erotic sentiment (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) between the two supreme deities, Pārvatī and Parameśvara. Some say, "This description of the union of the parents is utterly improper. Another form of impropriety is the description of place, time, and so forth, in a manner contrary to reality.
For if that were the case, it would be impossible to attract the disciples by means of the poetic work, because of the appearance of its unreality.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of defects existing separately from these [figures of speech].

It is because of the faults already mentioned. To explain: in the case of *upamā* (simile), there is the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatva*) when there is a lack of similarity or impossibility, or when the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is deficient or excessive in terms of genus (*jāti*) or measure (*pramāṇa*). In the case of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) and the substantiation of a matter imagined (*utprekṣita*), it is likewise inappropriate. These occur respectively, as follows: [Example for simile: The moon is like a lotus, and the lotus is like the moon. [Example for arthāntaranyāsa: The mountain is like a cloud, and the cloud is like a mountain. [Example for utprekṣā: He is like a lion, and the lion is like him. In these cases, the intended meaning is not properly established due to the aforementioned defects. Thus, the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" arises in sequence.
“I am stringing the moon of poetry, with its far-reaching rays of meaning.
“Your arrows fall like streams of blazing water.
“That king is as reckless in battle as a caṇḍāla.”
“The orb of the moon shines like a fragment of a potsherd.
“This peacock shines like Hara, with its neck blue.
“Your breasts are equal to mountains.”
“He who protects the darkness hidden in caves as if it were afraid of the day—
surely those of lofty spirit feel an exceeding sense of ‘mine’ even toward a lowly being who has come for refuge.”

In such cases as these, it is entirely inappropriate to justify the appearance of an imagined object as having its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), precisely because that object lacks actual existence.
Furthermore, the defect of *aprayuktatva* (non-usage) occurs when a *yamaka* (rhyme) is employed across three quarters of a verse, as for example: [Example omitted per instructions]
“At nightfall, that beautiful woman comes together with her affectionate kinsmen to the bower-mansion.”
In the case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), when the word *yathā* functions as the concluding marker of the fancy, it constitutes a lack of expressive power (*avācakatva*). For example:
"This king protects the earth like Dharma incarnate."
Thus, in the case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), there is the defect of "discordant phonemes" (*pratikūlavarṇatva*) when it contradicts the poetic style (*vṛtti*).
For example: "ovaṭṭai ullaṭṭai—"
In such cases as these,

and in the case of simile (*upamā*), when the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is either redundant or deficient, there is respectively the fault of "redundant word" (*adhikapadatva*) and "deficient word" (*nyūnapadatva*).
Examples in order:
“Śambhu, whose splendor is white like snow, shines with the light of his eye,
like an autumnal cloud accompanied by lightning, appearing as if covered by a fragment of a dark blue water-bearing cloud.”
In this case, because the Lord’s state of having a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭha*) is not established, the fourth quarter is redundant:
“Embraced by Kamalā, wearing a radiant pearl necklace, and the enemy of Mura, he shines like a dark cloud adorned with lightning.”
In this context, the presence of a defect in the simile (*upamāna*) must be stated.

In this very [category], there is "break in the sequence" (*bhagnaprakrama*) regarding the difference in gender and number between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), as well as the difference in tense, person, mood, and so forth.
Examples follow in order:
“Like the pure moon itself,” “like white moonlight is their fame,” and “there was an indescribable splendor as they two proceeded in their spotless attire.”
Like the sky and the moon when freed from mist at the time of a sacrifice.
In this case, the beauty of the variegated moon was not merely present at that time;
rather, it exists at all times:
"O slender one, you shine like a creeper."
“Here the creeper shines, but you shine even more.
“May your son live long, like the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.”
In this case, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya is indeed alive;
however, this is certainly not something to be enjoined by the word "jīvatu" (let him live).
But here, where there is no alteration of the common property despite a difference in gender or number, there is no fault.
Examples in order:
"The face shines like the moon.
"His appearance, possessing sweetness, is unlike that of other women."
They assumed a supreme beauty, as if they were her own graceful charms.

In the previous examples, because the connection of either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*) with the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is established [only implicitly], there is a clear failure to carry through the intended meaning. Likewise, in the case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), futility constitutes the fault of lack of significance (*apuṣṭārthatva*).
For example: "anaṇuraṇanmaṇimekhalamaviralaśiñjānamañjumañjīram... [etc.]
The red-footed partridge,
as it wanders about, produces groundless anxiety.

Thus, in the case of *samāsokti* (condensed expression), although the meaning of the other [the subject] is understood through the power of common attributes (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇa*), its explicit mention by word is redundant. In the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), since the contextual meaning (*prastutārtha*) is apprehended through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) alone, the verbal expression of that same meaning constitutes a tautology. Examples in order: [Example of *samāsokti*: "The lotus-stalk has become thin; the moonlight is pale; the night has grown long; and the body of the young woman is emaciated. Alas! Love, having become a single-minded devotee of the God of Death, has indeed become a great physician for the world. [Example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*: "O King, you who are like a lion, having torn apart the elephant-like enemy with your sharp claws, you now sport upon the mountain of his chest, which is white with the ichor of rut in the form of his blood. In the first example, the description of the lotus-stalk and so forth allows the reader to infer the state of the woman through common attributes; to then state her condition explicitly is redundant. In the second, the description of the king's prowess suggests his identity as a lion through implication; to name him "lion-like" directly is likewise redundant.
“The courtesan of the sky banished the sun from his dwelling, even though he possessed a body that was lovely to the eyes and provided comfort by dispelling heat, for he was now devoid of wealth.”
In this context, by the mere phrase "the western direction," her status as a courtesan is understood.
"When birds are summoned, even a mosquito is not kept away from the front; whether situated in the middle or at the head, a glass trinket assumes the rank of jewels.
Even a firefly does not tremble to move among the luminous bodies. Fie upon such commonality, which—like a mindless master who has failed to discern the inner truth—is devoid of discrimination!"

In this case, the designation of the Lord as "insentient" (acetasaḥ) is improper. Thus, in the instance of alliteration (anuprāsa), the absence of established usage constitutes a contradiction with what is well-known (khyātaviruddhatva).
For example:
The wielder of the discus bestowed upon that king the status of being presided over by the discus, the lineage of the lineage-shatterer, and the bull, for he whose banner is the bull.
And regarding those defects mentioned above, he states that in certain cases they are not defects and in others they are merits:

"When the speaker is joined with anger, or when the subject matter is highly agitated, or in the case of the Furious (raudra) and other such rasas, extreme harshness of sound becomes a merit. (VisSd 7.16)

And in these cases, because they consist of the nature of attachment (*āsvāda*) and [consequently] poison, their designation as "qualities" (*guṇa*) is merely figurative, since they assist through the excellence of the primary [flavor].
This is illustrated in sequence as follows:

“Cruelly piercing the heart of me—who am emaciated by separation from her and whose life-breaths are gasping in my throat—with arrows sharpened by the most intense passion, the pitiless and cruel five-arrowed one (Kāma) fills it completely.”
May he, who was once made terrifying by the mass of flames from the fire of his fierce eye, now remain with his entire being subject to the compassion of Śambhu for all living beings.
In this context, the speaker is angry regarding the erotic sentiment:

"May the *tāṇḍava* dance of Śambhu bestow auspiciousness upon you—[the dance] which, under the guise of the spray of water tossed up by the mass of restless waves of the celestial river as it resounds while being violently shaken from his head; which forcibly casts the stars, marked like constellations, into the sky; and which causes the fragments of the cosmic egg to whirl about through the force of the wind arising from the momentum of the rotation of his staff-like upraised legs."
In this context, a bold *tāṇḍava* dance should be expressed.
These two verses are my own. Even if they are disregarded as being unsuited to sentiments such as the Furious (*raudra*), their extreme harshness to the ear is actually a great merit here.
For example:
"Having cut again and again [the flesh] from the skin... and so forth.
Here, the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) is the loathsome (bībhatsa).
Furthermore, in contexts such as the beginning of a love-making or a social gathering, the use of indecorous words is likewise considered a merit.
For example: [text follows].
“When the hand has entered the narrow space and stirred within, the male organ, approaching,
shines forth with its means of accomplishment.”

For in this context of a gathering at the commencement of amorous play, the established rule of the *Kāmaśāstra* states: "One should dismiss a female companion by means of offering betel-leaf, and one should hint at secret matters through words with double meanings.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it should be understood that this applies to storytelling for tranquility (*śama-kathā*) and other such occasions.
In cases such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the faults of "meaninglessness" (*nihatārtha*) and "unconventional usage" (*aprayukta*) may not be considered defects.

For example: "Falling [into the water], one bows down to the waters of the celestial river—which split the mountains, which are purifying, victorious, highly esteemed, and deep—just like Hari, just like Hari, just like Hari."
In the case of Indra, the word *pavitra* has its primary meaning suppressed;
in the case of a lion, the word *mataṅga* is not used in the sense of an elephant.
Excellence (*guṇa*) would consist in the speaker and the expressed object being uncontradicted and possessed of knowledge.
For example: “They declare you to be primordial nature (prakṛti), which acts for the sake of the Puruṣa;
they know you alone to be the Puruṣa, the witness who remains indifferent.”
Or, even in the case of self-reflection (*svayam-parāmarśa*), the fact that [the meaning] is not immediately apparent (*apratītatvam*) is considered a merit;
as in: “He who was joined with the digits for the increase of the darkness, and was diminished by them for their destruction.”
I cultivate that moon of the self, which is pure and rests upon the supportless state.
And the state has been described once again.
When that which has been prescribed is restated, in cases of despondency, wonder, anger, dejection, as well as in the *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), compassion, and conciliation; VisSd 7.19.

In the case of *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is transferred to another), when joy is present, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is indeed a merit (*guṇa*). For example:
“Ruddy the sun rises,” and so forth;
here there is a restatement of what has been enjoined. “Ah! Ah!”
“O friend, my beloved has departed in the spring; he has not yet returned.
Here there is despondency.
“How wonderful, how wonderful! O fair-faced one, how is it that the moon is in the skyless [space]?”
Here there is astonishment [expressed by the thought]: "O fair-browed one, fix your eyes [upon me]. Here there is *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration).
In such passages as “His eyes are indeed his eyes,” there is suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning;
the same applies elsewhere as well.
Likewise, if there is ambiguity, it results in what is known as "disguised praise" (vyājastuti).
An example of this based on the quality alone is as follows:

“O King, now our two dwellings are equal: yours has a vessel of broad gold, while mine has a retinue whose hunger is satisfied; you have a thicket of sporting female elephants, while I have [the same].”
But when the principal grammarian is either the subject matter to be explained or the speaker,
then difficulty or harshness of sound is indeed considered a merit.
For example:

"There is something like *dīdhī* and *vevī*, or like the *iṭ* augment, which is not a recipient of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*; there is something resembling the *kvip* suffix, in the presence of which those two do not occur."
In this case, the meaning is difficult to grasp,
and the speaker is a grammarian; thus,
even though he is the one being instructed in this way.
"In this [sentence], 'I never forgot you, my teacher,' there is the quality of being unpleasant to hear (*duḥśravatva*). A grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) is the intended speaker (*vācya*)."
Thus, even though he is the speaker, vulgarity exists in his low speech. (VisSd 7.21)
It is simply a quality (guṇa), as in my own verse:
"This orb of the moon appears here like a mass of fresh butter."
These people, deluded by their hopes, fall like a stream of milk upon their expectations."

This is the statement of the critic (vidūṣaka). However, the lack of a stated reason (nirhetutā) does not at all constitute a defect in the meaning of a *khyāti* (cognition or description), as for example: "Now, at the time of twilight, the pairs of wheels are being separated."
In the well-known convention of poets, the quality known as "contrariety" (viruddhatā) is recognized.
And those things well-known by poetic convention:
blackness is described for the sky and for sin; whiteness is described for fame, laughter, and glory; and redness for anger and passion.
The lotuses, blue water-lilies, and other flowers found in rivers and oceans spread throughout every body of water;
flocks of birds such as swans disperse across all reservoirs; the moonlight is drunk by the *cakra* birds; and during the rainy season, the swans depart for Lake Mānasa.
The *aśoka* tree blossoms from a kick, the *bakula* from the wine of women’s mouths, necklaces adorn the limbs of youths, and the heart breaks from the torments of separation.

The bowstring is a garland of bees, the bow is [drawn], and the arrows are made of flowers; just as the heart of a young man is pierced by the arrows of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva), so too is it pierced by a woman’s sidelong glance.
The lotus blooms by day, the night-lily blossoms at night;
moonlight appears during the bright fortnight, and peacocks dance amidst the rumbling of clouds; yet there is no fruit upon the aśoka tree.

There would be no jasmine in spring, nor fragrance from the trees of the essence of scent [such as sandalwood] during the flowering and fruiting seasons; other such matters found in the conventions of poets should be inferred in the compositions of great poets.

The examples for these are clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākaras*). In words such as *dhanurjyā* ("bow-string"), the words "bow" (*dhanus*) and so forth are used for the purpose of conveying the state of being strung (*ārūḍhatva*) and the like.
For example: “When heaven and earth were filled with sounds arising from the twanging of the bowstring.
Here, although the meaning is already conveyed by the word *jyā* (bowstring), the inclusion of the word *dhanus* (bow) indicates that the string is dependent upon the bow.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other examples are implied].
"In 'That ear-ornament shines,' the word 'ear' (karṇa) is used here to convey its location on the ear.
Likewise, there are terms such as 'ear-ring' (śravaṇakuṇḍala), 'head-crest' (śiraḥśekhara), and so forth."
Thus, although it is established that the word *mālā* (garland) without any prefix denotes only a flower-garland,
in the phrase "The flower-garland shines upon you," the word *puṣpa* (flower) is used for the purpose of increasing the excellence of the flowers.
Similarly, in the term *muktāhāra* (pearl necklace), the word *muktā* (pearl) indicates that it is not mixed with other gems.
These should be employed as they stand. VisSd 7.26.
Elements such as the bowstring and so forth should be described only when they are situated within a fine poem,
but not those that are not so situated, such as the waist-belt, bracelets, and the like.
When a person is immersed in bliss and so forth, the deficiency of words (nyūnapadatā) may be considered a merit.
For example:

“O giver of honor! ‘No, no!’—she whose breasts were flattened by a tight embrace, from whom horripilation had burst forth, and whose beautiful lower garment was slipping down due to the excess of the essence of thick affection.”
"Is she sleeping, or is she dead? Or has she dissolved into my mind, or merged into it?"—thus she spoke in faint, gasping syllables.
In this case, "pīḍaya" (afflict) is deficient; in some instances, it is neither a fault nor a merit—
it is simply the deficiency of a word.
For example:
"She might remain hidden by her power due to the force of her anger, yet she does not stay angry for long; her heart is moist with affection for me, so she would rise to heaven.
Even the enemies of the gods would not be able to carry her off while she stands before me; and yet, she has become utterly beyond the range of my eyes—what is this play of fate?"
In this context, after the words "it might be that [the intention] is concealed by her power," the phrase "because this is not so" (*naitadyataḥ*) is deficient.

Even though these words are deficient, it is not a merit, because they fail to bring about the excellence of the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called deliberation (*vitarka*), which is suggested by this sentence.

Furthermore, there is no fault, because the cognition of the meaning of the sentence beginning with "tiṣṭhet" (he should stay) clearly manifests through the understanding produced by the sentence beginning with "dīrghaṃ na se" (not for long, etc.).
The quality (guṇa) is sometimes an additional syllable (pada). VisSd_7.27.
For example:
"I do not know whether it is because the wicked person acts impulsively toward matters that are beyond even the reach of the mind; but I do know this: he does not touch upon any cruelty."
In this context, in the phrase "not that I do not know," there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

In the second instance, by the word "I know," there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—namely, "it is not that I alone know"—and thus there is a specific aesthetic interruption (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).
The repetition of what has already been concluded is sometimes neither a defect nor a merit.
For example: “anyāstā guṇaratna-” and so forth.
Here, although the sentence is completed by the first half, the sentence of the second half is taken up again.
Thus, it should be understood that when only a qualifier is repeated, the fault is *samāptapunarātta* (resuming what was already finished), and not when an entire different sentence is repeated.
In some cases, being "pregnant" (garbhitatva) is a merit—as for example:

"The earth, with its four boundaries demarcated by the temples of the world-elephants, is being conquered; yet even as we speak, that [conquest] is already accomplished, for behold, our hair stands on end!"
What more need be said? Homage to that Rāma, for whom this wondrous narrative was composed as a gift to the Brahmin, from whom it first arose, and in whom its meaning finds its final rest.

In this context, the sentence beginning with "vadanta eva" (even as they speak) nourishes an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) by entering into another sentence; such is the nature of "falling excellence" (*patatprakarṣatā*). (Viśvavidyā-sadana 7.28)
In some cases, "so be it" (*tatheti*) constitutes a merit (*guṇa*).
For example, in the verse beginning with “*cañcadbhuja-*” and so forth,
the abandonment of verbal ostentation in the fourth quarter is a merit due to the delicacy of its meaning.

In some cases, there is no fault in expressing a transitory emotion by its own name, provided that its composition through the [transitory] effects (anubhāvas) and the determinants (vibhāvas) is not appropriate. (VisSd 7.29)

Where there is no clear comprehension when the [emotion] is presented by way of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*), and where the absence of nourishment provided by the excitants and ensuants is itself appropriate, there is no fault in expressing a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) by its own name. For example: * *yatrānubhāvavibhāvamukhena pratipādane viśadapratītirnāsti, yatra ca vibhāvānubhāvakṛtapuṣṭirāhityamevānuguṇaṃ tatra vyabhicāriṇaḥ svaśabdenoktau na doṣaḥ /* * *yathā—* [Example follows...]

“May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness—she who, at their first union with Hara, was made to cry out by her innate longing, turned back again and again by shame, drawn forward once more by the various words of her female kinswomen; she who, seeing her bridegroom before her, was filled with the essence of trepidation, and whose hair stood on end with thrill as she was embraced by the laughing Śiva.”

In this case, when eagerness (*autsukya*) is presented through its external manifestation (*anubhāva*) in the form of haste (*tvarā*), there is no immediate comprehension of it as being directed toward union (*saṅgama*),
because haste can also arise from fear and other causes; furthermore, the external manifestation of shame (*hrī*), such as turning away [from the beloved], can also arise from anger and other causes.

However, because the full development of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors for fear (*sādhvasa*) and laughter (*hāsya*) would generally be contrary to the primary sentiment (*rasa*) at hand, it is proper to express these by their own specific names.
It is a merit to mention a conflicting transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) as being sublated;
for example: “Where is the improper act of the moon-crested Lord, and where is his lineage? and so forth.

In this context, the suppression of the factors of tranquility— namely reflection, intelligence, apprehension, and fortitude— by means of longing, eagerness, memory, dejection, and anxiety, ultimately brings forth a preponderance of anxiety characterized by the height of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*),
whether through the recollection of one who has caused harm or through speaking of them with equanimity.

There would be no contradiction between two things that have attained the status of being the primary (aṅgin) and the subordinate (aṅga) to one another when they occur in succession—for example, in the verse beginning with "This is that [hero] who excels in taste... and so forth.

Here, although the erotic sentiment (*rasa*) has ceased because its substratum (*ālambana*) is gone, the subordinates (*aṅgas*) of that sentiment, being recollected, serve to intensify the grief (*śoka*), as they are conducive to it.

“With sweat-drops falling thickly from passion, with the broad surface of their thighs resounding from the blows of their hands, and with their lips repeatedly bitten by their teeth, the kings were possessed by wrath as if by a most beloved woman.”

In this context, the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is intended to be expressed through the similarity of its physical manifestations (*anubhāva*) with the anger that serves as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) for the hero who is the subject of description: “May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you during his moment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*): one, almost closed like a bud due to the closing of his meditation; the second, languid with the sentiment of enjoyment upon the lotus-face and the weight of the breasts of Pārvatī; and the third, inflamed by the fire of anger at the bow being drawn back to his ear.”
Here, there is love directed toward the Blessed One, nourished by the sentiments of tranquility (*śānta*), erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra*), and fury (*raudra*).

Or, for example: "Seized by the hand, he was cast aside; though violently struck, he took hold of the edge of her garment; grasping her hair, he was pushed away; falling at her feet, he was not even looked upon in her agitation."

May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortune—the fire which, like a lover who has recently committed an offense, was embraced by the young women of Tripura with their lotus-eyes filled with tears as they were cast down.
In this passage, the poet’s love directed toward the Blessed One is the primary element.

Since the Blessed One’s enthusiasm for the destruction of Tripura serves as a nourisher of that love, yet—due to its lack of full development and its failure to reach the status of a *rasa*—it remains a mere *bhāva*, it functions as a subordinate (*aṅga*) to the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment.
And the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment arises through the force of the comparison "like a lover."

Thus, because compassion also functions as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by virtue of its being a state of non-resting, there is no contradiction between the two—compassion and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)—since both serve to intensify the savoring of the emotional state (*bhāva*) consisting of the Lord’s enthusiasm and the love directed toward that object.

Now, one might ask: how can a contradiction be conceived between such a rasa, which is of the nature of a full, dense bliss consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), and another rasa?
In a single sentence, because they appear as distinct placements and lack simultaneity, it is impossible for them to mutually cancel one another;
nor can there be a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin),
since both rest independently in their fullness.
This is well said.

For this very reason, because these other rasas lack independence and repose, and because they consist merely of portions of the full rasa, the ancients designated them by the name *saṃcārī-rasa* (transitory rasas) due to their distinct nature.
However, for the venerable Śrī Caṇḍīdāsa—the foremost among the learned poets and the younger brother of my grandfather—they were designated by the name *khaṇḍa-rasa* (fragmentary rasas).

As they say: "If the subordinate element (aṅga) were to be suppressed, or if the combination (saṃsarga) were the primary element (aṅgin) when another rasa is present, then that [rasa] would not be experienced in its entirety; therefore, it is known as a 'fragmentary rasa' (khaṇḍarasa)."
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: according to the principle stated as "The first [rasa] is [produced] by means of the pathetic, the loathsome, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying," how can there be a coexistence in a single place of the opposing *vīra* (heroic) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasas—as in the following verse:
"On Jānaki’s cheek, which steals the luster of the tusks of a young elephant, her lotus-face bears a profuse and intense thrill of horripilation, blossoming with the smile of Love."
Repeatedly hearing and seeing the tumultuous clamor of the night-stalking army, the lord of the Raghus tightens the knot of his matted locks.
In such cases, there is a coexistence [of conflicting emotions].
To this it is replied: here, indeed, the opposition or non-opposition of rasas is established in three ways;
for some, by virtue of having a single objective basis (*ālambana*).
In some cases, there is contradiction through identity of substratum, and in others, through contiguity.
Among these, there is a contradiction between the heroic (*vīra*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments due to the identity of their objective support (*ālambana*).
Likewise, [there is a contradiction] of union with the comic (*hāsya*), the furious (*raudra*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*);
and of separation (*vipralambha*) with the heroic (*vīra*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the furious (*raudra*), and so forth—
[this being the case] when the objective basis (*ālambana*) is one and the same.
Furthermore, there is conflict between the heroic (*vīra*) and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) due to their having a single substratum;
between the peaceful (*śānta*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) due to their lack of interval and their having a single determinative cause (*vibhāva*);
and this threefold conflict of the heroic exists with respect to the marvelous (*adbhuta*) and the furious (*raudra*).
The erotic sentiment is [contrasted] with the marvelous, and the terrible with the loathsome.
Therefore, because the heroic and the erotic here have different objective bases (*ālambana*), there is no contradiction.

And thus, when the heroic is established as residing in the hero (*nāyaka*) and the terrible as residing in the antagonist (*pratināyaka*), there is no contradiction due to their having different substrates (*āśraya*).

Furthermore, regarding the fact that even Jīmūtavāhana—who was the very embodiment of tranquility—is shown to possess passion for Malayavatī in the *Nāgānanda*, there is no contradiction between the *śānta* (peaceful) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiments there, because the interruption caused by the insertion of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta*)—expressed as "Oh, what singing! Oh, what instrumental music!"—prevents their immediate succession.
This same principle should be understood to apply to other cases as well.

And in cases such as "the face pale and emaciated," since qualities like paleness serve as subordinate elements even in the context of *karuṇa-vipralambha* (love-in-separation characterized by grief), there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, in the case of imitation (*anukāra*), none of these defects constitute a defect at all.
This refers to all [the defects] beginning with "difficult to hear" (*duḥśravatva*),
as for example:
"Someone here prattles, 'I bow to Duścyavana,' and so forth."
In this context, the word *duścyavana* is considered unidiomatic (*aprayukta*).
Regarding other defects as well, the wise should understand their status as non-defects, their status as merits, or their status as being neither, according to propriety. (VisSd 7.32)
The state of being neither [defect nor quality] is the state of being neither a defect nor a quality.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Defects," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
The eighth chapter.
He states the qualities:
"Just as the qualities such as bravery belong to one who has attained the status of being the principal (aṅgin) [in a person], so too are the qualities [of poetry]."
Just as bravery and other such qualities are designated by the term "guṇas" because they serve as causes for the excellence of the self who has attained the status of being the principal (aṅgin),

so too the properties of rasa— which has attained the status of being the principal in poetry— namely its specific characteristics such as sweetness (mādhurya) and the rest, also possess the suitability that makes the composition of words conveying them fit for the designation "poetry.
This is the meaning.
And how these possess the nature of mere aesthetic flavor (rasa) has already been demonstrated. They are threefold: sweetness (mādhurya), vigor (ojas), and clarity (prasāda).
These are the qualities. Among them—
joy consisting of the melting of the mind is called sweetness (*mādhurya*).

As for what has been stated by someone—that "sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the cause of melting (*druti*)"—that is not correct, because melting, being non-different from the joy that constitutes the very nature of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), cannot be its effect. Furthermore, melting consists in the heart of the connoisseur (*sahr̥daya*) becoming as if moistened through the arousal of bliss permeated by the form of love (*rati*) and other such emotions; this occurs by abandoning distractions (*vikṣepa*) brought about by natural stiffness, or by [states] such as passion, anger, excitement, and laughter.
And that [compassion] is, respectively, greater in the erotic, the obstructed, and the peaceful [rasas]. (VisSd 8.2)
The terms "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*) and so forth are indicative;
by this, it should be understood that its presence also exists within the appearances of enjoyment and the like.
[This applies] to those letters at the head of the classes, excluding the final letter of each class and the letters ṭha, ḍa, and ḍha.
And when the *ra* and *ṇa* are light (*laghu*), the phonemes become the cause for the manifestation of that [syllable]. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 8.3)
Non-repetition or minimal repetition, as well as a sweet composition,
is as follows:
“The flickers of her sidelong glance, the auspicious ground for the god of love...”
They repeatedly produce a continuous stream of inner torment within young men.
Or as it is in my own verse:
“Causing the cluster of bees intoxicated with honey to hum in the vine-thicket, making the bodiless god of love embrace his limbs and swell with power,
gently stirring the blossomed lotus and scattering its mass of pollen, the breeze blows drop by drop of nectar in every direction.”
Ojas is said to be the radiance of the mind, which takes the form of its expansion.

However, this *ojas* increases progressively in the heroic (*vīra*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments. Here too, the words "heroic" and so forth are intended as illustrations.
