Nor is this the figure of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of "difference in what is non-different."
For instance, in such examples as “The beauty of her limbs is quite another,” there is an identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the object—such as beauty—as being distinct [from its source].

However, in this case, the state of being beloved and so forth is not identified with the Lord by the cowherd women and others, because at that time, the state of being beloved and so forth is real (*tāttvika*) in the Lord.
Some say: “This ornament is necessarily rooted in the striking effect (*vicchitti*) of another ornament.”

In the example cited, because of the intention to restrict childhood and the other qualities, there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of "dearness" and so forth as being distinct; thus, there is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

Even though that exists, the specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) consisting in the perception of multiplicity due to the difference in perceivers is the cause for the distinct ornament called *ullekha* (multiple description).
In the description of the Śrīkaṇṭha region: "It is a cage of diamonds by those who have sought refuge..."
The passage beginning with "the opening of the sky, as [described] by the Vātikas" is a distinct domain of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*);
and here, there is the application of the figure of speech known as metaphor (*rūpaka*).
However, in reality, scholars maintain that in cases such as "the opening of the sky," this is indeed an instance of the figure of illusion (*bhrāntimān*), and not a metaphor.
This is because superimposition (*āropa*), which is preceded by the cognition of difference, is the very cause of figurative usage (*gauṇī*) and primary metaphors (*mūlarūpaka*) and the like.

As the venerable Vācaspati Miśra stated in his commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*: "Furthermore, when a word denoting one thing is applied to another thing due to the connection with qualities perceived therein, and this is the common understanding between the speaker and the listener, that is figurative (*gauṇa*)."
"And that [superimposition] is preceded by the cognition of difference.
However, in this context, during the description of the region of Śrīkaṇṭha by the Vātikas, the attribution of "a gap in the sky" and so forth is produced solely by error (*bhrānti*).

And in this very same passage, in such instances as "the hermitage grove by the sages, the abode of love by the courtesans," there is the application of the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).

In such instances as "By depth you are the ocean; by majesty you are the mountain," where there is a manifold superimposition (*anekadholllekha*), the differentiation of the objects—such as depth and so forth—is the determining factor.
And here, there is the application of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Furthermore, in expressions such as "Guru in speech, Pṛthu in chest, Arjuna in fame," its scope is distinct from that of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
For here there is a conjunction of hyperbole (atiśayokti) rooted in paronomasia (śleṣa).
Apahnuti (concealment) consists in the denial of the subject at hand and the establishment of something else;
it is of two kinds.
In some cases, there is superimposition preceded by concealment; in others, concealment preceded by superimposition.
The examples follow in order:
“This is not the vault of the sky, but the ocean; these stars are not fragments of fresh foam;
this is not the moon, but the coiled king of serpents; and that is not a dark spot, but the Lord Murāri lying down.”
“Here shines the orb of the cool-rayed moon, kissing the crest of the western mountain, possessing the luster of a mass of foam;
it bears the smoke of the fire of love kindled throughout the night under the guise of its manifest mark.”
This verse is my own.

In this manner—such as in the form of “The ocean, whose body is the sky, shines forth, and therein the stars are the fragments of foam”—the negation of the subject matter (*prakṛta*) is to be understood.
Having somehow illuminated the meaning that is to be concealed, [one should proceed]. (VisSd 10.38)
If one should alter [the meaning] through paronomasia (*śleṣa*) or otherwise, that too is *apahnuti* (concealment).
As an example with paronomasia:
"At the time of the clouds, it is simply not possible to remain without having rained."
"You are longing, O fickle one! No, no, my friend;
the path is slippery."

In this context, regarding the phrase "by not having fallen" (*apatitayā*), having first stated "without a husband," it was subsequently altered to mean "by the absence of falling. An example of *aśleṣa* (non-connection) is as follows:
"What creeper here, its form shaken by the wind, does not meet with a tree?"
"Do you remember, friend, the festival of dalliance with your lover? Indeed, the arrival of the clouds has not been proclaimed."
The distinction is that in *vakrokti* there is a modification of another's statement, whereas here it concerns one's own statement; furthermore,
because even that which is to be concealed is first expressed by means of concealment, this constitutes *vyājokti*.
Furthermore, *niścaya* (ascertainment) is the re-establishment of the subject under discussion after having negated something else.
This is the poetic figure known as *niścaya* (certainty).
"Another" refers to that which is being superimposed.
As in my own verse: "This is a face, not a lotus; these are eyes, not two blue lilies."
O bee, why do you wander with joy near this lovely-eyed one?
Or as it is said:
"This is a necklace of lotus fibers upon my heart, not the lord of serpents; this is a garland of blue lily petals around my neck, not the luster of poison;
this is sandalwood powder, not ashes. O Anaṅga, do not strike me, who am bereft of my beloved, mistaking me for Śiva!"
Why do you run away in anger?
For this is not a doubt that culminates in certainty,
because in that case both doubt and certainty would reside in a single locus;
here, however, there is doubt on the part of the bee and certainty on the part of the hero.

Furthermore, even for bees and the like, there is no doubt regarding a cognition that exceeds [the perception of] a single alternative, because approaching [the object] from nearby would be impossible; therefore,
let it be merely an error.
Granted that there may be an error regarding the bee and so forth; however, in this case, it is not that error which produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*),
but rather the speech of the hero and other characters of that kind— this is what is perceived by those with sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*).

Furthermore, even if the falling of the bee and so forth, or its wandering, were not intended [to be literal], such a statement occurs only in the form of a heroine's coquetry (*cāṭu*). Nor is this a case of "suggestion through metaphor" (*rūpakadhvani*),
because there is no determination of the face as being a lotus.
Nor is this a case of *apahnuti* (concealment), because there is no denial of the subject at hand; therefore, this is a distinct ornament from those mentioned by the ancients.

When a person falls upon a mother-of-pearl shell with the cognition that it is silver, the statement by someone else, "This is a mother-of-pearl shell, not silver," is not an ornament, due to the absence of poetic charm (*vaicitrya*).
The poetic conceit (saṃbhāvanotprekṣā) consists in the imagining of the subject at hand as having the nature of another;
it is considered to be first of two kinds: the expressed (vācyā) and the implied (pratīyamānā).
When terms such as "as if" (*iva*) and so forth are employed, it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy); when they are not employed, it is *parā* (the other).
Furthermore, that which is to be fancied—whether a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*)—belongs to both types.
Then each of those eight [types] is further divided into eight through the conceit of existence and non-existence,
and again because the cause consists of qualities, actions, and essential nature.
They become thirty-two types.
Among these, an illustration for *vācyotprekṣā* (verbal fancy) by way of a mere direction is as follows:
"The thigh of the deer-eyed woman, with its fluttering hem of her garment, shines..."
It was a golden pillar of victory, adorned with banners, like that of the God of Love.
Here, because the term "Victory Pillar" (vijayastambha) has multiple meanings, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on genus (jāti).
"In wisdom, silence; in power, forbearance; in renunciation, the absence of praise—his virtues, because they are followed by further virtues, seem as if they were accompanied by their own offspring."
In this case, the presence of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is a poetic merit (*guṇa*).
[For example: "O Protector of the Faithful, in the waters of the Gaṅgā, there is the sound of your *niḥśāna* [sword]."
He is as if a sinner who has caused an abortion from the womb of a group of women who have bathed in water.

In this case, "he bathes" is an action (*kriyā*). In the example, "The face of the deer-eyed woman shines like another full moon," the word "moon" (*candra*) is a substance-word (*dravyaśabda*) because it denotes a single individual entity.
These [examples] concern the conceit of existence;
as for the conceit of non-existence, it is as follows:
"Alas, her two cheek-plates, having become such [as they are],..."
"Beholding each other as if they were mere shadows, they have both reached such a state of emaciation."
In this case, the phrase "not seeing" (*apaśyanto*) denotes the absence of an action;
other instances are similar.

When the cause (*nimitta*) takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), as for example in "in the waters of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgambhasi*), the sinfulness (*pātakitva*)—which is a quality—is the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that [the waters] are as if bathing.
In the verse beginning with "apaśyantau," the action consisting of the attainment of emaciation is the cause.
The same applies to other cases.
An example of suggested (pratīyamāna) poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is as follows:
“The slender-limbed maiden did not reveal her face because of the pair of her breasts;
she felt ashamed that no place had been given to the virtuous pearl necklace.”
In this instance, because of the absence of words such as "as if" (*iva*), there is a suggested (*pratīyamāna*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as in the phrase "as if out of shame.
Other cases are to be understood similarly.
Now, it was stated during the discussion on *dhvani* that all poetic figures (*alaṅkāras*) can indeed be of the nature of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Now, how is it that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is specifically understood as being suggested (*pratīyamāna*)?
It is said: in the case of suggested *utprekṣā*, such as in the verse beginning with "mahilāsahasra-," the sentence reaches its completion even without an explicit act of fancying.

Here, however, because shame is impossible for breasts, the phrase "as if by shame" is an *utprekṣā* itself; thus, this is the distinction between suggested *utprekṣā* and *utprekṣā* that is directly expressed.

Regarding this, he states the specific distinction among the sixteen varieties of expressed *utprekṣā*: "Among those, the varieties of the expressed [utprekṣā] are further divided; excluding those based on substance (*dravya*), all others are of three kinds, pertaining to the essential nature, the fruit, and the cause. (VisSd 10.43)

Among the varieties of expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*pratīyamāna*) *utprekṣā* mentioned above, regarding those sixteen varieties of the expressed *utprekṣā*, there are twelve varieties pertaining to the three [categories] beginning with genus (*jāti*).
Each of these twelve varieties is further divided into twelve based on whether they reside in the nature (*svarūpa*), the result (*phala*), or the cause (*hetu*), resulting in thirty-six varieties.

Since only the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a substance (*dravya*) is possible, there are four [types]; thus, taken together, there are forty-four varieties.
Here, an example of the fancy regarding the essential nature of a substance is found in the previous illustrations, such as "the victory pillar of Smara" (*smārasya vijayastambhaḥ*).
Expressions such as "as if with offspring" (*saprasavā iva*) and so forth concern the essential nature of a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*).
An example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) is as follows:
“Even Rāvaṇa’s swift arrow, having pierced his heart when discharged by Rāma,
entered the earth as if to announce this pleasant news to the serpents.”
Here, the fruit of entering the earth is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as having the form of an action, namely, "to tell.
An example of a causal poetic fancy (hetūtprekṣā) is as follows:
"This is that very spot where, while searching for you, I dropped one anklet upon the ground."
It appeared as if it had become silent, as if out of the sorrow of separation from your lotus-feet.
Here, the quality of "painful nature" (duḥkharūpa-guṇa) is poetically imagined as the cause;
other cases are similar.
Thus, there are two types of *svarūpagā* [similes] therein, depending on whether the motive (*nimitta*) is expressed or unexpressed.

Among those forty varieties, the sixteen types based on the essential nature (*svarūpa*) become thirty-two varieties through the inclusion or non-inclusion of the ground for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā-nimitta*).
Thus, taken together, there are fifty-six varieties of expressed poetic fancy (*vācyotprekṣā*).

Among these, an example of the inclusion of the ground is the previously cited poetic fancy "as if bathing" (*snātīva*), where the ground—the state of being stained with sin (*pātakitva*)—is explicitly mentioned.
Regarding non-inclusion (*anupādāna*): as in the case of "like another moon," no such excellence of beauty and so forth is included.
However, in the case of cause and effect, there is necessarily an inclusion of the motive (*nimitta*).

For instance, in "as if from the pain of separation" (*viśleṣaduḥkhādiva*), the motive is the state of observing silence; and in "as if to tell" (*ākhyātumiva*), the motive is the entry into the earth. If these two motives were not included, the sentence would be entirely incoherent.
He states the distinction among the sixteen varieties of the implied [meaning]: "And the varieties of the implied meaning each pertain to the fruit and the cause. (ViSd 10.44)

Just as in the example cited, "nanvaṅgyāḥ stanayugmena," where the cause is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as "as if out of shame," in this case [of the *hetūtprekṣā*] as well, the non-mention of the cause is not possible;
for if the particle *iva* and so forth are not employed and the cause is not stated, it would be impossible for the cognizer to ascertain that a poetic imagination has occurred.

Nor does *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) occur here; for when this [type of *utprekṣā*] is based on the identification with another attribute (*dharmāntara-tādātmya*) and lacks the use of words such as *iva*, it is accepted as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), provided there is a connection with a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). For example: "This king is another Indra."
And when the qualification is absent, there is a metaphor, as in: "The king is Indra.
Thus, in this manner, there are thirty-two varieties of suggested *utprekṣā*.
Each of those [types of] utprekṣās regarding the subject at hand is further divided into two according to whether there is an explicit statement or no statement.
As an example of the one with an explicit statement: “The broad [hips] of the deer-eyed woman... and so forth.

An example of this when not explicitly stated is found in my *Prabhāvatī*: "Pradyumna: Indeed, now that the mass of darkness covers the ends of the quarters, the world seems fashioned from heaps of collyrium, filled with powdered musk, spread over with *tamāla* trees, and enveloped in blue silken garments."
In this case, the pervasion of the object by the suggested quality—such as being fashioned by collyrium—is not explicitly stated.
Or, for example:
"Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains down collyrium."

In this [verse], the object (*viṣaya*) of the smearing by darkness—namely, its spreading—is not explicitly mentioned. The falling of collyrium and the descent of darkness [are the objects of comparison].
The grounds for these two poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*) are, respectively, the extreme density of the darkness and its contact with the lower surface in the form of streams.

However, some say: "Even though darkness is not actually the agent of smearing, it is imagined as the agent of smearing, and its spreading is the cause; likewise, the sky is also [imagined] as the agent of the action of raining.
This [figure], arising from another ornament, may possess even greater aesthetic charm. (VisSd 10.45)

Among these, an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) involving concealment (*sāpahnavā*) is as in my own verse: “Under the guise of tears, from the beautiful-eyed woman whose eyes were clouded by the smoke of the sacrificial fire, a flood of the water of loveliness seems to flow away, unable to find a place upon her body.”
An example of a *śleṣa-hetugā* (a cause based on double entendre) is as follows:
“The heap of pearls emerging from the narrow interior of her oyster-like shell— lovely-eyed one—
we know that it has acquired its quality [of luster] from dwelling upon her beautiful, conch-like neck.”

Here, in the quality of being possessed of [auspicious] marks, the word *śleṣa* (conjunction) serves as the cause for the poetic fancy (*hetūtprekṣā*) regarding the dwelling upon the conch-like neck and so forth.
In this instance, the word “*jānīmahe*” (we know/perceive) is the indicator (*vācaka*) of the poetic fancy.
Thus—
Words such as *manye* (I think), *śaṅke* (I suspect), *dhruvam* (certainly), *prāyaḥ* (mostly), and *nūnam* (surely) [indicate poetic fancy].
In some cases, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) beginning with a comparison (*upamā*), as for example:
"Not seeing on the far side of the ocean any clusters of blue lotus petals..."
The rows of forests possess the appearance of moss rising up at every moment due to the thousands of ripples caused by the warbling of birds.
In this instance, because the word *ābhā* functions as a term expressing comparison (*upamā*), there is a simile (*upamā*) at the outset;
however, since the existence of moss on the shore of the ocean is impossible, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting in the arousal of a supposition (*sambhāvanā*) at the conclusion.

This should be understood similarly in descriptions of separation, such as in "acting like armlets with their bracelets... and "the curved side-glance of the deer-eyed one became a blooming blue lotus upon her ear."

In the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (the presence of error), as in the example beginning with "mugdhā dugdhadhiyā," those who are mistaken—the cowherds and others—possess no knowledge at all of the object, such as the moonlight, since its attribution has been created by the poet alone.
Here, however, there is knowledge of the object even on the part of the one performing the conceit; this is the distinction between the two.
In doubt (*saṃdeha*), however, there is a cognition of two alternatives as being of equal status; here, by contrast, one alternative—which is possible yet not established—is predominant.
In poetic hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), once the object of comparison (*viṣayin*) has been presented, its unreality is subsequently perceived.
But here, the distinction is that [the perception occurs] at the very moment of cognition:
"Are the various tree-tops dyed? Is the sky bent down?
Is the earth filled up in its uneven places? Or have the quarters of the horizon been withdrawn by darkness?"

Regarding this, some say that because the state of being overcome by darkness (*timira*) in the trees and so forth is doubted in the form of "coloring" (*rañjana*) and the like, this is the figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt);
but that is not correct, because doubt consists precisely in the flashing forth of multiple alternatives (*koṭi*) with equal strength regarding a single object.

Here, however, there is a difference in the correlates of the pervasion of the trees and so forth, and the flashing forth of "coloring" and the like occurs through the swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) of the act of pervading and so forth.

Others, however, have said: “Because it serves as the locus for a poetic figure (*vicchitti*) consisting of the determination of multiplicity, this variety of doubt is distinct [from ordinary doubt], even though it exceeds [the number of] one side.

That too is incorrect—for *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability) is the cognition of identity with something else on the part of that whose own nature has been swallowed up, and since that exists here clearly, and since it is indicated by the word *nu* just as it is by the word *iva*, it is proper that this should be considered *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) alone.
Enough with this futile fabrication of unseen causes!
When the moon displays the grace of a water-lily petal within its orb, people call it a "hare," but that is not how I view it.
I, however, consider the moon to be one whose body is marked by the scar of a burn from the falling meteor-like glances of young women overcome by the pangs of separation from their lovers.

In this context, even though the word "anyathā" (otherwise) is employed, since the aforementioned form of *sambhāvanā* (poetic probability) is not perceived, this is merely a *vitarka* (speculation); it is not *apahnava-utprekṣā* (concealment-based poetic fancy).

When the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is established as a fact, it is called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). Identification is the apprehension of non-difference between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the former.
Furthermore, because the subject of this *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is indicated as being uncertain, it possesses the character of a "probandum" (*sādhya*);
however, here [in the case of *atiśayokti*], it is perceived precisely as certain, and thus possesses the character of a "proven" (*siddha*).
Moreover, the "swallowing up" (*nigaraṇa*) of the object in *utprekṣā* consists merely in the subordination of the object.
This also occurs here in such cases as "the face is the second moon," as the learned have said:
"Whether the object [of comparison] is not mentioned or even when it is mentioned..."
"By the mere act of subduing, they declare that [the object] has been swallowed."
Thus:
"Even where there is difference, there is non-difference; where there is relation, there is non-relation; and the reversals thereof. (Viṣṇu-siddhi 10.46)
The reversal of the sequence between the effect and the cause is fivefold;
from that [arise] their two reversals: [the fallacy of] difference where there is non-difference, and connection where there is no connection.
That is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). Herein is non-difference where there is difference, as in my own verse:
"How is it that the peacock's plumage shines above, while beneath it rests the crescent of the eighth-day moon?"
"Then a pair of tremulous blue lotuses, below that a sesame flower, and beneath that a sprout."
In this case, there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of the beloved’s mass of hair and so forth with the plumage of a peacock and so forth, through non-difference.
Or, for example: “As if bound by silence due to the pain of separation.
Here, the silence belonging to a sentient being is one thing [and the silence of the object is another].
And because the other is insentient, there is non-difference despite the difference between the two;
thus:
"In his youth, his beloved became possessed of passion along with the lower lip."
Here, "passion" (rāga) refers to the redness of the lower lip,
while "passion" (rāga) refers to the love for the beloved; thus,
there is an identity between the two.
An example of difference within non-difference is as follows:
"The beauty of her limbs is quite another, and the abundance of her fragrance is yet another;
the loveliness of that lotus-petal-eyed woman is truly extraordinary."

An example of "absence of connection where there is a connection" is as follows: "In the creation of this [woman], was the Creator the Moon, the bestower of luster? Or was he Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was it the month of spring, the source of flowers? For how could the ancient sage [Brahmā], dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sensual objects, be capable of fashioning such a heart-stealing form?"
In this case, although there is a connection with the creation by the ancient Prajāpati, there is a lack of connection [between the two].
An example of a connection where there is no connection is as follows:
"If a pair of blue lotuses were attached to the orb of the moon..."
then her beautiful-eyed face may be compared to it.”
In this context, if there is a connection based on a relation brought about by the force of the meaning through a supposition,
the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect occurs in two ways:
when the effect exists prior to the cause, and when both exist simultaneously.
For example, in sequence:
"The hearts of the fawn-eyed women were already agitated with longing;
only afterwards did the beauty of the blossoming *bakula* and mango buds appear."
“Simultaneously, he who moves with the gait of an elephant ascended both his father’s lion-throne and the circle of the earth.”
Here, some say: "The worldly excellence residing in the mass of hair and so forth is determined as being non-worldly (*alaukika*).

[If this were the case], there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the definition for instances such as ‘The beauty of the limbs is something quite other,’ when the mass of hair and so forth is determined by means of [the word] *kalāpa* (cluster/bunch).
This is not so; for even in that case, the beauty of the limbs is determined as being "other" (*anyatvena*).

For instance, in the place where "anyadeva" (something else indeed) occurs, if the reading were "anyadiva" (as if something else), then because the identification (*adhyavasāya*) would not be established as a proven fact, it is accepted as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

In the verse beginning "prageva hariṇākṣīṇām—" (At dawn, for the fawn-eyed women...), although the beauty of the *bakula* trees and so forth actually occurred first, it is identified as occurring later;
therefore, here too, due to the connection with the word "iva," it is a poetic fancy, and so it is elsewhere as well.
When it occurs regarding the objects under discussion or other things, [it is called *arthāntara*]. (VisSd 10.47)

When there is a connection with a single attribute (dharma) among other [objects] that are not the subject at hand, then it is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing). The attribute (*dharma*) takes the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*).
The example:
“Ointments, flowers, and the women who had become angry with their husbands— by that means, the wicks of the lamps awakened for a long time the god of love who had been asleep.”
In this case, because the description of twilight is the subject at hand, there is a connection between the relevant items—the unguents and so forth—and a single act of cognition:

"In whose mind does the softness of her limbs not appear, compared to the hardness of jasmine, the crescent moon, and plantain? Here, since the description of twilight is the topic under discussion, the various items under discussion—such as the ointments and so forth—are connected to a single act of perception: "In whose mind does the softness of her limbs not shine forth, when contrasted with the harshness of jasmine, the crescent moon, and plantain?"
In this instance, there is a connection with a single quality—harshness—among the unstated objects such as the *mālatī* flower and others.
Similarly:
"Charity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, fame and dharma from life."
One should extract the essence from this essenceless body by means of benefiting others.

In this case, there is a connection with a single quality in the form of "crossing over" between the acts of giving and so forth, which function as the objects of the action, and their connection with the single action of "carrying away.
This is called *dīpaka* (the illuminator) when it pertains to both the irrelevant and the relevant.
Now, if a single agent were to perform multiple actions,
the examples follow in sequence:
"Even now, out of arrogance born of his strength, that conqueror of the world continues to oppress the universe as he did before."
Like a virtuous wife, one's innate nature remains perfectly steadfast and follows the person even through different states of existence.
Here, there is a connection through the single action of following after, between the subject matter at hand—a perfectly steady nature—and the subject matter not at hand—a woman:
“When you, the lord of her life, had come from afar, that poor girl was pierced by the arrow of the Mind-born [God of Love].
In your bedchamber, she rises and sleeps; she comes and goes; she laughs and sighs in an instant.”
"This is mine.
Here, there is a connection with multiple actions—such as rising and so forth—belonging to a single heroine.
Furthermore, the threefold nature of qualities and actions, based on their presence at the beginning, middle, and end, has not been specifically defined here.

Since such a variety is possible in a thousand ways everywhere, that [figure] would be *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) when there is a similarity to be understood between two sentences. *Viśvavidyāsadana 10.49*
Even when a single common attribute is described separately,
as for example:
"Blessed are you, O daughter of the Videhas!"
"By her noble qualities, even the King of Niṣadha was drawn away;
what further praise can there be for this moonlight, since it causes even the ocean to tremble?"

In this context, attraction (*samākarṣaṇa*) and subsequent intensification (*uttaralīkaraṇa*) constitute a single function; however, they are indicated by distinct verbal expressions in order to avoid redundancy.
This [function] is also seen in the form of a *mālā* (garland), as for example:
"The sun is indeed stainless, the moon is bright, and the complexion is naturally beautiful."
For Śivagiri is indeed like the brother of Śiva’s laughter, naturally beautiful, just like a virtuous person.
In this context, terms such as *vimala* (pure) and *viśada* (clear) are [implied] by the very sense of the meaning.
By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), for example:
"Only the *cakora* birds are clever in the act of drinking moonlight."
"Without women from Avanti, those of beautiful vision are not clever in the sport of love."
An example (dṛṣṭānta), however, is the reflection of a thing possessing common properties (sadharmā).
The phrase "of that which possesses similarity" (sadharmasya) serves to exclude the figure of speech *prativastūpamā*.
This [figure, *dṛṣṭānta*] is also twofold, by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
The examples follow in order:
“Even when its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even before its fragrance is perceived, a garland of jasmine captivates the eye.”
“When you are seen, the deer-eyed woman’s torment of love falls away;
when the moon fails to rise, the cluster of night-lotuses suffers exhaustion.”
“How can our minds be attached to other beloved women when our affection is fixed solely upon Vasantalekhā?
Does a bee, greedy for the nectar of a blossoming jasmine, ever long for another vine?”
This verse is my own.
Here, because the phrases "manaḥ kuto naḥ" (whence our mind? and "kāṅkṣati vallimanyām" (longs for another creeper) terminate with identical forms, there is indeed a *prativastūpamā* (parallelism).
In this case, however, there is only a similarity between the pouring of streams of honey into the ear and the stealing of the eyes.
But there is no identity of form.
Here, between the statement of the capacity and the statement of the possessor of capacity, there exists the relationship of general and particular, which constitutes *arthāntaranyāsa*;
however, this is not the case for *prativastūpamā* and *dṛṣṭānta*, which is the distinction.
Whether the connection between things is possible or impossible in some cases, that [figure] by which the state of being an original and its reflection is made known is *nidarśanā*. (VisSd 10.51)
Among these, an illustration based on the connection with a possible object is as follows:
“Who here, in this circle of the earth, having tormented people in vain for so long, attains prosperity?
Making [the world] realize this by day, the sun has reached the western mountain.”
In this context, the connection of the sun with the act of making such a meaning known is indeed possible as its speaker,
because it possesses the quality of reaching the western mountain (Asta), which is capable of making such a meaning known.
And that [quality] makes known the relationship of image and reflection between the sun’s journey to the western mountain and the onset of calamity for those who are tormented.
The indication of an impossible thing (*asambhavadvastunidarśanā*), however, is of two kinds: occurring within a single sentence or across multiple sentences.
Among these, that which occurs within a single sentence is, for example:
"The curved cast of her sidelong glance imparts the charm of a garland of blue water-lilies."
Her lower lip possesses the charm of a young sprout, and her face the splendor of the moon, the treasury of arts.

In this context, since it is impossible for one person to experience the graceful gestures (*lalita*) and so forth belonging to Kuvalayamālā and others— such as side-long glances (*kaṭākṣa*) and casting of looks— by thinking "how could another bear the *dharma* (quality) of another?", the [poetic figure] makes known the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) between the side-long glances and Kuvalayamālā, by making one understand a grace and so forth that is similar to the grace of those [others].
Or as it is said:
"O Indra among kings, at your departure,
the gazelle-eyed wives of your enemies were released [from their grief]."
She has the gait of a royal swan with her feet, and the radiance of the moon with her face.
In this case, since the movement of a royal swan is not connected to the two feet, its presence [in them] would be untenable; therefore, a connection between the two is postulated.
And that [connection], being impossible [in reality], suggests a gait like that of a royal swan.
An example occurring across multiple sentences is as follows:
“Whoever desires to achieve through ascetic toil this body which is naturally charming without artifice,
that sage surely intends to cut down a thorn bush with the edge of a blue lotus petal.”

In this case, the connection between the two sentence-meanings indicated by the word *ca* (and) through identity is untenable; therefore, it results in a relationship of "original" (*bimba*) and "reflection" (*pratibimba*), such that the ascetic’s desire to achieve the state of being exhausted by penance is like a desire to cut down a *śamī* creeper with a stream of water from a blue lotus petal.
For example:
“This birth has been rendered fruitless by my desire to obtain the enjoyments of worldly existence; alas!
I have sold a wish-fulfilling gem for the price of a piece of glass.”
In this context, the conclusion is that by greed for worldly enjoyment, one brings about the futility of birth, like selling a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) for the price of glass.
Thus:
"Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?"
"Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean that is so difficult to traverse by means of a mere raft."
In this case, according to my view, the description of the solar dynasty results in the conclusion that it is like crossing the ocean by means of the moon.
And this [type of simile] occurs even when the action belonging to the object of comparison (upameya) is impossible in the standard of comparison (upamāna),
as for example:
“The sweetness experienced by those experts in flavors on the lip of that fawn-eyed woman was tasted [by them] in the juice of the grape.”

In this case, because the quality of sweetness belonging to the subject under discussion—the lower lip—is impossible in grape juice, it results in a comparison (*sāmya*) as in the previous examples. An example of the *mālārūpa* (chain) variety is as follows, by me:
“You cast a parrot into the mouth of a cat; you offer a deer to the fangs of a leopard.”
You abandon the horse, fixing your mind upon the horns of a buffalo amidst the expanse of worldly enjoyments.
In this case, the meaning of the sentence remains incomplete without the implication of the relationship between the original object and its reflection;

whereas in the case of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), the relationship between the original and its reflection is conveyed through the force of the sentence-meaning once that meaning has reached its completion.
Nor is this a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
In that regard, in examples such as "This necklace belongs to the fawn-eyed ones," there is no culmination in similarity; rather,
*vyatireka* (distinction) consists in either the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or its inferiority.
And that [unestablished reason] is of one kind when the reason is stated; when the reason is not stated, it is again threefold.
Since even the fourfold [śleṣa] is understood through similarity by way of word, meaning, and implication, it is twelvefold; thus, including śleṣa as well, there are twenty-four types.
Taken individually, there would be forty-eight types when combined.

Furthermore, the cause for the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) consists of the grounds for superiority residing in the *upameya* and the grounds for inferiority residing in the *upamāna*.
When both of these are stated, it is one [type].

When each [of the four types] is stated individually or collectively as "threefold," and when in these four types the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is conveyed by word, by sense, or by implication— making twelve varieties—
the word "also" (*api*) implies that this occurs even in the absence of *śleṣa* (pun), resulting in twenty-four varieties.

Since there are likewise twenty-four varieties based on the inferiority of the standard of comparison through this same method, the *vyatireka* (contrast) thus comprises forty-eight varieties in total.
The example is:
“Her face is stainless, unlike the moon which is stained.
Here, both causes are stated: the quality of being stainless residing in the object of comparison (the face), and the quality of being stained residing in the standard of comparison (the moon).
Furthermore, because it is expressed by the word "like" (yathā), this is verbal comparison (*śābdam aupamyam*).
In the reading "not comparable to the spotted moon" (*na kalaṅkividhūpamam*), it is implied through meaning (*ārtham*).
However, in the reading "he conquers the spotted moon" (*jayatīnduṃ kalaṅkinam*), since words such as "like" (*iva*) or "equal to" (*tulya*) are absent, it is suggested (*ākṣiptam*).

In this very instance, by omitting the word *akalaṅka* (stainless), there is a failure to state the reason for the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*); by omitting the word *kalaṅkin* (stained), there is a failure to state the reason for the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*);
and by omitting both, there is a failure to state both.
As in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia):
"And though her virtues are exceedingly firm, her virtues are not fragile like lotus fibers.
Here, the suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of *iva* (like), and thus the comparison is verbal (*śābda*).
There is a statement regarding both causes of elevation and degradation. The word "guṇa" (quality) is used in a double sense (*śliṣṭa*).
Other varieties are to be inferred as before.
These are examples of the excellence of the object compared over the standard of comparison.
As for its inferiority, here is merely a direction:
"It is true that the moon, though waning again and again, increases more and more."
Desist, be gracious, O beautiful one;
youth that has once passed does not return.
Herein, there is a superiority of the instability of youth, which serves as the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Therefore, regarding the definition of some who state that "the figure *vyatireka* occurs when the object of comparison exceeds the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or in the reverse case," the claim made by certain others that "the phrase 'or in the reverse case' is redundant" is not withstands critical examination.
For instance, in this context, what is intended to be expressed is precisely the existence or non-existence of excess or deficiency;
and here, the non-existence of youth in relation to the moon is quite evident. Or, let there be some manner of satisfaction regarding this example as it stands.

In such passages as, “The path of the messengers was whitened by the fame of Hanumān and others, and again by my laughter at my enemies,” what is the solution? It has been well said: “Or rather, there is deficiency.
Where, by the force of the sense of conjunction (*saha*), a single word should be expressive of two things: VisSd 10.54.
That is Sahokti (Simultaneity) when it is based upon a *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole).

Here, the *atiśayokti* is also twofold: rooted in the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) [of two things] and consisting in the inversion of the sequence between cause and effect. Furthermore, that which is rooted in identification is also twofold: based on *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) and otherwise.
He provides an example in sequence: "In her youth, her beloved partook of passion along with the lower lip.
Here, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *rāga*.

“Together with the night-lotuses and kadamba flowers, they cause the season to bloom; together with the masses of thick darkness, they dispel one’s fortitude; and together with the clusters of day-lotuses, they cause the heart to close—thus do the rays of the nectar-rayed moon move in every direction.”
"This is mine.
In this case, the distinction between "joy" (*ullāsa*) and the other [emotions] arises solely from the difference in their respective relations,
and not through the use of *śleṣa* (punning).
“Simultaneously with the king, she— her consciousness utterly lost through profound delusion—
descended to the surface of the earth like the flame of a lamp together with a drop of oil.”
And this [type of *sahokti*] can also occur through a garland (*mālā*), as in the example cited: "Together with the *kumuda* and *kadamba* flowers... and so forth; for instance:
"Rāma went to the dense forest together with Lakṣmaṇa."

In such cases, because there is an absence of the basis for hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), this is not a figure of speech. Vinokti is that where, without another thing, something is neither good nor bad. (VisSd 10.55)
"It is not that it is non-good or non-beautiful.

And thus, although the conclusion [of the statement] lies precisely in its being beautiful, nevertheless, by way of the absence of non-beauty, this is the intended meaning of the expression "beautiful": that any non-beauty belonging to something worthy of description is merely a defect arising from proximity to another.
Furthermore, its beauty exists by its very nature, as in: "Without the season of the clouds, the moon attained fullness;
without the heat of summer, the forest grove became lovely."
“Improper and unseemly,” as for example:
“O lady, you have done well by following your beloved who has transcended the world;
for what is the beauty of day without the sun, and what is the night without the moon?”
“Vain was the life of the lotus plant by whom the orb of the moon was not seen;
likewise fruitless was the birth of the moon itself, by whom a lotus plant was not seen in full bloom.”
Here, there is an excellence of aesthetic charm (*cākacakyātiśaya*) through the device of expressing mutual inseparability (*parasparāvinokti*).
Even in the absence of the use of the word "without" (*vinā*), when the sense of "without" is intended, this is indeed *vinokti*.
Likewise, it should be understood that *sahokti* (concomitance) also occurs when the sense of "together" is intended, even in the absence of the use of the word "together" (*saha*).
*Samāsokti* (Abridged Expression) occurs where, through similar actions, effects, or adjectives, the activity of another thing is superimposed upon the subject at hand. *VisDh 10.56*
Here, through a common action, there is the superimposition of the behavior of the unmentioned upon the mentioned.
For example:
"When the garment was shaken off from the breasts of the lotus-eyed one—breasts that possess the grace of golden jars—"
"You alone are blessed, O breeze from the Malaya mountain, who forcibly embraces every limb of this woman."
Here, there is a superimposition of the behavior of a forceful lover upon the wind-carrier (the breeze).
An example based on similarity of gender is as follows:
"What thought of women can there be for a spirited man who has not yet completed his desire for conquest?"
Without having traversed the entire world, the sun does not resort to the twilight.
Here, the treatment of the sun and twilight as the hero and heroine is based merely on their masculine and feminine genders; however,
the similarity of their attributes occurs through both punning (*śliṣṭatayā*) and commonality (*sādhāraṇyena*).
And it is threefold by virtue of containing a simile (*aupamyagarbha*); for example, through the use of *śleṣa* (punning), as in my own verse:
"Beholding before her the eastern quarter, its face blossomed from attachment to passion (*rāga*), with the veil of darkness slipping away upon being touched by the rays of the sun—"
Alas, the moon, its hue as pale as a withered lavalī fruit and its interior deeply turbid,
now resorts to the eastern quarter.
In this instance, there is the punning nature (*śliṣṭatā*) of words such as *mukharāga*.

Indeed, in this very context, if the reading were "timirāśukam" instead of "timirāvṛtim," even though there would be a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) of only one part [of the object], it would still be *samāsokti* (speech by compendium) alone, and not *ekadeśavivarti rūpaka* (metaphor residing in a single part).

For in that case, the relationship between the superimposed (rūpya) and the object of superimposition (rūpaka)—namely, the eye-disease (*timira*) and the cloth (*aṃśuka*)—is one of mutual concealment; because their similarity is so manifest, it rests solely within itself even without depending on the assistance of the other, and thus it is not capable of obstructing the cognition of *samāsokti*. However, where the similarity between the superimposed and the object of superimposition is not manifest, the metaphorical identification of one part would be inconsistent without the metaphorical identification of another part; therefore, even though it is not expressed by words, it necessarily requires the metaphorical identification of another part for its own sake.
In that case, it is indeed a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) based on a partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*).
For example:
“Of him who, in the inner apartments of battle, holds the tip of his sword-blade in his hand...”
"Even the enemy army, though facing toward passion, suddenly turns its back."
In this case, the similarity between the battlefield and the inner apartments is indeed indistinct.

Furthermore, in instances where there is a verbal representation (*rūpaṇa*) of many elements possessing clear similarity, while the similarity of one part is understood through implication (*ārtha*), that is precisely *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor; for the cognition of metaphor, by virtue of its pervasiveness, obscures the cognition of *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning).
If it is argued that there is indeed a clear similarity between the battlefield and the inner apartments due to the ease of movement in both,
this is true;
however, it must depend upon a careful consideration of the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
Indeed, it is not independent,
because— just as the loveliness of the moon-like face and so forth [is relative]— there is no inherent ease of movement for the army and the inner apartments [within it].
This is illustrated by a common example:
“Adorned by the song of bees wandering about her natural fragrance,
the lotus plant blossomed with a smile when the lord of the day arose.”

Here, because of the similarity of the qualifiers beginning with "nisarga" (natural), the cognition of the behavior of a heroine (*nāyikā*) in the lotus plant (*sarojinī*) is caused by the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the quality of "smiling," which belongs to women in general. Without that [superimposition], the cognition of the behavior of a heroine would be impossible through the mere similarity of qualifiers alone. Furthermore, the presence of an implicit comparison (*aupamya*) occurs in three ways:
Because it contains a mixture of simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Among these, as an example of its containing a simile:
"Adorned with the flowers of the luster of her teeth, and beautified by her sprout-like hands..."
The deer-eyed woman was beautifully attired with a mass of hair like a swarm of bees.

Here, because of her exquisite beauty, there is first a compound based on the internal presence of a simile (*upamā*), namely that "the luster of her teeth was like flowers. Immediately thereafter, by resorting to further compounds—such as "filled with flowers resembling the luster of her teeth"—the conventional treatment (*vyavahāra*) of the gazelle-eyed woman as a "creeper" (*latā*) is perceived through the power of these identical adjectives (*samāna-viśeṣaṇa*). An example of the internal presence of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is: "Filled with the honey of loveliness," and so forth.
Regarding the state of being a "conflation" (*saṅkara*), as in the verse beginning with "The flowers of the luster of her teeth" (*dantaprabhāpuṣpa-*), etc.:
in the reading "surrounded" (*parītā*) for the word "well-dressed" (*suveṣā*), since there is no evidence to establish either simile (*upamā*) or metaphor (*rūpaka*), one must resort to conflation;
the specific compound is to be analyzed as before.
The cognition of a creeper arises through the power of a different compound.

And among these, according to those who hold that there is no "partial metaphorical transformation" (*ekadeśavivartin*) in cases of simile or commixture (*saṅkara*), the first and third types constitute *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
However, the second type pertains exclusively to the domain of partial metaphorical transformation (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*).

Upon careful consideration, however, it is appropriate to accept that in the first type [of this figure], there is indeed a *upamā* (simile) occurring through partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartinī*).
Otherwise—[as in the following verse]:
"Autumn, bearing a rainbow upon her pale cloud-breasts, resembling fresh nail-marks..."
While delighting the spotted moon, she increased the heat of the sun even further.”
In this case, how can there be a perception of the behavior of a heroine (*nāyikā*) in autumn?
For it is impossible for a heroine’s breast to bear a rainbow (*śakracāpa*) that has the appearance of a fresh nail-mark.

Now, one might argue: "Even though the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) resides in the phrase ‘having the appearance of a fresh nail-mark,’ through a consideration of the actual state of things, it should be transferred to Indra’s bow."

If it is argued that—as in "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and similar cases, where the act of offering is already established by other means and the injunction is transferred to the curds—likewise, there will arise the cognition: "She bears fresh nail-marks shining like a rainbow," [and thus no fault exists]; we say no. For, rather than postulating such a strained construction (*kaṣṭasṛṣṭikalpanā*), it is superior to accept the *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) simile itself.

Or let there be a *samāsokti* (condensed expression) here in some way or another, as in the case of "with eyes as if with blue lotuses, with lotuses... and so forth, since no other interpretation is possible.
Furthermore, since there is no cognition of social convention (*vyavahāra*) in a mere simile, how could *samāsokti*, which depends upon that [simile], find a place?
As they say:
"Whether it be conventional usage or reality, that which is perceived through comparison is not mere comparison; it is *samāsokti* (synecdoche) or a clear *ekadeśopamā* (partial simile)."

Thus, if it is accepted that both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) involve the partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivarti*) of their constituent parts, then even when their bases overlap (*saṅkara*), its exclusion from the scope of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is established by logic. Consequently, since this [figure] does not fall within the domain of that which is "aroused by a qualifier containing a simile," it is of two kinds when the qualifiers are identical: that aroused by a punning (*śliṣṭa*) qualifier and that aroused by a non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) qualifier. Furthermore, when the effect (*kārya*) and the mark (*liṅga*) are identical, there are two further varieties; thus, *samāsokti* is of four types.
In all these cases, the superimposition of conventional usage is the cause.
And that [superimposition] is, in some instances, the superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly object upon a worldly object,
and in others, the superimposition of the conventional usage of a technical (śāstrīya) object upon a technical object.

There are four ways [of superimposition]: either the superimposition of the conventional usage of scriptural entities upon worldly ones, or the superimposition of the conventional usage of worldly entities upon scriptural ones.
Among these, even worldly entities are of many kinds due to the distinctions of rasa and so forth.
According to the treatises as well, *samāsokti* (synecdoche) is of many kinds, being well-known in the sciences of logic (*tarka*), medicine (*āyurveda*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).

To give a mere indication: in such examples as "Having shaken off his garment... and so forth, there is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a worldly matter—such as the conduct of a forceful lover—upon another worldly thing.
[And: "By whom you, the immutable, are perceived as uniform in all your functions, proceeding in an infinite number of ways..."
"Indeed, the elision of the case-ending was performed because it possessed priority;
therefore, I consider your definition to be certainly established."
In this case, there is a superimposition of the linguistic usage of a thing well-known from grammar onto a thing well-known from the scriptures and treatises;
so it is elsewhere as well.
In a metaphor (*rūpaka*), the form of the subject (*prakṛta*) is concealed by the imposition of the form and configuration of something else that is not the subject (*aprakṛta*).
In this case, however, by superimposing its own state, [the poet] distinguishes that [object] from its previous state precisely while its true nature remains obscured.
For this very reason, they say that here there is a superimposition of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-samāropa*), but not a superimposition of essential nature (*svarūpa-samāropa*).
In the case of *upamā-dhvani* (suggestion of simile) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is similarity even of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
But here, it is only the qualifier [that is suggested]. The distinction is that in Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant), what is suggested is the relevant subject,
whereas here, it is the irrelevant subject.
The *parikara* (periphrasis) is considered to consist of the aforementioned qualifiers used with intentional meaning (*sābhiprāya*).
For example:
"O King of Aṅga! O General! [and so forth].
"O Karna, you who mock Drona,
protect this son of Duḥśāsana from Bhīma!"
śleṣa (paronomasia) is the expression of multiple meanings by means of words that, by their very nature, possess a single meaning. VisDh 10.57.
The exclusion [of other types of figures] is established by the pun (*śabdaśleṣa*) in the phrase "by means of identity of nature and identity of meaning" (*svabhāvādekārthaiḥ*),
and by the term "recitation" (*vācanam*) [which excludes] *dhvani*.
An example follows:
“Performing virtuous deeds, removing the impurity of the quarters,
and blazing with abundant splendor, the Maker of Light shines forth.”
In this case, because there is no restriction by context or other such factors, both types of *rājasūya* are to be expressed.
"Sometimes the particular [is suggested] from the general, or the general from the particular;
the cause from the effect, or the effect from the cause; and likewise, the equal from the equal. (Viśvavidyā 10.58)

If the relevant subject is understood from that which is irrelevant, then there is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), which is of five kinds; the examples follow in order: 1. *Arthāntaranyāsa* (Corroboration): "The moon has risen, and the night has become beautiful; yet, alas, my beloved does not appear before my eyes. 2. *Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing): "The sun rises in the east, and the king rises in the eastern direction; both dispel darkness and grant light to the world. 3. *Dīpaka* (Illuminator): "The lotus blossoms, the lily blooms, and the bee hums; the day is bright, the night is dark, and the moon shines. 4. *Vyatireka* (Contrast): "The moon is pale compared to her face; the lotus is surpassed by her eyes; and the lily is eclipsed by her smile. 5. *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description): "The swan, having wandered through various lakes, now dwells in this pond; for the virtuous, even a small refuge becomes a great abode."
“Better is the dust that, struck by the foot, rises up and settles upon the head, than the embodied being who remains in his own place even when insulted.”
In this context, while a specific point was intended—namely, that even dust is better than her—the general has been stated:
"If this garland were a taker of life, why does it not kill me when placed upon my heart?
By the will of the Lord, even poison may sometimes become nectar, or nectar may become poison."

In this case, while the general principle is under discussion—that by the will of the Lord, even one who causes harm may act for benefit, and even one who acts for benefit may cause harm—a specific instance has been stated.
Thus, here we have an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general rule) based on the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
In a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example), however, a well-known object is taken up as a reflection.
But here, since the transformation of poison into nectar or nectar into poison is not established, its existence [as a poetic figure] does not occur.
"The moon is as if smeared with collyrium; the gaze of the deer-eyed women is as if dulled; the coral leaf is as if its ruddy luster has faded; the radiance of gold is as if turned dark."
And alas, a touch of harshness has begun to manifest even in the throats of the female cuckoos, as if before Sītā; and the plumage of the peacocks appears as if it were adorned with rubies.

In this case, from the possible effects residing in Indra and others—such as being smeared with collyrium—the relevant cause, which consists of the particular beauty residing in the face and so forth, is understood. "‘I am going,’ having been thus addressed by that deer-eyed woman, he left behind a sighing sound, glanced askance at me with one eye clouded by tears, and spoke with a taunt to the fawn, who had grown fond of him: ‘Today, let the love I have bestowed upon you be transferred by you to the circle of my dear friends.’”
In this [figure], a cause is stated for an effect consisting in the non-occurrence of something.
When an equal [subject] is introduced and an equal [object] is expressed, it is twofold: based on *śleṣa* (punning) and based merely on similarity (*sādṛśya*).
That which is based on *śleṣa* is also twofold: like *samāsokti*, when there is *śleṣa* only in the adjectives, and when there is *śleṣa* in the substantive as well, as in *śleṣa* itself.
For example, in due order:
"The mango tree is ever-fragrant, endowed with the beauty of spring,
possessing brilliant luster, glorious, and filled with abundant buds."
In this instance, by virtue of the pun (*śleṣa*) on the adjectives alone, there arises the cognition of a certain relevant hero from the irrelevant mango tree:

"Even if he were to deviate from manhood, even if he were to go downwards, even if he were not great in granting favors—nevertheless, he would uplift the entire world; such is the direction shown by that Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) through some [unfathomable] means.
Here, although the word *puruṣottama* is a pun upon the substantive as well, due to its widespread renown, Viṣṇu is understood first.
By that [description], a certain person worthy of praise is understood.
An example based on mere similarity is as follows:
"A single young pigeon is pursued by hundreds of hawks out of hunger."
The sky is devoid of any covering; alas, alas! The compassion of Brahmā is our only refuge.
In this case, from the dissatisfied pigeon, a certain [other] subject is understood. And this [figure] sometimes occurs even through contrast (*vaidharmya*):
"Blessed indeed are the winds in the forest, cooled by contact with the *kahlāra* lilies."
Those who touch Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, without being restrained.”
In this instance, by means of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the subject under discussion is understood through the contrast: "The winds are fortunate, while I am unfortunate.
This [type of *vyatireka*] is of three kinds, according to whether the expressed meaning is possible, impossible, or both.
Among these, the examples for the case of possibility are precisely those already stated.
An example of impossibility is as follows:
"I am a cuckoo, you are a crow; our blackness is equal.
Yet, those who are experts in the sweet warbling of birds will tell the difference."
In this instance, the dialogue between the crow and the cuckoo is impossible without the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of the subject at hand.
An example of both forms [simile and metaphor] together is as follows:
"There are many holes within, and many thorns without."
How might the fibers of the lotus stalk not be fragile?
In this case, without the superimposition of something relevant to the context, it is impossible for the holes within the lotus stalks to be the cause of the breaking of the string;
however, for others [the causes], it is possible. Thus, there is a dual nature.

Furthermore, because this [figure] has its life-breath in the superimposition of a conventional behavior (*vyavahāra*), just like *samāsokti*, it differs from *vastudhvani* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
In the suggestion of simile (*upamādhvani*), the non-contextual element is suggested;
likewise in the figure of speech known as *samāsokti*.
But in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), both [the contextual and non-contextual elements] are expressed.
The figure of speech known as "Praise in Disguise" (vyājastuti) has been explained; now [the next] is discussed again.
When praise and blame are both expressed through words,

yet praise is understood through blame, it is *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) based on the etymology "praise by means of a pretext. When blame is understood through praise, it is praise in the form of a pretext.
For example, in sequence:
"O King, even when you were angry, the wives of your enemies became as trusting as before— their pearl ornaments fallen from their breasts and their slender bodies covered in thorns."
This is mine.
“O cloud, this ‘praise by artifice’ has been uttered by me regarding you: that your waters are for the very life of the world. But this, O rain-cloud, is truly a great hymn of praise to you!”
That you earn the assistance of the King of Dharma by slaying travelers!
Paryāyokta (periphrasis) occurs when that which is already implied is expressed by means of an indirect turn of phrase.
An example:
"The clusters of *pārijāta* blossoms, which were cherished by Śacī through the enjoyment of her hair in the *Nandana* grove, were touched with disdain by his soldiers."

In this case, the fact that "Heaven was conquered by Hayagrīva" is the very subject at hand (*prastuta*) that is to be understood; however, for the sake of conveying a particular poetic charm (*vaicitrya-viśeṣa*), it is expressed through its effect—the army’s disdainful touch upon the *pārijāta* flower-cluster—rather than directly.
Nor is this a case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), where a cause is inferred from an effect, because in that figure the effect itself is what is not the subject at hand (*aprastuta*).
But here, because it serves to make known the extraordinary power of the subject being described, it is introduced as an effect, just like a cause.
Thus:
"By him, as he wiped away the teardrops—thicker than pearls—from their breasts..."
The necklaces of the wives of the enemy's women have returned, even without their strings of pearls, as they were cast off.

In this case, just as the cause—the killing of the enemy who is to be understood—is described, so too is the effect—the weeping of the enemy’s wife—deserving of description because it serves to reveal the king’s extraordinary power;
thus, this is indeed *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"O King, the princesses do not teach me; the queens remain silent. O Kubja, feed me! Why is nothing yet being eaten by the princes and their ministers?"
Thus, having been released from his cage by travelers in the palace of your enemy, the royal parrot gazes upon the figures in the paintings and addresses each one individually from the empty turret.
In this case, the reason presented is that upon hearing that you were intent on setting out, the enemies fled at once.
Some say, "The effect is also presented as being worthy of description.
Others, however, say: "By means of the account of the royal parrot, some power inherent in the subject matter is made known; therefore, this is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description)."
Whether the universal is qualified by the particular, or the particular by that [universal], or whether this effect is established by its cause, or the cause by its effect. (VisSd 10.61)
Based on similarity and its opposite, *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) is thus eightfold.
The examples follow in order: “Even one who is very small reaches the end of his task when aided by the great.”
Having come together with the great river, the mountain stream reaches the ocean.
Here, the general meaning contained in the first half-verse is rendered plausible by the specific meaning found in the second half-verse:
"Having thus spoken words consisting of only as many phrases as were necessary for the purpose, Mādhava ceased;
for the great, by their very nature, are speakers of measured speech."
“O Earth, be firm!
O Serpent, support her! O King of Tortoises, you must uphold this pair!”
"O elephants of the quarters, direct your desire to support it; the Noble One is drawing the bow of Hara to its full stretch."
In this context, the stringing of the bow of Hara, which serves as the cause, supports the effect, namely the stability of the earth and so forth.

In such passages as "One should not perform an action impulsively," the avoidance of haste—which is the effect—supports the cause, which consists of acting with deliberation (the absence of impulsive performance).
These are examples of *sādharmya* (similarity).
An example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is as follows:
“Even when propitiated in this manner, the wicked man afflicts the three worlds;
he may be pacified by retaliation, but not by a favor.”
In this case, the general statement is the support for the particular.

In the verse beginning with "One should not act impulsively," the fact that the absence of impulsive action results in the non-occurrence of misfortune—which would otherwise be a contrary effect—is the supporting factor.
The same applies to other instances.
When the reason constitutes the meaning of the sentence or its constituent words, it is called *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the causal mark).
In that regard, an example of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is as follows:
"O beloved, that blue lotus which shared the luster of your eyes has sunk into the water;
the moon, which imitates the radiance of your face, has been obscured by clouds."
Even those royal swans who have gone away with a gait that imitates your own amusements—fate does not permit me even the mere diversion of your likeness.
In this case, the sentences of the first three quarters serve as the reasons for the fourth quarter. An example of this being the meaning of the words (padārthatā) is my own verse:
“[The earth], made muddy by the masses of dust kicked up by the hooves of your horses...”
Hara does not bear the Gaṅgā upon his head for fear of its immense weight.”
In this second half-verse, the first half-verse serves as a single-word reason (*hetu*).
An example with multiple words is as follows, by me: "They behold the river of the water of your charity flowing along countless paths."
"O Lord, she protects her own self, the triple-pathed river, upon his formidable head."

In this regard, some do not favor *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) on the grounds that its purpose is already served by the *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) residing within the meaning of the sentence itself, specifically through the relation of cause and effect.
That is incorrect; for in this context, the reason (*hetu*) is threefold: the indicator (*jñāpaka*), the producer (*niṣpādaka*), and the corroborator (*samarthaka*).
In this context, the indicator is the domain of inference (anumāna),
the producer is the domain of the poetic figure "Poetic Reason" (kāvyaliṅga), and the corroborator is the domain of "Corroboration by another matter" (arthāntaranyāsa).
Thus, in this case, the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) and the *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) function as distinct cause-and-effect relationships.

For instance, in the verse beginning with “yattvannetra-,” the sentence of the fourth quarter would otherwise be incomplete and inconsistent due to its expectancy; therefore, it depends upon the sentences contained in the first three quarters as its means of fulfillment.
Regarding the verse beginning with "sahasā vidadhīta," [it says]:
"I tell you the truth: one should never associate with wicked people who are intent on harming others."

Just as in such examples, by the mere fact of being instructed, one becomes free from further expectation; thus, even though the matter is already understood by itself, the avoidance of immediate action is performed with supporting reasoning. Therefore, this *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is distinct from *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), as they function through different causal relationships.
[As it is said: "Hara does not bear the Gaṅgā upon his head out of fear of its great weight."
For that [earth] has indeed become muddy with the dust kicked up by the rows of your horses."

For here, by the inclusion of the word *hi* (for/since), the status of [the reason] as a logical ground (*hetutva*) is made explicit— just as in the expression "because of its being muddy"— and thus this is not a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), since a figure of speech consists precisely in a striking peculiarity (*vaicitrya*).
Inference (*anumāna*), however, is a cognition [arising] from the establishment of a probandum through a probans, characterized by a specific charm (*vicchitti*).
For example:

"We know that within the heart of this lotus-eyed woman shines the moon of her beloved's face; for by the spreading nets of its radiance over her limbs, there has come a paleness and a budding state in her lotus-eyes."
In this case, the striking beauty arises from the power of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Or, for example:
"Wherever the glance of young women falls, there sharp arrows fall."
And I think that Smara runs before them with his arrow unaimed.

In this case, there is aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) by virtue of the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*). The difference between the two is that in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), there is a perception of something as being uncertain, whereas here it is perceived as certain.
The designation [of the cause] by way of non-difference from the effect is the reason, together with that which possesses the reason.
As in my own verse: “The playfulness of youth”—here, the cause of subjugation (the heroine) is described as the act of subjugating [the hero];
this figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) is based on the identification (*adhyavasāya*) between playfulness and laughter.
If adverse action follows favorability, it is called *anukūla-prātikūlya*.
For example: "O slender one, when you are angry,
having inflicted a wound with your fingernails,
then bind his neck firmly with the nooses of your arms."
And because this particular variety of strikingness (vicchitti) manifests as distinct from all other ornaments, it is logical that it constitutes a separate ornament.
[This is for the purpose of] conveying a specific quality of the subject matter intended to be expressed. (VisSd 10.64)
Paralipsis (*ākṣepa*) is a semblance of negation; it is twofold, according to whether it concerns what is yet to be said (*vakṣyamāṇa*) or what has already been said (*ukta*).

Regarding the subject of what is yet to be said, there are two varieties: in one case, there is a negation of everything that was indicated in general, and in another, when a portion has been stated, there is a negation of the remaining portion.
And regarding the subject of what has already been said, in some cases there is a negation of the very nature of the thing itself.
In some cases there are two [types] of "telling the facts," thus making four varieties of objection (*ākṣepa*).
For example, in order:
“O friend, for the sake of my companion, who is distressed by hundreds of the arrows of Love, I say something: rest here for a moment! Or rather, what can I say to one whose heart is merciless?”
In this instance, there is a negation of the separation that was indicated in general by the friend regarding the matter about to be described:
"Alas! Upon seeing the fresh jasmine in full bloom during your absence, the deer-eyed one is now utterly [distraught].
Ah! What is the use of these futile words?"
In this context, the portion "she will die here" is not explicitly stated:
"O young man! I am not a messenger; 'your beloved loves you' is not my business.
She is dying because of you; we speak only these words of righteousness."
In this instance, there is a negation of the matter of acting as a messenger:
"How can that slender-limbed woman endure the nights during her separation from you?
What is the use of speaking before one who is so cruelly resolved?"
In this case, there is a negation of that which has already been stated in the narration.
In the first example, the specific point understood is that death is inevitable;
in the second, it is the impossibility of being expressed, and so forth.
In the third [instance], there is speaking the truth regarding the role of a messenger;
in the fourth, there is an excess of suffering.
And this is not a prohibition of what has been enjoined.
In this case, because the negation is merely apparent, another type is considered an "apparent injunction" (vidhyābhāsa) regarding an undesirable matter. (VisSd 10.65)
"So be it," as before, for the sake of understanding the specific detail;
namely: "Go, if you must go, my beloved."
“May your paths be auspicious, and may mine also be so; may my birth also take place in that very place where you have gone.”
In this case, because pleasure is undesirable, the injunction takes on a faltering form and results in a prohibition;
furthermore, the specific nature of the act of going is understood as something that must be absolutely avoided.
*Vibhāvanā* occurs when the production of an effect is described without its cause.
It is proclaimed to be twofold, because its causes are either explicitly stated or unstated.
Even when the arising of an effect is described as being without a cause, it is logically proper that it must depend upon some other cause;
and that other cause is of two kinds: sometimes stated and sometimes unstated.
For example—
“The waist of the fair-browed maiden was slender without effort, her eyes trembled with a subtle apprehension, and her body captivated the mind even without ornaments, at that stage of youth.”
In this case, the cause consisting of age and form has been stated.

In the very same context, with the reading "The body of the deer-eyed one shines," since the cause is unstated, there is the figure of speech called *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), which likewise occurs in two ways: [the absence of the effect despite the presence of the cause, and the absence of the cause despite the presence of the effect].
Because it has both stated and unstated causes;
among these, those with stated causes are as follows:
"Even the wealthy are free from arrogance, and even the young are not fickle."
Though they are powerful, they remain vigilant, possessing great majesty.
In this case, the possession of great majesty (*mahāmahimaśālitva*) is stated as the cause (*nimitta*).
However, in the reading of the fourth quarter of this very verse as "How many are there on the surface of the earth? (*kiyantaḥ santi bhūtale*), it is not so stated.
Furthermore, the state of having an inconceivable cause (*acintyanimittatva*) is not mentioned separately, as it is merely a specific variety of that which has an unstated cause.
For example:
"That flower-armed god alone conquers the three worlds;
though his body was taken away by Śambhu, his power was not taken away."
In this case, even by means of the removal of the body, the cause for the removal of strength is inconceivable;

and here, the absence of an effect is also established by way of the presence of something contrary to that effect. Likewise, in the figure of *vibhāvanā* (peculiar causation), the absence of a cause is established by way of the presence of something contrary to that cause.

And thus, because of the composition of longing—which is contrary to the cause [of joy]—in the verse beginning with "He who steals away childhood," there is *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit of the absence of cause).
