Furthermore, because of the composition of longing—which is contrary to the effect [of the stated cause]—in the verse beginning with "He who steals away childhood," there is *viśeṣokti* (poetic conceit of the presence of effect despite the absence of cause).
In this way, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti* here.
But a pure example must be sought.
A genus [is related] by four [terms], beginning with its own genus; a quality [is related] by three, beginning with its own quality. (ViSd 10.67)

When an action appears as if mutually contradictory with another action or a substance, or when one substance appears as if contradictory with another substance, this is "contradiction" (virodha), which has ten forms.
For example, in sequence:
"In separation from you, the Malaya breeze is a forest fire; even the moonbeams are hot;
the wind pierces her heart though it is gentle; and even a lotus petal is like the summer sun to her."
“O King, due to the constant engagement in numerous household chores caused by the lack of pestles,
the hands of the wives of the twice-born, though naturally hard, become as delicate as lotuses.”
“Who knows your true nature— you who take birth though unborn, who destroy your enemies though devoid of effort, and who remain awake though appearing to sleep?”
“Without the contact of her lover’s lap, the full-moon night for that fawn-eyed woman became filled with the flames of poison.”
This form of the intoxicating-eyed one, which is a feast for the pair of eyes and difficult to attain even by the activity of the mind, gladdens my heart and yet causes it to burn with pain.

In the verse beginning with “tvadvāji,” and specifically in the fourth quarter of the verse beginning with “vallabhotsaṅge,” if the reading were “madhyandinadinādhipaḥ,” there would be a contradiction between two substances (*dravya*).

Here, however, in the passage beginning with “tava viraha-,” since the words for wind and so forth denote multiple individuals, they are genus-words (*jātiśabda*); thus, there is a mutual contradiction between these—wind and the rest—and the forest fire, heat, heart-piercing, and the sun, which take the forms of genus, quality, action, and substance respectively.
It appears on the surface,
but its resolution lies in the fact that it is caused by separation.
In the passage beginning with "of the unborn" (*ajasya*), there is a contradiction between qualities such as being unborn and actions such as the taking of birth.
However, because the power of the Blessed One is so preeminent, there is a resolution.
In the verse beginning with "tvadvāji-," there is an apparent contradiction (virodha) in the statement, "Even Hara does not bear the Gaṅgā upon his head";
yet, this is resolved through the bold poetic assertion (kaviprauḍhokti) of the poet beginning with "tvadvāji-."
The rest is clear.

In *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect despite the absence of its cause), because it is presented through the absence of the cause, the effect itself is perceived as that which is sublated; and in *viśeṣokti* (the description of the absence of an effect despite the presence of its cause), it is the cause itself [that is perceived as sublated] through the absence of the effect.
In this case, however, the distinction is that both [factors] are mutually sublated.
"Incongruity" (asaṅgati) occurs when cause and effect occupy different locations,
as for example:
“She is young and we are timid of heart; she is a woman and we are faint-hearted; she bears a pair of full and elevated breasts while we are burdened with weariness;
she is overcome by the weight of her hips and unable to walk, yet we have become incompetent through faults that belong to others—how strange!”
And because this [figure] is an exception, when there is a contradiction between two things residing in a single locus, it is the figure of speech called *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction).
[Furthermore: "If there should be two qualities or two actions that are contradictory, belonging respectively to the cause and the effect... (Viśvavidyā 10.69).
When there is the failure of what has been undertaken and the occurrence of misfortune,
or when there is a conjunction of two discordant things, that is considered the "uneven" (viṣama) [figure].
For example, in due order:

"Having immediately received the touch of his hand in battle after battle, the blade of his sword— dark as a tamāla tree— gives birth to fame, white as the autumnal moon, which serves as an ornament for the three worlds."

In this case, the production of white fame from the sword-blade, which is the cause in its material form, contradicts the established principle that "the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect.
[And yet: "O lotus-petal-eyed one, you bestow upon me this intense bliss."
But this separation, produced by you alone, torments my body exceedingly.”
Here, from the cause of a woman’s form which produces joy, arises the separation that produces suffering:
"This ocean is a mine of jewels," so it was served with the hope for wealth;
let alone the wealth, my mouth has been filled with the waters of brine.
In this matter, not only was the desired gain of wealth not achieved,
but rather his mouth was filled with salt water:
"Where is the forest, adorned with the bark of trees, and where is royal splendor, worshipped by Great Indra?"
Alas, the conduct of the element that acts in opposition is surely most difficult to endure!
Here, there is a conjunction of two discordant things, the forest and royal splendor;
this is my view.
Or, for example:
“The belly of the one who lies upon the ocean, which was vast enough to swallow the worlds at the end of an eon,
was in turn drunk up by the gaze of a single city woman, her eyes slightly askance with the intoxication of passion.”
Praise that is appropriate to a worthy object should be proportionate;
for example:
"The moonlight has reached the moon, and the daughter of Jahnu has descended into the ocean, her fitting mate, now freed from clouds."
Thus, delighted by the union of equal virtues, the citizens there broke into a single voice that was harsh to the ears of the kings.
If that diverse [action] performed by one who is opposed [to the Buddha] is for the sake of a desired result, [then it would follow that the Buddha’s teaching is not supreme].
As it is said:
"He bows down for the sake of advancement, he gives up his life for the sake of livelihood,
and he suffers misery for the sake of pleasure— who is more foolish than a servant?"
When there is an excess of either the substratum (*āśraya*) or the superstratum (*āśrayin*), it is called "excess" (*adhika*). An example of excess due to the substratum is as follows:
"What more can we say of the greatness of this ocean, wherein Hari resides?"
"Having deposited the worlds within his belly, he sleeps quite unknown."
An example of excess of the substratum (*āśritādhikya*) is as follows: "In whose body the worlds, having withdrawn themselves at the time of the end of the age, rested in full expansion—
therein the joys arising from the arrival of the ascetic did not find room for the Enemy of Kaiṭabha."
Each of the two is mutually the cause of the other's single activity.
“She is graced by you, and you too are graced by her;
as the moon is graced by the night, so the night is graced by the moon.”

When something that is to be produced—whether it be possible or otherwise—is a single entity that serves as the locus for many, yet lacks a substratum; (then there is no other means). *Viṣṇusmṛti-sāra*, 10.73.
The accomplishment of an effect through destiny is thus a threefold distinction;
for example, in sequence:
"Those whose multitude of vast virtues [endures] until the end of the kalpa, even for those who have ascended to heaven..."
How could those poets not be worthy of homage, whose words delight the worlds?
“In the forest, by the banks of rivers, and even in the caves of mountains,
your enemies shall see you alone before them, resembling the God of Death.”
“My wife, my counselor, my confidential friend, and my dear pupil in the art of graceful accomplishments—
tell me, what has not been taken from me by Death, who is indifferent to compassion, in seizing you?”
But that contradiction occurs when an object is treated by someone in a manner different from how it was originally made.
If another person performs that same action by means of that very same method, but in a different manner—
as in “the mind-born god was burnt by her glance,” and so forth—
and if the effect is produced more easily, then it constitutes the *viruddha* (contradictory) figure. (VisSd 10.75)
It is indeed a contradiction:
"Stay right here; my beloved, I shall return quickly in just a few days. You are delicate and cannot endure hardship."
"O fortunate one, my very delicacy is the reason why you have come; for I, being delicate, could not endure the incomparable distress caused by separation."
In this instance, the hero states the heroine’s fragility as the reason for her inability to accompany him;
however, the heroine, on the contrary, presents that very same quality as the reason why accompanying him would be even easier.
This occurs when each preceding factor serves as the cause for each succeeding one.
Then there would be a "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*), as follows:
"From association with those of perfected intellect, learning arises; from learning, discipline arises."
Is the world's affection not due to discipline? And is it not from the world's affection [that discipline arises]?
—That, moreover, is the lamp-in-a-garland (mālādīpaka). VisSd_10.76.
The connection of several subjects with a single attribute, arranged in successive order,
is as follows:
"When you had entered into the combat, arrows were drawn upon your bow."
By him, enemies' heads were struck with arrows; by that [deed], the earth was won; by you, fame was attained."
In this context, the act of causing to attain is the primary factor;
each subsequent element serves as a qualification for each preceding one.
If it is either established or excluded, then that single series (ekāvalī) is of two kinds.
The examples in order are:
"The lake has blossomed lotuses; the lotus is frequented by bees."
Where the bees, accompanied by song, performed music that evoked the memory of love.
“That is not water which does not contain beautiful lotuses; that is not a lotus upon which a bee does not alight.”
It was not a six-legged bee that did not hum sweetly, nor was it not a humming that did not captivate the mind.
In some cases, even the substantive (viśeṣya) is seen to be established as an attribute (viśeṣaṇa) for each subsequent term and thus excluded [from its primary status], as in:
"The ponds become clear; lotuses bloom in the ponds."
Bees alight upon the lotuses, and they produce music among the bees.
In this same way, even in the process of elimination,
the progressive excellence of the object is called its essence.
For example: "In a kingdom, the essence is the earth; in the earth, the city; in the city, the palace;
in the palace, the bedchamber; in the bedchamber, the couch; and on the couch, the beautiful woman—the very all-in-all of the god of love."
"Enumeration in order" refers to that which follows the sequence of items previously mentioned.
For example:

"They open [their eyes]; pluck [the flowers] with your nails! They carry [them away]; cover them with the hem of your silken garment! They enter the pleasure grove; terrify them with the tinkling of your bracelets!"
"O fortunate one, such are the secret conversations among her friends with one another during your absence, amidst the *vañjula* trees, the southern breezes, and the cuckoos."
In some cases, the one resides in the many, and the many reside in the one, sequentially.
If it exists or is produced, then it is accepted as a sequential process (*paryāya*), as for example in this sequence:
"They remained for a moment on the eyelashes, their lips struck [by the lashes], then crushed by falling upon the fullness of the breasts."
The first drops of water, having stumbled over her folds, reached her navel in succession.
“Where graceful women, languid from the weight of their hips, used to stroll,
there in your enemy’s city, jackals, crows, and female jackals now run about.”
“Her hand, which had released its attachment to the stream of tears, was turned away from the red cosmetic on her breasts and from the reddish ball;
with its fingers scarred by the plucking of blades of *kuśa* grass, it was made devoted to the rosary.”
“Upon whom that bright necklace was placed by the wives of your enemies.”
Large teardrops are deposited upon their two breasts.”
And among these, in some cases the substratum (ādhāra) is both of a composite nature and a non-composite nature; in other cases, the superstratum (ādheya) is likewise.
For example:
In the phrase "sthitāḥ kṣaṇam" (they stood for a moment), the drops of water occurred sequentially upon a substrate that is not a unified whole, such as the eyelashes.
In the phrase "vicaranti" (they roam about), the tigers and other creatures, who are the objects supported, occurred sequentially within a city that is a unified whole.
The same applies to other instances.
And here, the distinction from the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra* (peculiar excellence) lies in the fact that a single thing occurs in multiple places only successively;
and its distinction from *parivṛtti* (exchange) lies in the absence of exchange. For it is said:
"Parivṛtti is an exchange involving equals, inferiors, or superiors. (Viśvavidyā-sadana 10.80)
The examples in order are as follows:
"Having cast a sidelong glance, the deer-eyed woman seized my heart;
but I, having given her my heart, have been seized by the fever of love."
In this verse, [the first half] is with equal [syllables], and the second half is with fewer [syllables]:
"And why should that aged Jaṭāyu, who has now gone to heaven, be mourned at all?"
By which [merit], through the sacrifice of a worn-out body, fame as radiant as the rays of the moon was purchased.”
In this context,
whether from an excess [of words], or from what is stated as a question or even as a non-question,
if there occurs an exclusion of something else similar to that object, then it is either verbal or objective.
Exclusion (parisaṃkhyā)—an example in order:
"What is the most enduring ornament here? Fame, not jewels. What is the duty to be performed? The conduct of the noble, which is well-done, not vice."
What eye is unimpeded? Wisdom, not the physical organ; for who other than you knows how to distinguish between the real and the unreal?
Here, the objects to be excluded are expressed verbally:
“What is always to be propitiated? Merit. Who is always to be served? The True Tradition (sadāgama). Who is to be meditated upon? The Blessed Viṣṇu. What is to be desired? The Supreme State.”
In this context, the purpose of exclusion is for the sake of [excluding] evil and so forth.
These two [types of vows] are preceded by a question;
as for those not preceded by a question, it is as follows:

“The devotion of the great is seen to be generally directed toward existence [liberation], not toward worldly prosperity; their passion is for the scriptures, not for the weapon of youthful women; and their concern is for fame, not for the physical body.”
“Strength is for the sake of pacifying the fear of the distressed; extensive learning is for the approval of the wise.
For that Lord, not only his wealth, but even his possession of virtues serves the purpose of others.”
And regarding its being rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a particular variety of charm, as in:
"While that king, who had conquered the world, was protecting the earth, there was a confusion of colors in paintings, and a breaking of the string in bows," and so forth.
If the answer is inferred from the answer itself to a question...
And that which is repeatedly impossible, even when a question is posed, constitutes an answer. (10.82)
As it was said by me: "My mother-in-law is unable to endure separation, and my husband has gone far away;
I am a young woman all alone—how can you have a dwelling here?"
By this, the traveler's request for lodging is understood: "What is uneven? The way of women. What is to be gained? A person who appreciates virtue.
What is happiness? A good wife. What is difficult to endure? A wicked person."
In this case, since there is no intention to exclude others, the distinction is one of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
Nor is this inference (*anumāna*),
for that [inference] is accepted only when there is the presentation of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
Nor is this *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication),
because the latter [the answer] does not produce the former [the question].
*Arthāpatti* (presumption) is held to be the comprehension of another meaning by way of the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*).

By the statement, "The staff has been eaten by the mouse," the eating of the cake (*apūpa*), which is concomitant with it, follows by implication; thus, another matter arises from a fixed common logic. This principle is called *daṇḍāpūpikā*. Here, there are two varieties: in one case, a non-contextual matter follows from a contextual matter, and in the other, a contextual matter follows from a non-contextual matter. The examples follow in order: [Example 1] *“The staff has been eaten by the mouse.”* [From this, the eating of the cake follows. [Example 2] *“The king has been conquered by a single arrow.”* [From this, the conquest of his entire army follows. [Example 3] *“The moon has been swallowed by Rāhu.”* [From this, the cessation of all activities follows. [Example 4] *“The crow has been killed by the cat.”* [From this, the destruction of the entire flock follows. [Example 5] *“The elephant has been captured by a lion.”* [From this, the destruction of the entire herd follows. [Example 6] *“The snake has been devoured by Garuḍa.”* [From this, the destruction of the entire serpent race follows. [Example 7] *“The sun has set behind the mountain.”* [From this, the cessation of all worldly business follows. [Example 8] *“The moon has risen.”* [From this, the resumption of all worldly business follows. [Example 9] *“The lotus has blossomed.”* [From this, the awakening of the bees follows. [Example 10] *“The lily has blossomed.”* [From this, the awakening of the bees follows. [Example 11] *“The sun has risen.”* [From this, the awakening of the bees follows. [Example 12] *“The moon has set.”* [From this, the closing of the lotuses follows. [Example 13] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the blue lotuses follows. [Example 14] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the blue lotuses follows. [Example 15] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the white lotuses follows. [Example 16] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the white lotuses follows. [Example 17] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the red lotuses follows. [Example 18] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the red lotuses follows. [Example 19] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the night-lotuses follows. [Example 20] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the night-lotuses follows. [Example 21] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the day-lotuses follows. [Example 22] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the day-lotuses follows. [Example 23] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the water-lilies follows. [Example 24] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the water-lilies follows. [Example 25] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the white water-lilies follows. [Example 26] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the white water-lilies follows. [Example 27] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the red water-lilies follows. [Example 28] *“The cloud has not rained.”* [From this, the closing of the red water-lilies follows. [Example 29] *“The cloud has rained.”* [From this, the blooming of the blue water-lilies follows. [Example 30] *“The cloud has not rained.”*
“This necklace rolls upon the circle of the breasts of fawn-eyed women; such is the condition even of pearls—what then can we say of us, the servants of Love?”
“He lamented with a voice choked with tears, casting aside even his innate fortitude;
even iron, when excessively heated, attains softness—what need is there to speak of embodied beings?”

And here, when the same logical principle (*samānanyāya*) is rooted in *śleṣa* (punning double entendre), there is a specific variety of aesthetic charm, as illustrated in the verse beginning with “This necklace”—for this is not inference (*anumāna*), because the same logical principle lacks the nature of a [logical] relation (*sambandha*).
Furthermore: “*Vikalpa* is the conflict between two [alternatives] of equal strength, brought about by ingenuity. (VisSd 10.83)
For example: “Let heads bow or bows bend; let commands be made into ear-ornaments or bowstrings.

Here, there is a contradiction because the bowing of heads and the bending of bows serve as indicators of peace and war respectively, and since peace and war cannot be performed simultaneously; yet this contradiction culminates in the adoption of one side or the other.

And here, the equality of strength (*tulyabalatva*) between the two—bowing the bow and bowing the head—is to be understood as being conceived through their mutual rivalry. Furthermore, the skillfulness (*cāturya*) here lies in its containing a comparison (*aupamya*).
Likewise, this applies to the phrase "let them be made ear-ornaments" (*karṇapūrīkriyantām*). Thus—
“May the eyes or the body of Hari bring about the pacification of your suffering.
Here, there is beauty supported by the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning).
“Let the unconquered wealth be given to the god or to the Brahmin.”
In this case, because there is an absence of skill (cāturya), this is not an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).

This is *samuccaya* (accumulation): when one means of accomplishing an effect already exists, if another [means] should also perform that action by way of the "partridge-in-the-grain-field" logic (*khalekapotikā-nyāya*), [it is *samuccaya*]. (VisSd 10.84)
Two qualities or two actions may occur simultaneously, or alternatively, a quality and an action may occur together; as in my own verse:
"O, you steady breeze!"
"Ah! Your birth is from the Sandalwood Mountain, your courtesy is unsurpassed in the world, and your acquaintance is with the waters of the Godāvarī;
yet you burn me limb by limb. If even you are like a fierce forest fire, what will this dark-souled forest-dweller, the cuckoo, say of me?"
In this instance, although there is a single cause for the burning—the production of sandalwood from the mountain—there is the employment of other causes such as courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*) and so forth.
Here, because all the causes are excellent, it is a "good conjunction" (*sadyoga*).

In this very same example, however, because of the employment of non-excellent factors such as intoxication (*matta*) and so forth in the fourth quarter, it is an "unfortunate conjunction" (*asadyoga*).
An example of the conjunction of the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadyoga*) is as follows:
“The moon grey with daylight; a woman whose youth has faded; a lake devoid of lotuses; a face that does not match its own beauty;
a lord devoted only to wealth; a virtuous person who is perpetually destitute; and a villain residing at the king’s court—these seven are thorns in my heart.”
On this point, some say: "The conjunction of the good and the bad consists in the beauty of the moon and so forth, contrasted with the ugliness of the villain.
Others, however, maintain: "The conjunction of the good and the bad consists in the inherent beauty of the moon and so forth, contrasted with the ugliness of their greyish hue and the like.

For in this case, since the greyish hue and other such qualities are entirely absent from the moon and its counterparts, it is precisely the specific strikingness (*vicchitti*) that produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

The concluding summary, “There are seven thorns in my mind,” treats all seven as thorns. However, the phrase “the villain has reached the king’s palace” conveys a sense of defect due to the deviation from the established order; for throughout the passage, the focus has been on the excellence of the subject (the king) alone.
And here, like the metaphor of the pigeons in a single barn, all the causes appear together in combination.
In the *Samādhyalaṅkāra*, however, the distinction is that while all [causes] are effective toward a single result, another [cause] occurs by way of the "crow-and-fig" maxim (*kākatālīya*).
For example: “O young woman, your eyes are reddened, yet your beloved’s face is darkened;
your face is cast down, my friend, yet the fire of passion blazes within him.”
In the first case here, there is simultaneity of two qualities; in the second, simultaneity of two actions.
An example of the simultaneity of both is as follows:
"O Lord of Kings, your eye— possessing a splendor like that of a white lotus— has suddenly become turbid toward your enemies;
and clearly, through its side-glances, calamity has fallen upon their bodies."
In such instances as "He shakes off the sword and spreads his fame," this [figure] is seen even when there is a single substratum;
yet, the *dīpaka* (lamp) does not apply here.

For these types of conjunction (*samuccaya*), which consist in the simultaneity of qualities and actions, are invariably rooted in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) characterized by the reversal of the temporal sequence of cause and effect; however, the *dīpaka* lacks such a foundation in hyperbole. *Samādhi* [is defined as]: when a task that would otherwise be difficult is accomplished due to the intervention of another factor through chance. (VisSd 10.85)
For example: "To dispel her pride, this thundering of clouds has arisen by good fortune as an aid for me as I am about to fall at her feet."
If one is unable to counteract an enemy, then the disparagement of that enemy's partisans serves to establish the enemy's own superiority.
“Of that very one” means of the enemy alone.
As it is said by me:
“This slender-waisted woman has surpassed my waist in slenderness.”
The lion, resembling her jar-like breasts, splits apart her two elephant frontal globes.
The conceptualization of a well-known object of comparison as the object of comparison itself, or the statement of its fruitlessness, is called *pratīpa* (the inverse). (VisSd 10.87)
For example, in sequence:
"That blue lotus which was submerged in the water is one whose luster is equal to your eye," and so forth.
“If that face exists, then the talk of the moon is silenced; alas, if that radiance exists, then gold is surpassed!

If those eyes exist, blue lotuses are defeated; if that smile exists, what is nectar? Fie on Cupid’s bow if those eyebrows exist! But why say more? Truly, the Creator’s course of creation has turned away from redundant things.”
In this case, because the moon and other objects convey their splendor solely through the face and so forth, those [objects] are rendered fruitless;

having thus stated the extreme excellence of an exceedingly superior object, some have declared it to be *pratīpa* (the inverse simile), even though the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is merely imagined. (VisSd 10.88)
As it is said:
"O Hālāhala, my dear, I alone am the teacher of the most terrible things."
Do not be arrogant;
for are there not words such as yours from wicked men in this world?
Here, the excellence of superiority is expressed by the first quarter-verse;
for if that were not stated, this would not be a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
For example:
“A Brahmin speaks like Brahmā,” and so forth.
*Mīlita* (the concealment of an object) is the hiding of a thing by something else possessing similar characteristics;
here, the object possessing similar characteristics may sometimes be adventitious.
An example of this in sequence is as follows:
"The mark of musk upon the chest of Hari, located on the breast of Lakṣmī,
was not perceived by Bhāratī because it was eclipsed by her own luster, which resembled a blue lotus."
In this regard, the Blessed One’s natural complexion is dark:
"The faces of amorous women, though flushed with anger, never caused doubt among young men— those faces whose [earrings] were always reddened by the rays of his ruby-studded earrings."
In this case, the redness of the ruby earring is adventitious;
the commonality consists in the identity of the subject with something else through its similar qualities. (VisSd 10.89)

For example: “Adorned with jasmine flowers in their braided hair and beautifully smeared with sandalwood paste, the women going to meet their lovers move about easily, unrecognizable in the moonlight.”
In *mīlita*, the inferior quality is concealed by a superior quality;
here, however, because both possess equal qualities, there is a failure to perceive their distinction.
In *tadguṇa*, due to the relinquishing of one's own quality, there is the assumption of a much superior quality.
For example: "He spoke, making the bees that hovered around the lotuses of his lips turn white with the rays of his prominent teeth."
In *mīlita*, there is the concealment of the subject matter (*prakṛta-vastu*) by another object (*vastvantara*);
here, however, the difference is that what is perceived is being overcome by the quality (*guṇa*) of the other object.
On the other hand, when the non-assumption of its form occurs despite the presence of a cause, it is *atadguṇa*.
For example: "Alas!
Even though my heart is filled with intense passion, O you who are white with virtue, how is it that you do not take delight in being seated within it?"
Or, for example:
"O royal swan, as you dive into both the white waters of the Ganges and the collyrium-dark waters of the Yamunā,
that same whiteness of yours neither increases nor diminishes."

In the former case, although the hero—who is denoted by the term *guṇagaura* (white with virtues)—appears as if he has attained redness due to contact with a heart intensely colored [by passion], that redness is not fully realized.

In the latter case, even though there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the swan, which is the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), does not assume the nature of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā despite its contact with them.
Furthermore, this differs from *viśeṣokti* (causation of a specific effect) because it relies on a particular strikingness (*vicchitti*) consisting in the non-apprehension of qualities.

And because there is no production of a different color from the uneven [object], when a subtle meaning is perceived through its form or gesture, it is indicated by some fortunate circumstance; that is called the "subtle" (sūkṣma). (VisSd 10.91)
Subtle, it is not perceived by those of gross intellect. Regarding this, by way of form, as for example:
"A certain woman, seeing the saffron [on her breast] broken on her neck by a continuous stream of sweat-drops trickling from her face..."
Manifesting his manhood to the slender maiden, her friend smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon her hand.

In this instance, the amorous advances (*puruṣāyita*) of one woman were indicated by another through a mark made with saffron; it was signaled on the hand by drawing the lines of a sword, the male emblem.
As for indication by gesture (*iṅgita*), for example: "Having perceived that the lover’s mind was fixed on the time of the tryst, the clever woman..."
The playful lotus, its secret intention conveyed by her smiling eyes, was closed.

In this instance, the lover's intention regarding the time for the rendezvous, indicated by the movement of his eyebrows and so forth, is revealed through the closing of the lotus that occurs at nightfall. Disguise (*vyājokti*) is the concealment of a matter that has become manifest despite efforts to hide it;
as for example:

“May Śiva protect you—he who, agitated by the interruption of his entire ritual engagement due to the disarray caused by the horripilation and other signs arising from being embraced by the hand of Pārvatī as she was being presented by the Lord of Mountains; and who, upon seeing him, was gazed upon with smiles by the circles of mothers in the mountain’s inner apartments, saying: ‘Ah! How cool are the hands of the Snowy Mountain!’”
This is not the first type of apahnuti (concealment), because the object that performs the concealment is not explicitly mentioned;
furthermore, its distinction from the second type of apahnuti was demonstrated during the discussion of that [second type].
Svabhāvokti (description of intrinsic nature) is the depiction of the form of one's own action regarding a difficult-to-understand object. (VisSd 10.92)

In the case of two difficult [similes]— where the object is known only to a poet, such as the behavior or nature of a child and so forth, which reside solely within those two [subjects] themselves— for example, my own verse:
“Having struck with his tail and repeatedly tearing at the surface of the earth with his forefeet, then suddenly crouching down upon himself and leaping swiftly into the sky with great prowess;”
With a roar of hissing "hum" sounds, driving away all creatures in every direction, this hyena, possessed by rage and with eyes red and swollen, has entered the forest.
That which consists in the appearance as if directly perceived of a marvelous object— whether past or future— is called the bhāvika.
For example:
"Victorious is the sage, the lord of yogis, the great-souled one born from a jar,
by whom those two divine beings, the fish and the tortoise, were seen within a single mouthful of water."
Or as it is said:
“I see collyrium here in your eyes;
I perceive your form as it will be when adorned with its full array of ornaments.”
Nor is this the quality called *prasāda* (clarity),
because it cannot be the cause of that [quality] when past and future things appear as if they were being perceived directly.
Nor is it the marvelous (*adbhuta*) sentiment (*rasa*).
This is because it serves as the cause for setting aside astonishment; nor is it the figure of speech known as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole),
due to the absence of *adhyavasāya* (imaginative identification).
Nor is it a mere error,
because that which has occurred and that which will occur are manifested precisely as having occurred and occurring;
nor is it a statement of essential nature (svabhāvokti).
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that [Svabhāvokti] is precisely the description, exactly as it is, of the subtle intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a mundane object;
however, this [Vibhāvanā] possesses a particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) consisting in the object appearing as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇa*).
Furthermore, if this strikingness is possible even when there is a statement of the intrinsic nature of an object in some instances, then there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of both.
“Though he possesses no sunshade, he is seen here as if surrounded on all sides by white parasols;
though he has no fly-whisk, he is always being fanned—what a marvelous man he is!”
In this case, since the description concerns that which is already appearing as if perceived, this is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*),
because the very nature of [this ornament] consists precisely in appearing as if perceived by virtue of the description.
However, where there is an appearance as if perceived even in the description of that which is not appearing as if perceived, it is appropriate for this to be an ornament.
As illustrated in the verse beginning with "āsīdañjanam" and so forth, the *udātta* (the exalted) is said to be the description of a superhuman excellence;
or else, it occurs when the conduct of great beings serves as an accessory (*aṅga*) to the subject at hand. (Viśvanātha’s Śāradātilaka 10.94)
The examples in order:

“In that [city], the pleasure grove increases in size through the waters flowing from the moonstones of its pavements, which have eclipsed the circle of clouds and are drenched by the falling moonlight.”
“Being praised by the first Creator, whose lotus-throne is split from his navel,
that Puruṣa, having withdrawn these worlds through his yogic sleep appropriate for the end of the age, reclines upon him.”

When the sentiments (rasa), the transitory states (bhāva), their semblances (tadābhāsa), as well as the subsidence of a state (bhāvaśama), attain a subordinate status, then they become poetic ornaments (alaṃkāra). (10.95)
The *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita* [are the figures of speech], in that order.

Their semblances (*tadābhāsau*) are the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) and the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*). Among these, the figure of speech *rasavat* arises from the presence of rasa, as for example:
“In this, that drawing forth of the tongue,” and so forth.
Here, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is a subordinate element (aṅga) of the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa).
The same applies elsewhere as well.
It is called *preyaḥ* (the more beloved) because it is exceedingly dear.
As in my own verse:
“Her eyes, with pupils wide and languidly half-closed, and her creeper-like arms slackened by the slight pressure of the bond around my neck;”
Constantly recollecting her face, its cheeks covered with droplets of perspiration, he finds no peace within."

Here, the erotic sentiment of union (saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra) is a subordinate element (aṅga) to the emotion (bhāva) called remembrance; and that [remembrance] is a subordinate element to the erotic sentiment of separation (vipralambha).
"Ūrja" means strength; because it possesses such [strength] when proceeding through what is improper (anaucitya), it is called ūrjasvin.
For example:
"In the forest, having abandoned their own wives, the Pulindas take pleasure in the throngs of women belonging to your enemies, being devoted to every art."
In this case, the semblance of the erotic (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the emotion (*rasa*) of love directed toward the king;
the same applies to the semblance of an emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).
This is the resolution (*parihāra*).

For example: “The pride of your enemies was seen repeatedly through the constant brandishing of their swords, the knitting of brows, and their threats and roars; yet that pride vanished somewhere in an instant upon seeing you.”
In this context, the subsidence of the emotion (bhāva) called intoxication (mada) serves as a subordinate element (aṅga) for the emotion of love directed toward the king.
Furthermore, when there is the arousal, the conjunction, or the mixture of emotions, they are designated by those same names.

The figures of speech named Bhāvodaya (emergence of emotion), Bhāvasandhi (juxtaposition of emotions), and Bhāvaśabalatā (intermixture of emotions) are as follows; their examples in order: “Having heard your name from somewhere, those enemies, who were engaged in drinking wine with their friends, fell into a miserable state.”
In this instance, the arising of fear (*trāsa*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the dominant emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the king:
“May Pārvatī always protect us— she who is eager for the touch of her lover’s body from a previous birth, yet remains bashful in the presence of her friend.”
Here, the *saṃdhi* (fusion) of longing (*autsukya*) and bashfulness (*lajjā*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the deity:
“Someone might see me! O fickle one, O restless one! Who am I? A young maiden. Give me your hand to support me! Alas, alas! This is a transgression; where are you going?”
"Thus, O Lord of the Earth,
the daughter of one who dwells in the forest and is your enemy speaks as she gathers certain fruits and tender shoots."

In this instance, the intermingling (*śabalatā*) of doubt, envy, fortitude, memory, fatigue, dejection, awakening, and eagerness serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the king.

Regarding this, some say: "Since figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) assist the rasa and other elements only through the medium of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the expressive words (*vācaka*), whereas the rasa and other elements are themselves only assisted by the expressed and the expressive, it is not proper for them [the rasa and others] to possess the status of being subordinate elements."

Others, however, maintain: “In this context, the designation of ‘ornament’ (alaṅkāra) based merely on the assistance rendered to rasa and so forth must be accepted as figurative, in accordance with long-standing tradition.

Still others hold: “The status of being an ornament exists primarily through the mere assistance rendered to rasa and so forth; whereas in cases such as metaphor (rūpaka), it is due to the superimposition of the expressed meaning (vācya) and so on, according to the maxim of the goat’s udder on the neck.”

But those who are learned [in this matter] maintain: "In cases such as *samāsokti*, the designation 'ornament' (*alaṅkāra*) applies because the subordinate elements—such as the sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth—which are assisted by their own manifestors, the denoted meanings, the expressive words, and so on, contribute to the principal element (the primary sentiment) by way of embellishing the denoted meaning and the expressive word;
however, in *samāsokti*, it is merely the behavior of the heroine and others that constitutes the ornament, not the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) itself."
They maintain that this is because it lacks the manner described above.
For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated: "Where the primary meaning of the sentence is something else, and rasa and the like are merely subordinate members..."
"In that poetry, the ornament is rasa and so forth; such is my opinion."

If, moreover, the status of being an ornament (*alaṅkāratva*) were based merely on providing assistance to rasa and so forth, then it would follow by the same logic that this would apply to the expressive words (*vācaka*) and other elements as well.

And thus, the claim made by some— that "when rasa and so forth are the primary element (*aṅgin*), there is the ornament *rasavat* and so on, but when they are subordinate (*aṅga*), there is the second ornament, *udātta*"— is also refuted.
If these very same figures of speech are mutually intermingled, then there are two distinct figures: *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) and likewise *saṅkara* (commixture).

Just as even among worldly ornaments, when they are mixed together, each possesses its own distinct beauty and thus constitutes a separate ornament, so too, when the aforementioned poetic ornaments are mixed with one another, there arise two distinct ornaments known as *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) and *saṃkara* (blending).
Among these—
“The coexistence of these [figures] without mutual dependence is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling).
Of these— namely, verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) and semantic figures (*arthālaṅkāra*)— as for example:”
“May the Lord, whose eyes are like smiling blue lotuses, the swan that destroys the darkness of saṃsāra, the slayer of Kaṃsa, protect us from the lower realms.”
Here, there is *yamaka* (rhyme) in "pāyād apāyāt," and alliteration (*anuprāsa*) in "saṃsāra" and so forth; thus, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two verbal ornaments.
In the second quarter, there is a simile (*upamā*).
And in the second half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *rūpaka*; thus, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of two semantic figures (*arthālaṅkāra*).
Since both [types of figures] are present in this way, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* of verbal and semantic figures (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*).
[The same applies] when figures of speech stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), as well as when they reside in the same substratum (*ekāśrayasthiti*).
And when there is doubt, there is again a threefold confusion.
The relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is as follows:
“When the ocean was being encircled by the slough of the serpent king, which had slipped from his body due to the force of his dragging,
the Mandākinī quickly coiled around the base of his foot for a long time, as if to alleviate the pain caused by the churning.”
Here, by the concealment of the snake-skin (*nirmokapaṭṭa*), there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of the Mandākinī; thus, this is an *apahnuti* (concealment).

And that [concealment] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *śleṣa* (paronomasia), because it brings about the paronomasia that what is, in reality, the wrapping around the base of a mountain peak is the wrapping around the base of a foot.

Furthermore, the *śleṣa* itself is a subordinate element of the *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which consists in the identification of the wrapping around the base of a mountain peak with the wrapping around the base of a foot.
And the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) "as if for the sake of allaying the pain of churning" is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
And that poetic fancy, by suggesting the behavior of a hero and a heroine between the ocean and the Mandākinī, is a subordinate element of the implied metaphor (*samāsokti*).
Or, for example:
“The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its forerunner;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, that even so there is no union!”
In this case, it is an auxiliary to both *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and *viśeṣokti* (speech of distinction).
An example of the commingling of doubt (*saṃdehasaṅkara*) is as follows:
"This shines in the sky, piercing the dense darkness..."
The lunar orb, which brings delight to the eyes of the beautiful-eyed women.

In this case, is it *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) due to the identification of the face with the moon; or is it *rūpaka* (metaphor) because, having pointed out the face with the word "this," one superimposes the nature of the moon upon it;
or rather, is it *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), because the two subjects—the face and the lunar orb—both being contextual (*prakṛta*), are connected by a single common attribute?

Is it, rather, an *ulka* (illuminator) because the moon is not the subject under discussion; or is it *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), since the unstated face is understood through the similarity of its qualifiers;
or is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), wherein the subject under discussion—the face—is apprehended through the description of the unstated moon?

Alternatively, since the time that inflames the god of love has been described by way of a description of the moon—which is its own effect—this is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis); thus, because there is doubt among many possible figures of speech, there is a *saṃdehasaṅkara* (blending through doubt).
Or, for example, in the phrase "I see the moon-face," there is a doubt: is it the *upamā* (simile) "the face is like the moon," or is it the *rūpaka* (metaphor) "it is the moon itself"?
When either the corroborator (*sādhaka*) or the subverter (*bādhaka*) exists, there can be no further doubt.
For example, in the phrase "he kisses the moon-like face," the act of kissing is favorable to the face; thus, it is a corroborator of the simile (*upamā*).
However, that which is contrary to the moon is an obstacle to the metaphor (*rūpaka*).

In the expression “The moon-face shines,” the attribute called “shining” is a facilitator of the metaphor because it can exist in the face through figurative application (*upacāra*); thus, it does not obstruct the simile (*upamā*). [For example:
“O King-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī embraces you intensely.”

In this case, an embrace of a woman by the hero is inappropriate for the purpose of similarity; thus, because an embrace of Lakṣmī is impossible in the case of a king, it subverts the figure of simile (upamā).
Since it is possible in the case of Nārāyaṇa, it constitutes a metaphor (rūpaka).
Likewise—
"In the lotus-face of the deer-eyed woman, the flickering eye shines.
Here, because the eye is possible in the face, it serves as a proof for the simile (upamā); yet, because it is impossible in the lotus, it acts as a sublation (bādhaka) of the metaphor (rūpaka).

Thus, in such cases as "the lotus-face is beautiful," because of the rule "that which is compared with [words like] *vyāghra* etc. forms a compound when the common attribute (*sāmānya*) is not employed," a compound of simile (*upamā-samāsa*) is impossible; therefore, this is an obstacle to the figure of speech "simile" (*upamā*). Consequently, in this instance, there is only a compound of metaphor (*rūpaka-samāsa*) according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.
The entry into a single substratum is as described by me:
"If she were to look at me even for a brief moment with a mere sidelong glance, then a dense bliss would flash forth, obscuring all other objects of sense;
what kind of embrace could there then be from that lotus-eyed one, wherein the garments are rent by her jar-like breasts rising with horripilation?"

Here, in the phrase "even with a sidelong glance for even a moment," there is a convergence (*anupraveśa*) of *cheḳānuprāsa* (alliteration based on single consonants) and *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration based on multiple consonants) upon a single locus, taking the letter *kṣa* from the word *nirīkṣeta*.
Thus, in this very instance, there is a convergence of *anuprāsa* and the figure of speech *arthāpatti* (presumption).
Or, for example:
In the phrase “saṃsāradhvāntavidhvaṃsa-,” there is a combination of metaphor (rūpaka) and alliteration (anuprāsa).
Or, for example, in the phrase “kurabakāravakāraṇatāṃ yayuḥ,” there is a combination of two instances of rhyme (yamaka): one being "rabakā ravakā" and the other being "bakāravakāra.
Or, for example—
“On days when the travelers’ companions have become eager for new provisions,
let the flocks of peacocks dance as their songs are set forth with joy.”
In this regard, in the phrase "among the travelers and the moonlight" (*pahiasāmāiesu*), there is a simile (*upamā*) based on a single substratum, namely "the travelers and the moonlight";
however, the form "among the travelers and the assembly" (*pathikasāmājikeṣu*) has entered into the realm of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
This is a composition created by the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja, son of the illustrious Candraśekhara Mahākavicandra.
Having examined this Sāhityadarpaṇa, the wise shall easily understand the entirety of the principles of literary aesthetics.
As long as Śrī, whose face resembles the bright moon, adorns the body of Nārāyaṇa,
so long may this celebrated composition delight the minds of poets and remain renowned in the world.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, composed by the sovereign of rhetoricians, the Great Minister for Peace and War, the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja.
